docs.title: Manual installation on Linux
docs.text:
Once the dependencies are installed and the package downloaded, it is unpacked and the installer is run:

tar -xvzf pandorafms_satellite_server_X.XNG.XXX_x86_64.tar.gz
cd satellite_server/
./satellite_server_installer --install

Then /etc/pandora/satellite_server.conf has to be edited and the server_ip token set with the address of the Pandora FMS Server, and the service is started with:

systemctl start satellite_serverd

The log is in /var/log/satellite_server.log.

docs.title: Installation on MS Windows
docs.text: The installer (signed since version 762) includes Nmap and the Visual C++ Redistributable from MS Visual Studio 2015-2022. It is run with administrator rights, the licence is entered, the server address and the scanning rules are configured, and the machine is restarted. If WMI queries fail, the Satellite Server service has to be run with an Administrator account.

docs.title: Offline installation of the EndPoint
docs.text:
The EndPoint is installed from the tarball package, valid for any Unix/Linux/macOS, and it does not require compilation.

tar xvzf pandorafms_one_agent_linux-latest.tar.gz
cd unix
./pandora_agent_installer --install
systemctl start pandora_agent_daemon

libnsl may have to be installed manually, and if the sources are used (.src.tar.gz), there are additional Perl dependencies, among them YAML::Tiny and Thread::Semaphore. On FreeBSD and NetBSD the file location and the start-up script change: the EndPoint stays in /usr/local/bin/pandora_agent, its script in /usr/local/etc/rc.d/pandora_agent, the configuration in /usr/local/etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf, and pandora_agent_enable="YES" has to be added to /etc/rc.conf.

After the installation, /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf has to be edited to point to the server and, as a recommendation, to activate remote configuration:

sed -i "s/^remote_config.*$/remote_config 1/g" /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf
systemctl enable pandora_agent_daemon

docs.title: Unattended Windows
docs.text:
The Windows installer supports unattended mode since EndPoint version 5.1:

"PandoraFMS_One_Agent_Windows-lts.x86_64.exe" /S

Custom path:

"PandoraFMS_One_Agent_Windows-lts.x86_64.exe" /S /D=C:\PFMS_agent

Parameters written to the EndPoint configuration: --ip (server_ip), --group (group), --alias (agent_alias) and --remote_config (remote_config). Example:

"PandoraFMS_One_Agent_Windows-lts.x86_64.exe" /S --ip 192.168.0.59 --group Applications --alias Mifunne --remote_config 1

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Once the installation is finished, open the console at http://<server>/pandora_console/ and confirm that it loads the login screen, where the initial user is admin with the pandora password.

Warning

Change the password on the first login, and if you installed with a custom user or a different path, check that the services start before you call it done. The fault that is not reviewed today turns into an incident on Monday.

docs.title: Uninstallation
docs.text: The installers are not copied during the installation, so their --uninstall cannot be used afterwards. Uninstallation has to be done by hand: these are the files and folders each component leaves behind and the commands to remove them (as root). If several components live together on the same machine, do not delete the shared directories until they have all been removed.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
• Binaries in /usr/bin: pandora_server, pandora_exec, pandora_supervisor, pandora_db, pandora_ha, pandora_manage, pandora_revent, pandora_encrypt_db, braa, pandorafsnmp, pandorawmic, pandora_iot_server, pandora_netflow_server, tentacle_server, tentacle_client, clean_pandora_server, clean_tentacle_serverd and clean_tentacle_rmm.
  • Libraries and utilities: /usr/share/pandora_server.
  • Services: /etc/systemd/system/pandora_server.service, pandora_ha.service, tentacle_serverd.service, tentacle_rmm.service, pandora_iot_server.service and pandora_netflow_server.service.
  • Tasks and rotation: /etc/cron.hourly/pandora_db and /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_server.
  • Configuration: /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf, pandora_server.env, pandora_server_extra.env, /etc/pandora/conf.d and /etc/tentacle.
  • Data, logs and PID: /var/spool/pandora, /var/log/pandora and /var/run/pandora_supervisor.pid.
systemctl stop pandora_server pandora_ha tentacle_serverd tentacle_rmm \
  pandora_iot_server pandora_netflow_server
systemctl disable pandora_server pandora_ha tentacle_serverd tentacle_rmm \
  pandora_iot_server pandora_netflow_server
rm -f /etc/systemd/system/{pandora_server,pandora_ha,tentacle_serverd,tentacle_rmm,pandora_iot_server,pandora_netflow_server}.service
systemctl daemon-reload
rm -f /usr/bin/{pandora_server,pandora_exec,pandora_supervisor,pandora_db,pandora_ha,pandora_manage,pandora_revent,pandora_encrypt_db,braa,pandorafsnmp,pandorawmic,pandora_iot_server,pandora_netflow_server,tentacle_server,tentacle_client,clean_pandora_server,clean_tentacle_serverd,clean_tentacle_rmm}
rm -Rf /usr/share/pandora_server
rm -f /etc/cron.hourly/pandora_db /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_server

And, if no other component remains, the shared configuration and data:

rm -Rf /etc/pandora /etc/tentacle /var/spool/pandora /var/log/pandora

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
It depends on how it was installed:

  • RPM (RHEL / Rocky Linux): it is removed with the package manager.
dnf remove pandorafms_console
  • Tarball (Ubuntu): it was copied to /var/www/html/pandora_console and it left its log rotation behind.
rm -Rf /var/www/html/pandora_console
rm -f /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_console

The console shares the /var/spool/pandora/data_in directory with the server (collections, conf, md5, netflow). Do not delete it if there is a server, and it does not touch the database, which goes separately.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
The installation creates the pandora database and the pandora user, and if MySQL or Percona only served Pandora FMS:

systemctl stop mysqld
mysql -u root -p -e "DROP DATABASE pandora; DROP USER 'pandora'@'localhost';"
dnf remove 'Percona-Server*'        # RHEL/Rocky. On Ubuntu, apt remove percona-server-server or mysql-server
rm -Rf /var/lib/mysql /etc/my.cnf /etc/my.cnf.d

If the database is on another server or holds data from other applications, limit the operation to DROP DATABASE and DROP USER.

docs.title: Satellite
docs.text:
• Binaries in /usr/bin: satellite_server, tentacle_client, pandorafsnmp, wmic, pandorawmic and clean_satellite_serverd.
  • Configuration: /etc/pandora/satellite_server.conf, satellite_server.env, satellite_server_extra.env, /etc/pandora/satellite_plugins and the agents directory /etc/pandora/conf.
  • Start-up: /etc/init.d/satellite_serverd (with its link in /etc/rc.d) and /etc/systemd/system/satellite_serverd.service.
  • Rotation, logs and temporary files: /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_satellite, /var/log/satellite_server.log and /var/spool/pandora/tmp/satellite_server.
systemctl stop satellite_serverd
systemctl disable satellite_serverd
rm -f /etc/systemd/system/satellite_serverd.service
systemctl daemon-reload
rm -f /etc/init.d/satellite_serverd
rm -f /etc/rc.d/rc?.d/S90satellite_server
rm -f /usr/bin/{satellite_server,tentacle_client,pandorafsnmp,wmic,pandorawmic,clean_satellite_serverd}
rm -Rf /etc/pandora/satellite_plugins /etc/pandora/conf /var/spool/pandora/tmp/satellite_server
rm -f /etc/pandora/satellite_server.conf /etc/pandora/satellite_server.env /etc/pandora/satellite_server_extra.env
rm -f /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_satellite /var/log/satellite_server.log

The /opt/pandorafms/perl5 directory of the satellite is shared with other components, so delete it only if none remains installed.

docs.title: EndPoint
docs.text:
On Linux and Unix it leaves:

  • Binaries in /usr/bin: pandora_agent, pandora_agent_exec, pandora_revent, tentacle_client and clean_pandora_agent_daemon.
  • EndPoint home: /usr/share/pandora_agent (plugins, collections, commands, ref).
  • Configuration: /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf and pandora_agent.env.
  • Start-up: /etc/systemd/system/pandora_agent_daemon.service (or the script in /etc/init.d).
  • Rotation, logs and man pages: /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_agent, /var/log/pandora/pandora_agent.log, /usr/share/man/man1/pandora_agent.1.gz and tentacle_client.1.gz.
systemctl stop pandora_agent_daemon
systemctl disable pandora_agent_daemon
rm -f /etc/systemd/system/pandora_agent_daemon.service
systemctl daemon-reload
rm -f /usr/bin/{pandora_agent,pandora_agent_exec,pandora_revent,tentacle_client,clean_pandora_agent_daemon}
rm -Rf /usr/share/pandora_agent
rm -f /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.conf /etc/pandora/pandora_agent.env
rm -f /etc/logrotate.d/pandora_agent /var/log/pandora/pandora_agent.log
rm -f /usr/share/man/man1/pandora_agent.1.gz /usr/share/man/man1/tentacle_client.1.gz

If there is a server or satellite on the same machine, do not delete /etc/pandora or /var/spool/pandora entirely.

MS Windows does include an uninstaller, which in unattended mode runs like this:

"%ProgramFiles%\pandora_agent\uninst.exe" /S

Or from the EndPoint binary:

pandoraagent.exe --uninstall

docs.title: Introduction and architecture
docs.text: Pandora FMS is not something you understand by looking at a screenshot of the console. You understand it when you know where every piece of data comes from, who brings it in and where it is stored. This chapter walks that path: what can be monitored, with which piece, and which topology is needed for the data to arrive. The following parts cover each topic in depth. This is the map.

docs.title: Introducing Pandora
docs.text:
Pandora FMS monitors systems, networks, applications and services. The unit it works with is not the machine, it is the agent: a logical container of modules. It is attached to a group and, optionally, to one or more IP addresses. An agent can receive local data (from an EndPoint installed on the machine) or remote data (from a network check), and the usual thing is that it receives both.

Every module stores a single metric, with a unique name inside its agent. Its value is interpreted through thresholds: that is where the NORMAL, WARNING and CRITICAL states come from, plus the UNKNOWN state when a module stops receiving data. Those states generate events and trigger alerts. Everything else in this chapter is a way of feeding that mechanism.

docs.title: Remote monitoring
docs.text:
The server does it: it goes out and asks. Nothing is installed on the device, you only need network visibility towards it. It is the natural route for network devices and for anything that will not take software on top.

With SNMP you query the OIDs the vendor exposes. And you listen to the traps the device sends on its own, without anyone asking for them. On MS Windows machines remote checks are done through WMI, with credentials. And for everything else there are the classic network checks: ICMP (ping, latency, jitter), TCP with challenge and response to confirm a port is answering, and static web checks, which verify availability and content, not a full user transaction.

One difference worth being clear about from the start: a remote check lives or dies by the network. If there is no path to the device, there is no data, and no amount of retries from the console will fix it. The topologies further down exist for those cases.

docs.title: Monitoring with EndPoints
docs.text:
The EndPoint is the program installed on the machine that runs the checks from the inside. That is where the real power is. Any data you can obtain with a command or a script is within reach, inventory included: installed software, disks, services. And it can act on the system when asked to: start a service, delete a temporary file.

The EndPoint packs everything from the interval into a single XML file and sends it to the server with Tentacle, on port 41121/TCP. The default interval is 300 seconds. Since version 784 some checks accept much shorter intervals, down to 15 seconds: ICMP (latency and ping) and numeric SNMP ones. Asynchronous modules never go below five minutes, and the console warns you if you try to force it.

With EndPoints there are three working modes for the modules that arrive in the XML. In learning they are created on their own. In normal they are only created if they are declared in the console. In self-disabled it works like learning, but the agent shuts down if everything turns unknown. Choosing one or the other is an operations decision, not a configuration detail: it defines who is in charge of what gets monitored, the machine or the console.

docs.title: Monitoring cloud environments and APIs
docs.text: Cloud providers and external services will not let you put an EndPoint inside, and often they will not let you probe them over ICMP either. The way in is the API they publish, and for that Pandora FMS uses its module and plugin library: there are plugins for specific cloud platforms and a generic API request plugin (ApiRequest) for whatever does not have one. The result is stored as one more module, so it inherits thresholds, alerts and everything above. If the service has an API, it can be monitored. If it does not, what gets checked is the availability of the access point.

docs.title: Application monitoring (Discovery)
docs.text:
Discovery is the leap from monitoring what you already know to finding out what is out there. The wizard explores the network, finds machines and devices, identifies the operating system and applies a monitoring template to whatever it finds, which starts reporting without going through the creation form. Beyond the network, Discovery is used to inventory virtual environments, databases and applications before monitoring them.

The value is in the start: on a large network, creating hundreds of devices by hand is weeks of work with guaranteed oversights. Discovery turns that into a short review and a list of exceptions.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Monitoring without presenting the data is collecting for its own sake. Reports, dashboards and visual consoles are the part that turns information into decisions: trends, SLA compliance and capacity planning.

Every user can build their own dashboard with widgets: graphs, status summaries, maps. Reports group data from several agents and modules, with different calculations and formats. For what has not happened yet there are prediction modules: capacity, trending and arithmetic operations on other modules. The capacity one answers the useful question: how many days until the disk fills up, if everything stays the same. They are there to warn before the incident, not to explain it afterwards.

docs.title: The event console
docs.text:
The event console shows, in real time, what is happening. It is a snapshot, not a history. Events are classified by severity (from maintenance and informative up to critical, through warning) and they are the raw material of alerts, which add notification and escalation.

It may look like an old feature in a modern tool, and it is. It is also still the fastest way to answer the question "what has broken?" without opening twenty graphs. Many tools in the market do not have an event console like this one, and you notice it exactly when you are in a hurry.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Pandora FMS collects logs from multiple sources in a single console, sorted by the timestamp at which they were processed, keeping the original timestamp from the file as well. The text is stored as it is, with no structure, in OpenSearch, which is what supports the volume.

The syslog server analyses the system log of the machine where it is installed and the log server lets you correlate logs and fire alerts on them. It is the raw material for SIEM and the troubleshooting tool for when the problem is not in the state of a module, but in what the system was saying while it was failing.

docs.title: Network topics (Netflow, SNMP, IPAM, NCM, remote shell)
docs.text:
This groups what looks at the network as the subject, not as the medium:

  • NetFlow and sFlow analyse traffic in real time from the data the devices send (or from a probe with port-mirroring). The collector listens on 9995/UDP. It is the way to know who is talking to whom and how much, when SNMP only tells you how many packets cross an interface.
  • SNMP is the query protocol and the one that receives traps (162/UDP) for all network equipment.
  • IPAM (version 731 or later) manages the IP addresses of your networks: it discovers the hosts of a subnet, detects when they stop answering, resolves their names and makes a guess at the operating system. It works whether or not those machines are monitored.
  • NCM (Network Config Management) goes into devices over Telnet or SSH to back up their configuration, restore it and run commands, with templates per vendor and model. It needs the Heavy server running.
  • The remote shell covers manual access: a web terminal for equipment managed over Telnet or SSH, and graphical remote control with Pandora RC for Windows, Linux and macOS.

docs.title: SIEM
docs.text:
A SIEM collects, filters, normalises, correlates and presents security events. What Pandora FMS adds to the concept is that collection is already done. The logs that feed the SIEM are the same ones the platform already gathers. The security event engine builds on that previous work, in place of setting up a second system alongside it.

For the installation it is recommended that EndPoints are at least on version 783 to make the most of all the features. The SIEM is activated from the console and enables its own servers. With it come the normalisation templates, the security events and their correlation.

docs.title: RMM
docs.text:
RMM stands for Remote Monitoring and Management. In Pandora FMS it is the piece that allows scheduling tasks from the console and having the agents run them locally, reporting the result afterwards. It comes into play from version 778 and relies on three components: the RMM agent, the RMM server (which stores the scripts and the executions) and the Tentacle RMM service, which connects the two over port 41123/TCP.

It is the basis for the remote management of many machines at once: distributing software, applying changes and keeping a record of what was executed on each machine, without going into them one by one.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Pandora FMS started as a monolith (server, console and database on the same machine) and that is still the most sensible way to begin. But no component is condemned to live next to the others: they are separated when the network, the volume or the organisation ask for it. The architecture decision is not made by the product, it is made by your infrastructure.

docs.title: Console
docs.text: The web console is the visible face and also the door to automation: the same console you use by hand is the one that exposes the API for scripts to work with. Permissions live there (groups, profiles and tags) and decide who sees and who administers what. And it can be deployed on several servers, to spread the load or to serve different groups of users.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
The Pandora FMS server is a single application with several specialised servers inside, running as concurrent processes and with their own number of threads. Their configuration lives in pandora_server.conf, in /etc/pandora.

These come enabled by default:

  • Data Server: processes the XML packages sent by EndPoints and turns them into data, events and alerts.
  • Network Server: runs remote checks: ICMP, TCP, SNMP, WMI, web checks and prediction modules.
  • Heavy Server: takes care of the tasks that need more muscle: plugins, NCM and inventory.
  • Network High Performance Server: moves ICMP and SNMP in bulk, designed for high volumes.
  • Discovery Server: explores the network and runs scheduled discovery tasks.

These come disabled, to be switched on only when needed:

  • SNMP Console: receives SNMP traps through snmptrapd and processes them.
  • Event Server: relates events and fires the associated alerts.
  • Alert Server: runs all monitoring alerts, so that a slow alert does not hold up the checks.
  • Log Server: the one that allows generating alerts from logs.
  • Syslog Server: analyses the syslog of the machine where it is installed and stores it in OpenSearch.
  • NetFlow Server: collects and processes NetFlow and sFlow flows.
  • WUX Server: runs complex web transactions in a real browser, with Selenium Grid.
  • SIEM Server and SIEM Event Server: normalise logs and generate security events.
  • MADE Server: the anomaly detection engine (Monitoring Anomaly Detection Engine).
  • RMM Server: hosts the scripts and the executions that RMM agents download.
  • Mainframe Server: monitoring of mainframe environments (z/OS).
  • Sync Server: goes out to fetch data from isolated networks, as explained in the topologies below.

There is a third group, the servers that depend on the master server:

  • Policy Manager: applies policies to agents. When a change affects hundreds of agents at once, the work goes into a queue of operations and this server is the one that serves it.
  • Migration Server: moves agents between the nodes of a Command Center, taking the tasks from a prioritised queue. It only exists in Command Center environments.
  • Autoprovision Server: the auto-provisioning server. It receives agents that arrive with no destination and decides which node they are created in, according to the configured strategy: round-robin, the least loaded node, or custom rules (by alias, by subnet…).

All three start alongside the master of a node or of a Command Center, which is where their work makes sense.

The list has been getting shorter with the versions. Since 784 several servers were grouped into others to stop wasting memory on processes that were no longer needed. Prediction, WMI and web checks went into the Network Server. Plugins, NCM, inventory and export went into the Heavy Server. And ICMP and SNMP went into the Network High Performance Server.

On load distribution: there can be several servers of the same type working at the same time. Within each type one is the primary and the rest are secondary, but they all work. If a secondary goes down, the primary absorbs what it had assigned. High availability acts on another layer: with two nodes in active/passive, the one still alive takes on all the work. The status and load of every server are visible from the console itself, because the system monitors itself like it monitors anything else.

docs.title: EndPoint
docs.text:
The EndPoint is the program running on the monitored machine. We have already seen it in the first half of the chapter: it collects data locally, packs it into an XML and sends it to the server over Tentacle at every interval. When it has no direct path to the server, it can send its data through a satellite server or through another EndPoint acting as a proxy.

It is the piece you have to install, update and, now and then, uninstall without leaving a trace. The installation part is in Installation. What matters here is that its presence is the border between local and remote monitoring.

docs.title: Satellite server
docs.text:
The satellite server is an autonomous server installed close to the remote network. It does not need to connect to the database: it runs the checks and sends the results as XML over Tentacle, just like an EndPoint would. It is the answer when you cannot reach some devices over the network and cannot install anything on them either.

It has two virtues worth knowing. The first is speed: it can run up to 500 checks per second, and although it only sends data to the server every so often, if it detects a state change it reports it immediately. The second is that it discovers itself: it finds devices over SNMP or WMI, creates the corresponding agents and generates interface, traffic, CPU, memory and disk modules with no intervention.

And it is managed remotely. The satellite asks the server every few seconds (every 30 by default) whether there are changes in its configuration or in that of the agents it has discovered. It applies what arrives from the console. It is the satellite that starts the connection, so no port has to be exposed in the remote network. And when it needs to be reached from the server, for instance for the SNMP wizard, it is also the satellite that opens a reverse SSH tunnel.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Everything the platform collects ends up in the database, the component everything else depends on. Pandora FMS works with MySQL, MariaDB or Percona, and in practice two of them are used: the real-time one and the historical one, to which data is moved once it no longer needs to be queried by the second.

The database can be replicated for high availability in active/passive or set up in an active/active cluster with load balancing. Together with the historical database, this is where you decide how much detail you keep and for how long: cheap on disks, expensive in slow queries.

docs.title: Command Center
docs.text:
The Command Center is the layer above all of the previous. It manages several Pandora FMS installations (the nodes or instances) from a single interface: seeing them together, synchronising their configuration and operating on all of them. Every node keeps its own database and its own server. The Command Center does not replace them: it coordinates them. That is how you reach hundreds of thousands of devices without looking at them node by node. And how you can provide multi-company service from a single access point.

Synchronisation goes in two directions. The Command Center queries the database or the API of each node for what it administers: agents, modules, alerts, policies. And it receives by replication what is continuously generated, such as events.

Users, groups, templates and tags live on both sides, because they have to be where they are used. That said, it is an advanced environment with its own requirements: it is installed on RHEL 8 or Rocky Linux 8.

docs.title: Topologies, diagrams and monitoring models
docs.text: We have reached the point that decides everything else. The topology is not chosen out of taste. It follows from a single question: in which direction can the connection be established. The rest of the chapter is the answer, case by case.

docs.title: Accessible networks
docs.text:
This is the comfortable case and the one covering most installations. There are two variants, and they can live together:

  • The Pandora FMS server reaches what it monitors, so it can do centralised remote monitoring.
  • Or the EndPoints installed on the machines reach the server, so they report without a problem.

If your network meets one of the two (or both), you need nothing else from this section.

docs.title: Networks that are hard to reach
docs.text:
Here the connection exists, but not in the direction that would suit you. It is solved with an intermediate piece. Which one depends on where the break is:

  • If the server cannot reach the network, a broker agent is deployed on a machine with access to both sides.
  • If the EndPoints cannot reach the server, the proxy mode of the EndPoints is used, or a satellite server acting as an intermediary.
  • If what you have is several networks the server cannot poll at the same time, the answer is more than one satellite server, or several Pandora FMS servers connected to the same database.
  • When the satellite can go out but cannot be reached, it supports a reverse SSH tunnel (since version 785). It is the satellite that opens the port on the server and redirects it to its own SSH. That way the console can reach it to launch the SNMP wizard or the SNMP console.

docs.title: Unreachable networks
docs.text:
When the remote network cannot start communication towards the server, the approach is turned around with the Sync Server. The main server takes the initiative and goes to fetch the data from a Tentacle server deployed in the isolated network, which acts as a temporary store. Information accumulates there until the main server downloads it. What has been downloaded disappears from the store.

The difference from the satellite is exactly that: the satellite sends, the Sync Server fetches. If neither direction is possible, there is no monitoring to be had, and it is worth knowing that before promising it.

docs.title: Large environments
docs.text:
Volume breaks small solutions, and it is not fixed with a single trick. The first thing is to spread the work across several Pandora FMS servers, all against the same database, and to count on high availability so the platform stays up when a node fails: the one still alive relocates the work of the fallen one automatically.

From there, every problem has its shape. The Command Center solves the large cases:

  • Command Center with several nodes: every installation keeps its database and its capacity, and the Command Center presents and manages them as one. It is the answer to several teams, several customers or several sites with different administration.
  • Remote networks that require local polling: a network of satellite servers reports to a node living in that same network. The node does not need to reach every device, only the satellite next to it.
  • High-speed polling with filtering: the satellite runs the checks very fast and does not send every reading. It filters at the source and reports to the node only state changes. That is how you monitor in detail where the data flow would not allow it any other way.

docs.title: Other organisational cases
docs.text:
Not everything that complicates a deployment is the network, and it is worth not confusing the two:

  • Dual reporting: an agent can send its data to two different Pandora FMS servers, even though only one of them manages it. Useful in migrations and in environments with two houses.
  • Fragmented management: sharing the administration of part of the equipment among different staff. It is not an architecture problem, it is a permissions problem, and it is solved with groups, tags and profiles.
  • Distributed polling: several servers running remote checks against the same database, to spread the work without duplicating the installation.

The useful summary of the whole chapter fits in one sentence: before designing anything, draw how Pandora FMS reaches every network and how the information comes back. If that drawing is clear, the architecture chooses itself. If it is not, whatever scheme you copy from a manual will last you until the first firewall change.

docs.title: Version and support policy
docs.text: Updating a monitoring environment in production is not like updating a laptop. Pandora FMS is spread across pieces: console, server, database, EndPoints, satellites and, in a Command Center, several nodes. "Updating Pandora" is not an action, it is a decision: which pieces move, in which order and with how much room to go back. The good news is that not everything has to be updated at once. The bad news is that some pieces do have to move together.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The pieces of an installation do not have the same tolerance for lagging behind:

  • Console, database schema and server are one unit. They are updated together and to the same version. Mixing them is asking for trouble.
  • EndPoints can run behind the server for a while. They report their version in every XML and the server stores it, so an estate with EndPoints on several versions is the normal thing in any installation with a history. That said: new features do not work until the EndPoint is updated. For SIEM, for instance, EndPoints are recommended to be at least on 783. And updating thousands of EndPoints is a deployment in itself, not a restart.
  • Satellite servers do not accept just any combination: a 785 satellite is not compatible with earlier versions of Pandora, and the other way round the new satellite features simply do not work. They are updated with their own installer, not with Warp Update.
  • In a Command Center, every node is an installation and the Command Center sits above them. After updating, the environments have to be re-centralised, so the maintenance window belongs to the whole set, not to each piece on its own.

The practical consequence is the same in every case: choose a target version, decide which pieces go into the window and do it with the backup in front of you. The procedure is not repeated here: it is in Updates.

docs.title: LTS version
docs.text:
LTS (Long Term Support) versions are released once a year and prioritise stability and validation: they gather what the intermediate versions have already been through and consolidate it into a better tested base. They are the recommended ones for production.

Their support goes beyond that year:

  • They are maintained with LTS patches: security fixes, relevant issues and critical bugs, published as needed.
  • An LTS is supported for two years, and that support can be extended by another two through a long-term support contract, which may involve additional cost.
  • And what it does not include: features from newer versions. A patch brings security and critical fixes. It does not bring down to the LTS improvements that only exist in newer versions.

Two nuances that are often confused and are worth being clear about:

  • The support expiry date shown in Management → About is the licence's, not the version's: it is tied to the licence payment. It tells you whether the installation is covered, not when you have to update.
  • What usually sets the real limit is not Pandora, it is the operating system. If the vendor stops supporting it or stops publishing security patches, the longest-lived LTS is left without solid ground. Before stretching the support of a version, look at the system's life calendar.

If there is no specific reason for the opposite, this is the choice. And to stay on this track without having to think about it, Warp Update has the Limit to LTS updates option, which discards intermediate versions when updating.

Supported operating system. The current LTS (800) is installed on RHEL/Rocky 9 and 10 and on Ubuntu 22.04:

Version RHEL / Rocky Ubuntu 800 LTS (current) 9 and 10 22.04

The full matrix, which changes with every version and every system, is in the support and version policy. And it refers only to the server and its associated elements: database, high availability, reporting consoles, Command Center, historical database, OpenSearch. Support for agents and EndPoints does not change with it.

docs.title: Feature Release (FR) version
docs.text:
Feature Release versions are published roughly every two months and bring in new features, improvements and fixes. They are meant for those who need continuous access to the evolution of the product.

When it makes sense in a real environment, because choosing it has a price:

  • When a specific feature is needed before it reaches the LTS, and waiting for the yearly cycle is not an option.
  • When there is a pilot environment where the new thing can be tested without putting what sustains the service at risk.
  • When the team accepts that every two months there is an update to review, test and apply.

What is not a good idea is running a critical environment on FR without that room for testing: you notice it exactly when there is no way back.

Choosing one or the other is not a decision for life: every year, when the LTS comes out, it is time to review whether that FR is worth keeping or whether it no longer brings anything the LTS does not have. And when in doubt, the rule is the usual one: stability is not negotiable in what sustains the service; new things are tested where you can go back.

docs.title: Patches
docs.text:
Between one version and the next you do not wait for the following release: fixes arrive as patches. A patch corrects something specific (a vulnerability, a relevant issue or a critical bug) without changing version family.

How they are named. The version number rules and the patch adds a consecutive number: LTS 800 receives 800.1, 800.2 and so on. Feature Release versions also have patches, following the same logic, but only in specific situations.

Where to see what each one brings. Every version has its release notes page, and that is where each patch is detailed:

  • Release notes, version by version: for instance LTS 800 "Aquarius".
  • Updates and release notes index: pandorafms.com/en/releases.
  • Full product changelog: pandorafms.com/en/changelog.
  • Operating system support and version policy: pandorafms.com/es/politica-soporte-versiones-os.

How they are distributed. Always with Warp Update, and that is where the convenience is: the full circuit is in Updates.

  • Connected: from the console, Warp Update → Update online. The wizard downloads and applies the patch.
  • Disconnected, or with every package reviewed beforehand: packages are downloaded by hand and uploaded to the wizard (Warp Update Offline) or applied with the manual procedure. It is the mandatory route in isolated environments and the usual one where security requires auditing before installing.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text: Updating Pandora FMS is not an emergency, it is maintenance. And like any maintenance, it is done when it is due and with the backup already taken, not on a Friday afternoon because a version just came out. This chapter explains the two ways of bringing an installation up to date: the automatic one and the manual one. And what to do with the pieces that do not follow the same path: the EndPoints and the satellite servers.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
A Pandora FMS installation has three pieces that are updated together: the web console, the database schema and the server. Since version 784 the server groups several services into fewer processes. So updating the server means updating the whole package.

There are two ways of doing it:

  • Warp Update: wizards from the console itself that download, apply and verify the update. This is the recommended route.
  • Manual update: the same packages, applied by hand, component by component. It is more laborious and demands more care, but it gives you full control of the process and works when the wizard cannot be used.

Neither of the two touches the EndPoints or the satellite servers: each has its own mechanism, and they are at the end of the chapter.

The current version, the schema MR and the licence support expiry date are shown in Management → About. It is worth having that screen at hand before and after any update: it is the one that tells you where you came from and where you have arrived.

And before starting, the usual thing, but said plainly: take a snapshot of the machine or a backup of all the components. If something goes wrong, the simple way to fix it is to go back. And that only works if there is a point to go back to.

For the Warp Update section to show up in the menu, Enable update manager must be switched on in Management → Settings → System Settings → Advanced. If it is not, the console hides the whole update block and it looks as though the feature does not exist.

docs.title: Warp update
docs.text:
Warp Update updates the web console, the database schema and the server automatically, through wizards. It is reached from Management → Warp Update and it has three working screens, plus one for options.

Warp Update Online downloads and installs from the official repositories, so the console needs outbound internet access. Registering with an email address is required to use it. The wizard shows the installed version and the versions it can be brought up to: only LTS ones, or consecutive ones too, depending on the configuration. And the release notes, under Show details, before deciding.

Warp Update Offline does the same without a connection to the repositories. The administrator downloads the packages and uploads them to the wizard. To download them, an email address is required and the unique access code the console associates with the licence must be copied. With that code you get into the repository, which reports the installed, the next and the latest version, and lets you download three files:

File What it updates package_XXX.XXX.fms The web console and the database schema. pandorafms_server-XXXXX.tar.gz The server. .sig The signature of the two previous ones, to check they have not been altered.

They are uploaded one by one from the wizard (Browse it), you check that what the screen shows matches what you want to apply, and the process is launched. It is better to update the console and the schema first, and the server afterwards. Each file has to fit within the post_max_size and upload_max_filesize limits in /etc/php.ini, or the upload will fail with nothing more than a size error.

Warp journal leaves a trail of what has been done: version updated, whether it was server or console, whether it came from online or offline, who launched it and when. It is the first stop when something does not add up after an update.

The Options of Warp Update are few and delicate:

  • Limit to LTS updates: restricts the update to LTS versions, which are the ones with extended support.
  • Allow no-consecutive patches: offline only, it allows jumping from one version to a non-consecutive one. It is off by default, and that is fine.
  • Warp Update URL, Use secured Warp Update and Proxy server: these are not fields to touch out of curiosity. Before changing them, check with support.

docs.title: Manual update
docs.text: The manual update uses the same packages the offline mode downloads, but applied by hand in the terminal, as root. The order is not negotiable: console, database schema and server. The procedure is valid for EL 7, EL 8, EL 9 and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS.

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
The .fms package is copied to the console directory, unpacked, and replacing everything is accepted:

mv package_XXX.XXX.fms /var/www/html/pandora_console/
cd /var/www/html/pandora_console/
unzip package_XXX.XXX.fms
# when asked about each replaced file: A (All)

Then the package number is updated in the database, replacing XXX with the target version:

mysql -u root -p -D pandora -e "UPDATE tconfig SET value=XXX WHERE token='current_package'"

docs.title: Database schema
docs.text:
The MR updater is run:

/usr/bin/php /var/www/html/pandora_console/godmode/um_client/updateMR.php

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
The server package is unpacked, installed and the service restarted:

tar -xzvf pandorafms_server-XXXXX.tar.gz
cd pandora_server/
./pandora_server_installer --install
systemctl restart pandora_server

docs.title: EndPoint
docs.text: They do not go through Warp Update, and there is no need to go machine by machine. The comfortable way is the self-update with file collections and the pandora_update plugin. The new EndPoint binary is dropped into a collection. The EndPoint runs the plugin with the name of that collection and compares the binary in the collection with the one it is running. If they differ, it stops, replaces itself and restarts with the new one. Every architecture needs its own collection (one binary for 32-bit Windows and another for 64-bit, for instance), and the process leaves a record in a log that can be watched with an async_string module. The new version can also be installed by hand, with the installer of each operating system (Linux, MS Windows). In an environment with hundreds or thousands of devices, that is work the collection does on its own.

docs.title: Satellite server
docs.text: The satellite is not touched by Warp Update either: it is updated with its own installer, the same one used to install it. In the update to 785 there is also a policy migration step, because Dataserver-type modules of Satellite agents became Satellite-type modules. Until that migration is completed, policy changes do not reach those agents.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Once the job is done, check Management → About to confirm the package and the MR, and Management → Servers to see the version in the Version column of every server. If the three pieces do not match, the update is not finished.

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text:
Pandora FMS is licensed by devices, not by metrics. That decision has very practical consequences in the architecture. A 24-port switch can report hundreds of modules without costing more licence than the switch. And adding logs, security or inventory does not make it more expensive, because they are included. What you pay for is how many devices are monitored and, in some cases, through which route.

This chapter does not talk about prices: that is sales territory. It talks about which licence model fits which architecture, which is what conditions a deployment.

To get your bearings before going into detail, this is the correspondence between what has to be monitored (and what is contracted separately) and the licence that applies:

If what has to be monitored is… You need… And on top of that… Servers, applications, cloud, virtualisation Pandora ONE (the top one) — Network equipment with nothing installed Pandora NMS Can be counted by modules Workstations (PCs) Pandora RMM Includes RC SaaS; on-premise RC is paid separately Several installations with a single view Command Center Additional licence to the nodes', per active node Security (SIEM) Pandora SIEM A percentage of Pandora ONE, Pandora RMM or Pandora NMS SAP, IBM i or z/OS The plugin for each one Sold separately Remote control of machines Pandora RC Separate: RC SaaS comes with the Pandora RMM licence, on-premise RC is paid separately Incident and asset management Pandora ITSM Has its own licence Not wanting to maintain anything Pandora MaaS Subscription only

docs.title: Perpetual and subscription licences
docs.text:
The on-premise version supports two models. The software and the features are the same in both cases:

  • Licence (perpetual): bought once. Support and maintenance are renewed every year, to keep receiving patches and new versions.
  • Subscription: paid every year. Both come out roughly the same over five years. So the choice is about cash flow (less initial investment) or about who books the expense, not about features.

The cloud version (Pandora MaaS) is subscription only, with an annual commitment: nothing is installed or maintained there, and the platform updates itself.

An on-premise licence includes, at no extra cost:

  • Technical support 8×5 through the ticketing tool, with no limit on incidents. The 24×7 with a dedicated phone line is contracted separately. The scope, the hours and what is left out are in the licence agreement.
  • Updates: patches and new versions.
  • All the features, without cuts: log collection and monitoring, security, Discovery, satellite servers, remote EndPoint deployment, inventory and RMM, among others.
  • Access to the module library, the knowledge base and the Enterprise code.

Two things from that list are worth keeping. The satellite server is not licensed separately: it is part of the licence, not an add-on. And the web user experience feature (WUX) is included inside Discovery.

And what happens if you stop paying. The two models behave differently. With an on-premise licence the software keeps working and you only lose support, patches, new versions and access to the Enterprise library. With pay-per-use, if you do not pay, the software stops working.

The legal conditions (warranty on the software, scope and exclusions of support, and liability) are developed in the licence agreement.

docs.title: How it is counted: agents or modules
docs.text:
The licence screen of the console is what rules. The field that decides how it is counted is Limit mode: agents or modules.

By agents. The number of agents is counted, and each agent can carry as many modules as it needs: there is no cap. An agent is any monitored device: a server, a router, a switch, an access point, a NAS. In virtualisation, every virtual machine with its own IP address. Devices watched over SNMP also count as an agent, even though they have nothing installed on them.

By modules. The number of modules is counted, not the number of machines. A 5,000-module licence is split however you like. 5,000 agents with one module each. Or 50 agents with 100 modules each. Or any combination in between.

Which one suits you? It depends on how the estate grows:

  • The agent licence gives you "no nasty surprises" scaling when the detail multiplies inside a single machine. A database server with twenty databases can report hundreds of modules without spending more licence than the server.
  • The module licence is more effective and easier to understand when you want to watch a little of many devices. If all you want from each camera is a ping, every camera ends up being an agent with one module. Counting modules there is cheaper and clearer than counting agents.

The two models do not work for every licence:

  • The Pandora NMS licence does allow module-based licensing.
  • The Pandora RMM licence is not compatible with module-based licensing.

Two more rules that affect the count:

  • Minimum: the minimum licence to contract with support is 100 agents, or its equivalent in modules when counting by modules.
  • Per environment, not per server: an installation is licensed as a whole, not piece by piece. Nodes sitting in passive for high availability do not count: an environment with replicas or redundancy runs on a single licence. The exception is the Command Center, licensed by number of active nodes (replicas do not count there either).
  • Mixed licence: types of licence can be combined in the same installation (for instance 10 Pandora ONE, 50 Pandora NMS and 500 Pandora RMM), but counting methods are not mixed, nor are payment models. The installation is all agents or all modules, and all perpetual or all subscription.

docs.title: Additional licences
docs.text: There are pieces that are not included in the monitoring licence and are contracted separately.

docs.title: Command Center
docs.text:
Its licence is additional to the nodes' monitoring licence (Pandora ONE, Pandora NMS or Pandora RMM) and is counted by active nodes. Replicas for redundancy do not add up. Each node handles on the order of 2,000 agents, though it can do more depending on the environment.

An example makes it clear. An environment of 10,000 agents with 4 nodes is licensed with a single 10,000-agent licence: the licence is for the environment, not for each node. Plus the Command Center licence for those four nodes. If there were also nodes in passive for high availability, they would not count.

docs.title: Pandora RC
docs.text: Remote control (Windows, Linux and Mac desktops and shells from the browser) is a product with its own licence: it is not part of the monitoring licence even though it is used from the same console. The Pandora RMM licence includes RC in SaaS mode. On-premise RC is independent and paid separately.

docs.title: SAP
docs.text: The SAP plugin is not part of the monitoring licence either: it is sold and licensed separately.

docs.title: IBM i and z/OS
docs.text: The IBM i (AS400) and mainframe (z/OS) plugins follow the same path: separate licence. Along with SAP, they are the exceptions to the "everything included" of the monitoring licence. They are not our own development.

docs.title: Pandora SIEM
docs.text: The security feature is licensed as a percentage of the monitoring licence (Pandora ONE, Pandora RMM or Pandora NMS) and is activated from the console.

docs.title: Pandora ITSM
docs.text:
Incident, asset and project management is another product, with its own licence. It integrates with Pandora FMS but is not part of the monitoring licence.

What does not have to be licensed separately, even though it may look like it: the satellite server, log collection, discovery, inventory and remote agent deployment. They are included.

docs.title: Pandora ONE, Pandora NMS and Pandora RMM
docs.text:
The three licences are best understood together. What separates them is not what you can do with the platform, but which devices they apply to:

  • Pandora ONE is the top licence: it covers every kind of device, with EndPoint or through remote checks. It applies to everything that is not specifically network or workstation.
  • Pandora NMS only includes remote checks: it is meant for systems that are exclusively network (routers, switches, network elements) with nothing installed on them. It allows module-based licensing. If one of those devices also needs a local check, that is covered by combining licence types (see the mixed licence above).
  • Pandora RMM is aimed at workstations (PCs), not servers: it is the licence for Mac and Windows desktop machines.

The rule that ties them together is simple: the FMS licence (Pandora ONE) is calculated as every agent that is not Pandora NMS or Pandora RMM. A mixed estate does not force you to choose a single licence: they can be combined. But every device pays the type that corresponds to it.

Around those three there are further modalities. Pandora Free, with the same features as Pandora ONE but free up to 50 agents or 600 monitors. Pandora MaaS, the managed cloud version. And the entry-level editions (Pandora Open, maintained by the community, and Pandora MINI), which are another conversation.

docs.title: Licence installation
docs.text:
The licence is installed from the console itself, in Management → Setup → License (Licence). The first thing needed is the AuthKey: the key Pandora FMS (or its distributor) sends by email or in a PDF. It is a number between 12 and 15 digits, and it only works once. With it the licence for your installation is generated.

A new installation runs as Pandora Free (50 agents limit) until a real licence is installed. If nothing is touched, it is not broken: it is unlicensed.

The wizard starts with Request new license, which opens the activation dialog. There it shows a piece of data worth noting down: the installation's request key, a short code of the #1ceebbee8 kind. With that and the AuthKey there are two paths.

docs.title: Online
docs.text:
The AuthKey is typed into the Authentication key field and Online validation is pressed. The console generates the licence, validates it against the server and leaves it installed.

From then on it does not have to be touched again: it refreshes on its own. The Sync license online button forces that check and confirms that everything is in order. It answers "License is up to date" if there are no changes and "License updated successfully" if there were. The two errors seen at this step are "Error while connecting to licence server", when the console cannot reach the server, and "Invalid response while validating license", when it reaches it but the response is not valid.

docs.title: Offline
docs.text:
When the console cannot reach the internet, the request key shown by the dialog is used. It is copied and taken to the Warp portal (the same one that serves the update packages) or sent to support. Whatever they return is the licence. That key is pasted into the Customer key field on the licence screen and saved.

There is no online validation, so the licence stays exactly as it was installed. It is worth keeping the key they returned and repeating the request when it is time to renew.

After saving, the licence screen shows the picture of what is contracted: expiry date, Platform Limit (the limit) and Current Platform Count (what is there, with enabled and disabled items). Then License Mode, Limit mode (agents or modules) and License Type (console or Command Center). And the limits per type: One Limit, NMS Limit, RMM limit and SAP limit.

Three more things that save support calls:

  • If the licence is a Command Center one, the nodes do not have to be activated one by one: the Command Center licence activates them automatically.
  • Do not start the pandora_server daemon with the Enterprise version installed before enabling the Enterprise part of the console: it will throw errors.
  • If the installation is a Command Center, the licence is propagated from the Command Center to all the nodes.

For prices, fees and changes of model you have to talk to sales: this page explains what each licence covers and how it fits the architecture, not what it costs.

docs.title: Database schema
docs.text:
All the information in Pandora FMS (agents, modules, alerts, events, users, policies) lives, in the end, in a handful of MySQL tables. It is tempting to look directly there when the interface does not give the quick answer you need: a report with custom SQL, a diagnostic SELECT at three in the morning, a script that needs to know in which column the server stores the last contact of an agent. This chapter is the map of that territory: which tables exist, what each one is for and how they relate to each other.

Before touching the database

The schema changes between versions (new columns, tables that appear or disappear, types that are adjusted) with no notice other than the changelog of each build. This page documents the version given in the header of the table reference, which is always aligned with the real code. To read or write Pandora FMS data from outside, the recommended way is the REST API: it is stable between versions and it does not require knowing the internal schema. Accessing the database directly is a last resort, with no compatibility guarantee, and you must never write directly on tables managed by the product: the server and the Web console take for granted that they are the only ones writing there, and a row touched by hand can leave the data aggregation, a counter or a task queue in a state they cannot interpret themselves. For read-only queries, always prefer a replica or the historical database over the main database in production.

One detail surprises you the first time: the Web console stores the texts (agent and module names, descriptions...) with the special characters converted to HTML entities, so Router & Firewall appears in the table as Router & Firewall. Keep it in mind when filtering by name. And modules deleted from the console do not disappear instantly: they stay marked with delete_pending = 1 until the server removes them, which is why module queries exclude them.

This chapter covers the main database, the historical one and the Command Center one. It does not cover third-party databases that Pandora FMS integrates with (external SIEM, CMDB, etc.): those have a schema of their own and are out of the scope of this documentation.

docs.title: Overview: databases, engine, files and version
docs.text:
A Pandora FMS installation can have up to three different databases, all of them with the same engine:

  • Main database (pandora): the only mandatory one. It stores the complete configuration and the recent monitoring data.
  • Historical database (optional, enabled with history_db_enabled): same schema as the data tables of the main one, designed to retain time series beyond what the main one purges. See Historical database.
  • Command Center database: in installations with Command Center, each node keeps its own main database and the Command Center adds one of its own with tmetaconsole_* tables. See Command Center.

The supported engine is Percona Server for MySQL 8 (recommended, especially above 4,000 agents) or MySQL 8 / MySQL 8.4 since build 785; the complete requirements table is in Installation.

The schema is defined in two files that are loaded once, at installation: pandoradb.sql (structure: the 271 tables) and pandoradb_data.sql (seed data: module types, default configuration, catalogues). From there on, two tokens of the tconfig table (db_scheme_version, for example 8.0NG, and db_scheme_build, for example PD260915) identify the installed schema version, and the console compares them with the package version to warn about outdated databases.

Between major versions, schema changes arrive as extras/mr/<number>.sql files, one per build. The console stores in tconfig the MR token with the highest number already applied and, on each update check, offers as pending the files with a higher number; when they are applied, the file moves to extras/mr/updated/ and the MR token is updated. They are not run by hand unless the update procedure says so explicitly.

docs.title: Map by functional area
docs.text:
The 271 tables of the schema are not organised in different SCHEMA or separate databases (they all live in the same database), but they do follow a clear functional distribution. The following table groups the tables by the area they cover; it is a construction of this documentation to make navigation easier, not a structure declared in the engine.

Functional area What it covers No. of tables Agents and monitoring (core) Agents, modules, their configuration and their data 37 Groups and organisation Group and category hierarchy 4 Alerts Alert templates, actions and commands 16 Events Event log and its life cycle 10 Policies Configuration deployed in bulk on agents 13 Users, profiles and sessions Accounts, permissions and active sessions 16 Notifications and messaging Internal notices and messages between users 11 Reports and visualisation Reports, graphs, dashboards, visual consoles 34 Discovery and reconnaissance Network discovery tasks 9 Network maps and GIS Network maps and geolocation 17 Cluster and high availability Agent cluster configuration 3 Command Center Nodes, synchronization and migration between nodes 14 Credential manager Store of reusable credentials 1 Servers, configuration and maintenance Servers, global configuration, backups 13 SNMP traps Traps received and their normalisation 2 IPAM (IP address management) Managed networks, subnets and IP addresses 8 NCM (Network Config Manager) Network device configuration 12 RMM (Remote Monitoring & Management) Remote management of machines 7 SIEM Security event rules and decoders 12 Security and vulnerabilities Detected vulnerabilities and patches 3 Downtime planning Scheduled maintenance windows 3 Tags Tagging of modules and policies 3 Services Services made up of other elements 2 Agent self-configuration Self-configuration rules for new agents 3 Remote commands (Web console) Remote commands runnable from the console 2 Collections and plugins File collections and plugin catalogue 2 Languages and translation Interface translations 3 Miscellaneous / internal utilities Support tables with no area of their own 11

For the detail of columns, types, keys and comments of any table in this list, the table reference gathers the 271 tables grouped by this same area, with a direct link to each one.

docs.title: Core tables in detail and relationship diagram
docs.text:
A handful of tables concentrate most of the usual queries. Knowing them by heart saves more than one trip back to the full reference:

  • Agent and module inventory. tagente stores one record per agent (id_grupo references tgrupo; modo is the learning mode of the module at creation, not a state of the agent: see Codes and enumerations). Each module of that agent is a row in tagente_modulo (id_agente references tagente, id_tipo_modulo references ttipo_modulo, the catalogue of module types). The last known state of each module lives in tagente_estado: one row per module, with id_agente_modulo and id_agente pointing to the previous tables by naming convention, with no declared FOREIGN KEY.
  • Module data. The time series are split into four tables according to the type of data: tagente_datos (numeric), tagente_datos_string (string), tagente_datos_inc (incremental) and tagente_datos_log4x (logs). All four are indexed by id_agente_modulo + utimestamp, also with no declared FOREIGN KEY: the volume they move every day advises against that check on each insert (see Historical database).
  • Alerts. An alert template (talert_templates) is assigned to a specific module through talert_template_modules (id_agent_module references tagente_modulo, id_alert_template references talert_templates; times_fired, last_fired, disabled and standby also live there). Each assignment triggers one or more actions via talert_template_module_actions, which point to talert_actions and, from there, to talert_commands.
  • Events. tevento is one row per generated event, with id_agente, id_grupo, id_agentmodule and id_alert_am as references by convention (with no declared FOREIGN KEY). event_type is a closed ENUM with the possible event types; criticity and estado are the codes described in the next section.
  • Policies. tpolicies is the header of a policy; tpolicy_agents and tpolicy_groups define the agents or groups it applies to, and tpolicy_modules and tpolicy_alerts the modules and alerts it deploys on them.
  • Credential manager. tcredential_store stores each credential under its identifier as primary key; product is an ENUM with the supported credential types (CUSTOM, AWS, AZURE, GOOGLE, SAP, WMI, SNMP). The complete functional detail is in Credential manager, and its encryption in Database encryption; here only the shape of the table matters.

The following diagram summarises those relationships. Continuous lines mark a FOREIGN KEY declared in the schema; the rest are relationships by column naming convention, with no restriction declared in the engine.

docs.title: Codes and enumerations
docs.text:
Several columns store integers that only make sense with their table of meanings at hand.

Module status (column estado of tagente_estado): values that the server really stores.

Code Meaning 0 Normal 1 Critical 2 Warning 3 Unknown 4 Not started: initial value when the module is created, before receiving the first data

The console constants AGENT_MODULE_STATUS_* add further values, but they are filter values of the interface, not something the column ever stores: 5 (not started, in filters), 6 (not normal, a grouping value), 7 (forced normal) and 100/200/300 (critical, warning or normal with some alert fired). Do not confuse column and filter: if estado is queried directly by SQL, only the values 0 to 4 will appear.

Agent status: no column stores it. The Web console calculates it from the counters of tagente (normal_count, warning_count, critical_count, unknown_count, notinit_count, total_count and fired_count, the one for fired alerts), which the server keeps up to date. To find out the state of an agent with SQL, look at those counters.

Agent mode (column modo in tagente): 0 normal, 1 learning, 2 self-disabled (autodisable). The column has 0 by default, but in practice agents are born at 1: it is the value the server uses when creating an agent from an XML and the Web console when adding it by hand.

Module type (table ttipo_modulo): catalogue with id, internal name (for example generic_data), numeric category and data type (numeric, boolean, string). There are about forty types; the complete catalogue is in the ttipo_modulo row of the table reference.

Event status (column estado in tevento): 0 new, 1 validated, 2 in progress.

Event type (column event_type in tevento, closed ENUM): going_unknown, unknown, alert_fired, alert_recovered, alert_ceased, alert_manual_validation, recon_host_detected, system, error, new_agent, going_up_warning, going_up_critical, going_down_warning, going_down_normal, going_down_critical, going_up_normal, configuration_change, ncm.

Event criticality (column criticity in tevento): 0 maintenance, 1 informative, 2 normal, 3 warning, 4 critical, 5 minor, 6 major. The values 20, 21 and 34 are combinations used by the console filters (20, not normal; 21, critical or normal; 34, warning or critical) and they are not criticalities of a specific event.

Fired alerts: there is no single "status" column for an alert. It is deduced from talert_template_modules.times_fired (firing counter) and last_fired (timestamp of the last one); standby and disabled control whether the alert can fire at all.

docs.title: Historical database: what moves, when, and how it is purged
docs.text:
The historical database is optional (history_db_enabled in tconfig, next to history_db_host, history_db_port, history_db_name and the rest of the connection parameters, configurable from Settings → System settings → Historical database). When it is active, the server moves the time series data of the modules (tagente_datos, tagente_datos_string) to it as a periodic task of pandora_db.pl, and, where applicable, events and traps as well. The exact detail of the movement is Enterprise functionality and it is not in the community tree, so it is not documented here.

In the main database, the same periodic process purges the data whose retention period has expired, with these default limits:

Parameter By default Purges days_purge 45 days tagente_datos string_purge 7 days tagente_datos_string event_purge 7 days tevento days_delete_not_initialized 7 days Agents that have spent that time without starting days_compact 0 (disabled) Compaction of old data

The historical database, when it is active, has its own purge cycle (the same function, run on the historical connection) with its own limits (history_db_days, history_db_string_days): it does not inherit the days of the main database.

To size how much each database is going to grow according to the number of agents and modules, see Volume analysis and high-capacity design, which is not repeated here.

docs.title: Command Center: its own tables and synchronization
docs.text:
The Command Center has a database of its own, with tables prefixed tmetaconsole_* that replicate or cache information from the managed nodes (they never replace the equivalent tables of each node, which remain the original source of that data).

The key tables are:

  • tmetaconsole_setup: registration of each node, with its URL and the connection credentials to its database, API and console (encrypted if database encryption is active).
  • tmetaconsole_agent: agents synchronized from the nodes, together with their source node.
  • tmetaconsole_agent_secondary_group: secondary groups replicated from the nodes.
  • tmetaconsole_ha_databases: high availability databases registered per node.
  • tmetaconsole_license_limit_cache: cache of the aggregated licence limit of all the nodes.

The synchronization and the migration of elements between nodes use a second group of tables: tsync_queue (synchronization queue), tmigration_queue and tmigration_module_queue (migration queues of agents and modules between nodes), tmerge_error, tmerge_steps and tmerge_queries (node merging) and tnode_relations (relationship between each element and its source node). When the migration moves module data between nodes that have the historical database enabled, the operation also touches that historical connection at source and destination, not only the main database of each node.

The registration and management of nodes from the interface are covered in their own Command Center chapter; this section does not repeat that procedure.

docs.title: Encrypted data
docs.text:
This chapter is, by convention of the whole site, the only place where tables and columns are named: the rest of the pages, including Database encryption, refer here instead of repeating them. With encryption active, these columns store the encrypted value instead of the original one: passwords of plugin modules and SNMPv3 credentials in tagente_modulo and tpolicy_modules; passwords of Enterprise inventory modules; agent custom fields marked as password type in tagent_custom_data; several password tokens in tconfig (SMTP mail, LDAP/Active Directory, historical database, console replication, API, update proxy, Pandora RC, remote commands, access hash between nodes); the connection passwords of each node in tmetaconsole_setup; and user, password and additional fields of each credential in tcredential_store.

All of them are stored as TEXT or VARCHAR: encryption does not use any dedicated binary type, it produces base64 text. That has a direct consequence for whoever queries the database by hand: a SELECT over any of these columns returns the encrypted value, not the original one. To read it in plain text the encryption and decryption mechanism is needed, not an SQL query: see Database encryption for the complete list of protected data and the activation procedure.

docs.title: Useful read-only queries
docs.text:
A handful of queries cover most one-off diagnostic needs. All of them are read-only and respect the warning at the beginning of the chapter: prefer a replica or the historical database over the main one in production.

Agents that have not contacted for more than one day:

SELECT nombre, direccion, ultimo_contacto
FROM tagente
WHERE disabled = 0
  AND ultimo_contacto < NOW() - INTERVAL 1 DAY;

Modules in critical status right now:

SELECT a.nombre AS agente, m.nombre AS modulo
FROM tagente_estado e
JOIN tagente_modulo m ON e.id_agente_modulo = m.id_agente_modulo
JOIN tagente a ON e.id_agente = a.id_agente
WHERE e.estado = 1
  AND m.disabled = 0
  AND m.delete_pending = 0;

Events by criticality in the last 24 hours:

SELECT criticity, COUNT(*)
FROM tevento
WHERE utimestamp > UNIX_TIMESTAMP(NOW() - INTERVAL 1 DAY)
GROUP BY criticity;

Alerts that have fired at least once, with their last firing:

SELECT m.nombre AS modulo, t.times_fired, FROM_UNIXTIME(t.last_fired) AS ultimo_disparo
FROM talert_template_modules t
JOIN tagente_modulo m ON t.id_agent_module = m.id_agente_modulo
WHERE t.times_fired > 0;

Data of a module in a date range:

SELECT FROM_UNIXTIME(utimestamp) AS fecha, datos
FROM tagente_datos
WHERE id_agente_modulo = ?
  AND utimestamp BETWEEN UNIX_TIMESTAMP('2026-01-01') AND UNIX_TIMESTAMP('2026-01-31')
ORDER BY utimestamp;

Number of agents per group:

SELECT g.nombre AS grupo, COUNT(*) AS agentes
FROM tagente a
JOIN tgrupo g ON a.id_grupo = g.id_grupo
GROUP BY g.nombre
ORDER BY agentes DESC;

Custom fields of a specific agent:

SELECT f.name, d.description
FROM tagent_custom_data d
JOIN tagent_custom_fields f ON d.id_field = f.id_field
WHERE d.id_agent = ?;

Modules without data (unknown) grouped by group:

SELECT g.nombre AS grupo, COUNT(*) AS modulos_desconocidos
FROM tagente_estado e
JOIN tagente_modulo m ON e.id_agente_modulo = m.id_agente_modulo
JOIN tagente a ON e.id_agente = a.id_agente
JOIN tgrupo g ON a.id_grupo = g.id_grupo
WHERE e.estado = 3
  AND m.disabled = 0
  AND m.delete_pending = 0
GROUP BY g.nombre;

docs.title: What is this FAQ
docs.text:
This FAQ gathers the questions that come up most often about Pandora FMS. They come from the two knowledge bases the team maintains (the community one and the official support one) and they are reviewed one by one before being published. It is not a dump: only what is still true goes in here, checked against the code of the current version.

Three things to get the most out of it:

  • It is ordered by topic, not by origin or age. The index is right below.
  • Every answer goes to the point: what to check, in what order and with what command. When the topic has its own chapter on the site, it is linked, so that a procedure already told is not repeated here.
  • What no longer applies is left out. The original entries are years old: discontinued operating systems, old versions and features that no longer exist. If something is missing, it is because it should not be there.

And to get your bearings before searching: if you are going to install Pandora FMS for the first time, start with Part 01; if you are looking for the exact detail of a token or an option, Part 09. This FAQ is for when something does not work or you do not know where to start.

docs.title: The sections
docs.text: Section What it is about 12.2 Server and database The server that does not start, restarts on its own or goes down, and the database that runs slow, without maintenance or with a damaged table 12.3 Agents and systems The agent that does not show up, Tentacle, the XML and BADXML queues, duplicates and what is specific to Windows and Linux 12.4 Web console and licences Passwords and access, a blank console, a full disk, HTTPS, AD/LDAP, notifications and the licence: checking and renewing it 12.5 Modules and network ICMP, WMI, web checks, templates, MIBs that do not load, traps that do not arrive and port 162 12.6 Alerts and events Alerts that do not fire, those that fire too often and the format of the alert email 12.7 Reports, logs and email PDFs that are not generated, file collections, the log viewer and email that does not arrive 12.8 Large environments Command Center, nodes, centralized mode, event replication and high availability 12.9 Automation and plugins Command line (CLI), API, macros and agent and server plugins 12.10 Bulk operations Deploying agents, changing configurations in bulk, cleaning the data_in and deleting what is left over

docs.title: Bulk operations
docs.text:
Deploying agents, changing configurations and cleaning up in batches, without going one by one.

They are powerful operations, so make a backup before the first one.

docs.title: Deploying agents in bulk
docs.text:
Pandora FMS does it from the deployment centre of Discovery, and two things have to be ready before using it:

  1. An agent repository: in Configuration → EndPoints repository the installers are uploaded, one per operating system.
  2. The credential store: in Configuration → Credential store the users and passwords of the target machines are saved. It is the same store that Discovery uses.

With that, the deployment goes through the machines, installs the agent of their system and leaves it reporting. It is the difference between preparing a hundred machines by hand and reviewing the result of a hundred installations.

docs.title: Updating the configuration of all the agents
docs.text:
There are two cases and they are solved in a different way:

  • Modules, plugins and alerts: it is done with policies. They are applied to the agents of the same operating system and the modules are written in their configuration without touching them one by one.
  • Special parameters of the agent file: here you have to go to the server. It is worth making a copy first of two directories: /var/spool/pandora/data_in/conf (where the server saves the configuration of each agent) and /var/spool/pandora/data_in/md5 (the checksums). With the backup done, the bulk change is applied and the agents are left to pick it up.

docs.title: Deleting the agents that have never reported
docs.text:
The candidates can be located through the database: they are the agents whose modules are all uninitialised. First run a read-only query to identify them. The database uses InnoDB and its tables are related: do not delete rows directly from tagente.

SELECT id_agente, nombre, notinit_count, total_count
FROM tagente
WHERE notinit_count = total_count;

That condition covers the two typical cases: the agent for which no module was created and the one that has them all in not initialised status. Review the list and delete the agents from the agent operations in the console, so that the product also cleans the related tables.

docs.title: Changing the IP of many modules at once
docs.text:
If a device changes address and hundreds of modules monitor it, they are not touched one by one. It is updated from Admin tools → DB interface:

UPDATE tagente_modulo SET ip_target = '10.0.0.1' WHERE ip_target = '10.0.0.2';

The new address goes in ip_target and the old one in the WHERE. It is worth running a SELECT first with the same WHERE to see how many modules are going to be touched. Make a copy of the database before running the UPDATE.

docs.title: Cleaning data_in when it has filled up with XML
docs.text:
