docs.text: Remote configuration has a natural extension for large deployments: autoconfiguration, which applies group, policies or extra configuration to every new EndPoint as soon as it registers, according to rules defined beforehand, without touching them one by one. It is explained in detail in Auto-provisioning mechanisms.

docs.title: Monitoring the basics of the system
docs.text:
Before thinking about scripts of your own or exotic integrations, it is worth covering the obvious: how much CPU and free memory there is, how much disk is left, whether a process or a service is still alive. It is 80% of what is asked of an EndPoint, and a good part of it arrives done: without configuring anything, the template it is installed with already collects the basics.

What comes from the factory Linux (Go and Perl) Windows CPU usage CPU Load module (with vmstat), plus CPU IOWait and Load Average CPU Load module (WMI query) Usage of each disk (%) pandora_df_used plugin df_percent_used.vbs plugin Memory usage (%) pandora_mem_used plugin (includes swap) mem_percent_used.vbs plugin Network traffic pandora_netusage and net_usage plugins network.vbs plugin TCP connections TCP_Connections module TCP_Connections module Known services autodiscover --default plugin: detects the usual services (databases, web servers…) and watches their status, their CPU and their memory Same, with autodiscover.exe --default Hardware information (CPU, RAM, disks, interfaces) hardware_info plugin, once a day Same, with hardware_info.exe

Even so, it is worth knowing how each thing is done by hand: to watch a specific disk, process or service, to adjust thresholds or to replace the template with one of your own. What follows describes the native modules of each EndPoint: first what is common to all three and then what changes according to the operating system.

docs.title: Modules common to all EndPoints
docs.text:
Go, Perl and Windows share these five modules with the same syntax:

Module What it measures module_cpuusage CPU usage percentage. module_freememory Free memory, in MB. module_freepercentmemory Free memory, in %. module_freedisk Free space on a partition or drive, in MB. module_freepercentdisk Free space on a partition or drive, in %. 
module_begin
module_name CPU
module_type generic_data
module_cpuusage
module_end

module_begin
module_name Free memory
module_type generic_data
module_freememory
module_end

module_begin
module_name Free memory (%)
module_type generic_data
module_freepercentmemory
module_end

module_begin
module_name Disk / free (%)
module_type generic_data
module_freepercentdisk /
module_end

module_freedisk and module_freepercentdisk need to know which drive to look at: on Linux and Unix, the mount point exactly as it appears in df (/, /var); on Windows, the drive letter (C:). The rest of the definition (which disk, which partition) is not guessed: if the mount point or the letter does not exist on the machine, the module generates no data.

module_cpuusage optionally accepts the number of the core to measure (0 the first, 1 the second…); with no value, or with all, it aggregates the usage of all cores into one.

docs.title: Monitoring specific to Linux and Unix (Go and Perl EndPoints)
docs.text:
On Linux and the rest of Unix, module_proc and module_service are the same module with two names: they look, among the running processes, for one whose full command line (as ps aux shows it, from the binary name onwards) matches the parameter exactly. The result is 1 if there is a match and 0 if there is not; it is not a count of processes, so it makes no difference whether there is one instance of the process running or five. There is no asynchronous mode and no watchdog: if the process dies, the next cycle reflects it, and that is where the watching ends.

module_begin
module_name SSHD running
module_type generic_proc
module_service /usr/sbin/sshd -D
module_end

The whole command line, not just the name

module_service sshd finds nothing if the real process runs as /usr/sbin/sshd -D. The line has to be copied as ps aux shows it, arguments included.

Two modules exclusive to Unix add detail about that same process: module_cpuproc (CPU usage) and module_memproc (resident memory, in MB). Both require the same kind of exact match as module_proc, and if the process is not running, the module generates no data that cycle. Also exclusive to Unix is module_occupiedpercentdisk, the counterpart of module_freepercentdisk: the used percentage instead of the free one.

module_begin
module_name SSHD, CPU usage
module_type generic_data
module_cpuproc /usr/sbin/sshd -D
module_end

module_begin
module_name Disk / used (%)
module_type generic_data
module_occupiedpercentdisk /
module_end

For everything a native module does not cover there is module_exec: it runs the command or script given to it and takes its standard output as the datum. On Linux and Unix it runs through /bin/sh, and on some systems (Debian and its derivatives, above all) that /bin/sh is dash, not bash: if the command uses bash syntax ([[ ]], arrays, source…), it fails silently or with a different result than expected in an interactive terminal. The safe way to avoid it is to wrap the command in bash -c.

module_begin
module_name Established connections
module_type generic_data
module_exec bash -c "ss -tn state established | wc -l"
module_end

docs.title: Monitoring specific to MS Windows
docs.text:
On Windows, module_service and module_proc stop being the same module and each one looks at a different thing.

module_service checks the status of a service by its short name (the internal one, the one shown in the "Service name" column of the services manager, not the display name), in quotes if it contains spaces. It returns 1 if the service is running and 0 if it is stopped or does not exist.

module_begin
module_name Print Spooler
module_type generic_proc
module_service Spooler
module_end

module_proc looks by process name, with the .exe extension included (notepad.exe, not notepad), and unlike Unix it does return the number of running instances, not a simple yes/no.

module_begin
module_name Notepad instances
module_type generic_data
module_proc notepad.exe
module_end

Both modules accept an asynchronous mode on Windows (module_async): instead of waiting for the next interval, the EndPoint watches for status changes and sends the datum as soon as they happen. On services it relies on the event log notifications of the Service Control Manager; on the Windows editions that do not offer them (the Home ones), the EndPoint switches on its own to checking the status every 10 seconds. Asynchronous modules are not supported on broker agents.

The watchdog (module_watchdog yes) is built on top of the asynchronous mode, and it turns the module into an active watcher. Watch the value: without it, the watchdog does not activate.

  • Services. If the service stops, the EndPoint starts it again by itself; no command has to be given.

    module_begin
module_name Print Spooler
module_type generic_proc
module_service Spooler
module_async yes
module_watchdog yes
module_end

  • Processes. It has to be told how to relaunch it with module_start_command (without it, the EndPoint discards the module and notes it in its log). module_startdelay and module_retrydelay set, in milliseconds, the wait before the start and between retries, and module_retries the number of attempts. The process is launched as the EndPoint service itself, that is, as SYSTEM; to launch it in the session of the user who has the desktop open, module_user_session yes is added.

    module_begin
module_name Notepad
module_type generic_proc
module_proc notepad.exe
module_async yes
module_watchdog yes
module_start_command c:\windows\notepad.exe
module_startdelay 3000
module_retrydelay 2000
module_retries 5
module_end

Windows does not have module_cpuproc, module_memproc or module_occupiedpercentdisk: for the CPU or memory usage of a specific process on Windows you have to resort to module_perfcounter or module_wmiquery (see further down).

docs.title: Creating your own modules
docs.text:
The first thing decided when creating a module is its type (module_type): it tells the server what kind of datum it receives and how to calculate its status. These are the ones used in an EndPoint:

Type What it receives How it is interpreted generic_data A number. The value as it is; the status comes from the thresholds. It is the default type. generic_proc 1 or 0. Direct status: 1 is normal and 0, critical. For "is it alive?". generic_data_string A text. The text as it is; the status comes from the text thresholds. generic_data_inc A counter that only grows. The rate of change per second between two readings (bytes/s, requests/s…). generic_data_inc_abs A counter that only grows. The absolute difference between two readings, without dividing by time. async_data, async_proc, async_string The same as their generic_* equivalents. Data that does not arrive at fixed intervals (events, status changes). They never go to unknown: if no data arrives in twice their interval, they go back to normal (async_recovery 1 on the server, the default value). log Log lines. It is not a monitoring datum: it goes to log collection.

The two incremental ones need a previous reading to calculate anything, so the first datum they send is discarded. The full list of Pandora FMS module types, including the remote monitoring ones, is covered in Introduction and architecture.

Every module, native or your own, is declared with the same wrapper: module_begin opens the definition, module_end closes it, and in between go module_name (mandatory), the data module itself (module_exec, one of the native modules above…) and, optionally, module_description, module_type (by default, generic_data, a numeric value) and the threshold tokens: module_min_warning, module_max_warning, module_min_critical, module_max_critical mark the warning and critical ranges; module_str_warning and module_str_critical do the same by text comparison or regular expression for string-type modules. module_unit adds a unit to the value shown in the Web console (%, GB…) and module_group groups related modules under the same heading in the agent view. All three EndPoints accept these tokens with the same name and the same effect.

module_begin
module_name Disk /var free (%)
module_type generic_data
module_freepercentdisk /var
module_min_warning 20
module_min_critical 10
module_unit %
module_group Disk
module_end

By default, every module runs on every EndPoint cycle, that is, every interval seconds. To space it out there is module_interval, which is not measured in seconds but in cycles: it is a multiplier of the general interval. With interval 300 (five minutes), a module with module_interval 4 runs one out of every four cycles, every 20 minutes. It is useful for costly checks or checks that do not change often, without touching the pace of the rest of the modules.

module_begin
module_name Packages pending update
module_type generic_data
module_exec apt list --upgradable 2>/dev/null | grep -c upgradable || true
module_interval 12
module_end

If what is needed is a fixed interval in time, independent of interval (once a day, every hour), there is module_absoluteinterval, which is explained in Scheduled monitoring.

For what no native module covers, module_exec accepts any command or script installed on the machine and turns its standard output into the module datum; it is the way in to local plugins, whose development is covered in Creating local plugins.

Two rules before the examples. The first: the command has to return a single value, on a single line. The second, the one that causes the most grief: if the command ends with an exit code other than 0, the EndPoint discards the datum even if it has written something. On Linux and Unix the command is launched with sh -c; on Windows, with cmd.exe /c.

Users with an open session on a Linux server, with a warning from five upwards:

module_begin
module_name Connected users
module_type generic_data
module_exec who | wc -l
module_min_warning 5
module_end

Is there a backup from the last 24 hours? The module returns 1 or 0 and, since it is of type generic_proc, the 0 puts the module in critical without defining thresholds:

module_begin
module_name Recent backup
module_type generic_proc
module_exec [ -n "$(find /backup -name '*.tar.gz' -mtime -1)" ] && echo 1 || echo 0
module_end

On Windows, is the computer waiting for a restart to finish applying updates? reg query returns an error code when the key does not exist, which is exactly the normal case, so the && … || turns the result into a 1 or a 0 that always ends well:

module_begin
module_name Pending restart
module_type generic_data
module_exec reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WindowsUpdate\Auto Update\RebootRequired" >nul 2>&1 && echo 1 || echo 0
module_min_warning 1
module_end

The exit code, always under control

A grep -c that finds nothing writes 0, but it exits with code 1 and the EndPoint throws the datum away. If a command can fail in the normal case, force the output with && echo … || echo … or end the pipe with a command that always ends well, such as wc -l.

docs.title: Creating modules from the Web console
docs.text: With remote configuration active (see above), the Web console allows creating and editing these same local modules without touching pandora_agent.conf by hand: the form generates the same tokens seen in this section and the EndPoint picks them up on its next remote configuration check. Without remote configuration, the only way is to edit the file directly on the machine.

docs.title: Advanced monitoring of MS Windows
docs.text:
The Windows EndPoint adds a handful of modules that have no equivalent in Go or in Perl, because they depend on technologies specific to Windows.

module_wmiquery runs a WQL query against WMI and module_wmicolumn indicates which column of the result to take as the module value:

module_begin
module_name Free physical memory (KB)
module_type generic_data
module_wmiquery SELECT FreePhysicalMemory FROM Win32_OperatingSystem
module_wmicolumn FreePhysicalMemory
module_end

If the query returns several rows, the module collects one datum per row; for a single value it is best for the query to return only one.

module_perfcounter reads a Windows performance counter directly (the same ones the Performance Monitor shows). Counter names are in the system language: the example is for a Windows in Spanish. For counters that express a rate ("per second"), module_cooked 1 delivers the value already calculated instead of the raw counter.

module_begin
module_name Bytes received on the network
module_type generic_data
module_perfcounter \Interfaz de red(*)\Bytes recibidos/segundo
module_cooked 1
module_end

The Windows event viewer is read with module_logchannel (the recommended one) or with module_logevent, which is kept for compatibility. Both filter by log (module_source, the only mandatory one), type, event code, application or pattern, and their main use is log collection, which has a chapter of its own: Log collection and monitoring.

Finally, module_exec_powershell runs the given command or script through PowerShell (powershell -C "<command>"), for everything that is better solved with a cmdlet than with a cmd.exe command:

module_begin
module_name Stopped services
module_type generic_data
module_exec_powershell (Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Stopped'}).Count
module_end

docs.title: EndPoint plugins
docs.text:
A local plugin is similar to module_exec in that it is a program installed on the machine that the EndPoint runs on every cycle, but with an important difference: it does not return one datum, but whole modules. The plugin writes the XML of one or several modules (name, type, datum, description…) to its output and the EndPoint adds it as it is to its data file. That is why a single plugin such as pandora_df_used creates one module for each disk it finds. All three EndPoints accept it with module_plugin, and as with module_exec, if the plugin ends with an exit code other than 0, its output is discarded.

The shortest form is a loose line, which runs on every cycle:

module_plugin nagios_plugin_wrapper Disk_tmp /usr/lib/nagios/plugins/check_disk -w 20% -c 10% -p /tmp

If the way it runs has to be adjusted, module_plugin also goes inside a module_begin / module_end block, next to the tokens that control execution: module_interval (every how many EndPoint cycles: 2, one out of every two), module_absoluteinterval (an interval of its own, such as 1d), module_timeout (seconds of margin before giving it up as failed) or module_crontab. In that case module_name and module_type are not needed: the name, the type and the datum are put by the plugin itself in its XML. The installation templates already do it that way:

module_begin
module_plugin hardware_info
module_absoluteinterval 1d
module_end

module_begin
module_plugin autodiscover --default
module_timeout 30
module_end

The Linux and Unix package already brings several plugins ready to use in its plugins folder (some, such as pandora_df_used or autodiscover, have already appeared in the default monitoring table) and it is enough to cite them by name, with no path. Among them is nagios_plugin_wrapper, which runs an already-written Nagios plugin (its first argument is the module name; the rest, the call to the plugin with its parameters) and turns its exit code and its text into a Pandora FMS module, without rewriting anything. On Windows, the plugins the package brings are VBScript scripts and loose executables in the util\ folder (the same df_percent_used.vbs, mem_percent_used.vbs or autodiscover.exe from the previous table); a plugin of your own in PowerShell is invoked like any other command, with module_plugin:

module_plugin powershell.exe -File "%ProgramFiles%\pandora_agent\util\mi_plugin.ps1"

Writing a plugin of your own, in any language, is covered in Creating local plugins.

docs.title: File collections
docs.text:
To avoid copying a plugin by hand on every machine there are collections: packages of files that are uploaded once to the Web console and assigned to the EndPoints that need them, which download them and leave them ready for a module_plugin to use. All three EndPoints accept them; how they are created, assigned and used from policies is explained in its chapter, Collections.

Remote configuration, a prerequisite

Collections are distributed over the same channel as remote configuration (see Remote configuration from the Web console): without it active, there is no way to push a collection to the EndPoint.

docs.title: Conditional monitoring
docs.text:
A precondition (module_precondition) decides whether the module gets to run; a condition (module_condition) evaluates the result already obtained. Both share the same syntax, in all three EndPoints:

Form Syntax It is met when Numeric comparison <operator> <value> <command> The value meets <operator> <value>. Operators: >, <, = and != (there is no >= or <=). Interval (<minimum>,<maximum>) <command> The value is between the two limits, not including them. Regular expression =~ <pattern> <command> The value matches <pattern>.

What changes is where the value comes from and what the command does:

  • In a precondition, the EndPoint runs the <command> first and compares its output. If a module has several, all of them have to be met; if any fails, the module does not run that cycle.
  • In a condition, the value is the datum the module has just obtained. If it is met, the EndPoint launches the <command> separately, as a response action (restart something, clean a directory…); the module datum does not change.

A precondition to avoid false alarms: the module checks whether there is a recent backup on a network resource mounted at /backup, but only if that resource is mounted. If it is not, the module does not run that cycle, instead of marking as critical a backup it has not even been able to look at:

module_begin
module_name Recent backup
module_type generic_proc
module_precondition = 1 mountpoint -q /backup && echo 1 || echo 0
module_exec [ -n "$(find /backup -name '*.tar.gz' -mtime -1)" ] && echo 1 || echo 0
module_end

A condition as a response action: the module measures how full the root disk is and, if it goes over 90%, the EndPoint deletes compressed logs older than 30 days. The datum is sent anyway; the deletion is a separate effect:

module_begin
module_name Disk / used (%)
module_type generic_data
module_occupiedpercentdisk /
module_condition > 90 find /var/log -name '*.gz' -mtime +30 -delete
module_min_warning 85
module_end

docs.title: Intensive monitoring
docs.text:
Intensive monitoring serves to find out before something falls without multiplying the data that is sent. It is activated with the global token intensive_interval, in seconds and shorter than interval: the EndPoint starts going round every intensive_interval seconds. On each round it runs the modules marked with module_intensive_condition, but it only sends their datum when their compliance with the condition changes, or when their normal interval is due. With intensive_interval at 0 (the default value) it is the same as interval and there is no intensive monitoring. The condition uses the same syntax as those in the previous table, without a command.

# General part of the file
interval 300
intensive_interval 10

module_begin
module_name Ping to the gateway
module_type generic_proc
module_exec ping -c 1 -W 1 192.168.1.1 >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo 1 || echo 0
module_intensive_condition = 0
module_end

docs.title: Scheduled monitoring
docs.text:
There are two ways for a module not to follow the normal pace of the EndPoint.

module_absoluteinterval gives it an interval of its own, in real time and not in cycles like module_interval. It accepts a number with a suffix (30s, 15m, 6h, 1d) or, with no suffix, a number of interval cycles. Underneath, the EndPoint translates it into cycles by rounding up: with interval 300, a module_absoluteinterval 7m runs every two cycles, that is, every 10 minutes. So it is best not to expect more precision than that of interval itself.

What really sets it apart from module_interval is memory: all three EndPoints save the time of the module's last run in a reference file (.ref), so that the interval is respected even if the EndPoint restarts. A daily module runs once a day, not once a day plus one for each restart. The special value once makes the module run a single time and turns it into an asynchronous one.

module_begin
module_name Web certificate: days to expiry
module_type generic_data
module_exec echo $(( ( $(date -d "$(openssl x509 -enddate -noout -in /etc/ssl/certs/web.pem | cut -d= -f2)" +%s) - $(date +%s) ) / 86400 ))
module_absoluteinterval 1d
module_end

module_crontab goes one step further: the module only runs when the time matches a five-field cron expression (minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week); the rest of the cycles it does nothing. It is the right thing for what makes sense at a specific time, such as a nightly close or a weekly report.

module_begin
module_name Weekly report generated (Monday, 9:00)
module_type generic_proc
module_exec [ -f /var/reports/weekly.done ] && echo 1 || echo 0
module_crontab 0 9 * * 1
module_end

docs.title: Post-processing, flip-flop and other module settings
docs.text:
A handful of tokens, common to all three EndPoints, fine-tune how the datum is treated once obtained, without touching how it is obtained. They are the configuration-file equivalents of the form fields described in 2.20, Common module configuration:

Token What it does module_postprocess Factor by which the server multiplies the numeric value when it receives it (to convert bytes into MB, for example). The EndPoint sends it as it is along with the datum. module_ff_interval, module_ff_type, module_each_ff, module_min_ff_event* They adjust the flip-flop: how many consecutive status changes are needed for the server to fire an event, instead of one for each change. module_timeout Seconds of margin for the module command or plugin to finish before giving it up as failed. module_save <variable> Saves the module value in the given environment variable, so that the modules that run afterwards use it.

module_async, already seen in the monitoring of Windows services and processes, is exclusive to that EndPoint: it turns the module into a watcher that warns as soon as it changes status, instead of waiting for the cycle. Neither Go nor Perl implements it.

docs.title: The EndPoint as a network monitoring point
Remote checks from the EndPoint
docs.text:
An EndPoint can also watch another machine on the network from where it is installed, without that machine having an EndPoint of its own. The difference between systems is one of substance, not of nuance: Windows brings native modules for this; on Linux and Unix, with Go or with Perl, there are no equivalents and they are built with module_exec.

On Windows, module_ping launches a ping against the given host and gives 1 or 0 depending on whether it gets a response; module_ping_count and module_ping_timeout adjust the number of attempts and the waiting time. module_tcpcheck checks whether a TCP port responds, with module_port to indicate which one and module_timeout for the waiting margin. module_snmpget launches an SNMP query and takes the returned value as the module datum, with module_snmp_version, module_snmp_community, module_snmp_agent (the host) and module_snmp_oid.

module_begin
module_name Ping to the gateway
module_type generic_proc
module_ping 192.168.1.1
module_ping_count 2
module_ping_timeout 1
module_end

module_begin
module_name Server web port
module_type generic_proc
module_tcpcheck 192.168.1.10
module_port 443
module_end

On Linux and Unix the same result is achieved with module_exec, supported by the system tools. Here the same rule applies as in any other module_exec: the exit code decides whether the datum is sent, so it has to be forced explicitly instead of trusting the command's own exit code.

module_begin
module_name Ping to the gateway
module_type generic_proc
module_exec ping -c 1 -W 1 192.168.1.1 >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo 1 || echo 0
module_end

module_begin
module_name Server web port
module_type generic_proc
module_exec nc -z -w 2 192.168.1.10 443 && echo 1 || echo 0
module_end

module_begin
module_name Uptime over SNMP
module_type generic_data
module_exec snmpget -Ovq -c public -v 2c 192.168.1.10 sysUpTime.0
module_end

For network monitoring from outside the target machine (with no EndPoint needed) there is remote monitoring, in Network monitoring.

docs.title: Broker mode
docs.text:
An EndPoint in broker mode stops reporting as a single agent and starts generating and sending, in the same cycle, one or several additional agents: each broker_agent <name> in pandora_agent.conf starts a child agent with its own configuration, derived from that of the main EndPoint (same server, same interval, same transfer mode), but with its own name and its own modules. It is what allows, for example, a single EndPoint installed on a gateway to report data from several devices behind it, each one as its own agent in the console.

All three EndPoints accept it. On the Windows EndPoint, broker agents do not accept asynchronous modules: a module with module_async in the configuration of a broker is discarded.

broker_agent Router-planta-1
broker_agent Router-planta-2

docs.title: Proxy mode
docs.text:
In proxy mode, the EndPoint stops limiting itself to sending its own data and also starts acting as a Tentacle intermediary for other EndPoints on its network that do not reach the server directly. On starting with proxy_mode 1, it starts its own local Tentacle server (tentacle_server) listening on proxy_address and proxy_port (by default, all interfaces and port 41121, the same as the server's), and it forwards what it receives towards server_ip and server_port. proxy_max_connection limits the simultaneous connections it accepts (by default, 10) and proxy_timeout the waiting time of each one (by default, 1 second). The EndPoints that rely on the proxy only need to point their server_ip to the machine acting as proxy, instead of to the real server.

# On the EndPoint acting as proxy
proxy_mode 1
proxy_address 0.0.0.0
proxy_port 41121

docs.title: Secondary server
docs.text:
secondary_mode decides whether the EndPoint also sends its data to a second server, in addition to the main one (server_ip), and under what circumstance:

Value Behaviour never (default) It is only sent to the main server. on_error The main one is tried first; only if it fails, it is sent to the secondary one. always It is sent to both servers, always.

The secondary server is configured with its own mirrored set of tokens (secondary_server_ip, secondary_server_port, secondary_transfer_mode, secondary_server_ssl, secondary_server_path, secondary_server_user, secondary_server_pwd), independent of the main server's. It is the way to keep reporting when the main server is not available, or to feed two different Pandora FMS installations at once, without depending on proxy mode or on a full distributed architecture.

secondary_mode on_error
secondary_server_ip 10.0.0.5
secondary_transfer_mode tentacle

docs.title: Remote actions on the EndPoint
docs.text:
The Perl and Windows EndPoints can listen for orders through a small UDP server: it is activated with udp_server 1 (it comes deactivated), it listens on udp_server_port (41122 by default) and it only serves the addresses in udp_server_auth_address (0.0.0.0, the default value, accepts any). The Go EndPoint has no UDP server.

The orders it understands are few and deliberately limited:

Order What it does Perl Windows REFRESH AGENT Forces an immediate run of the cycle: the EndPoint collects and sends its data without waiting for the interval. Yes Yes (see note) START PROCESS <name> / STOP PROCESS <name> Runs the command defined in process_<name>_start / process_<name>_stop. Without that token, the order is rejected. Yes Yes START SERVICE <name> / STOP SERVICE <name> Starts or stops the given Windows service, only if it is authorised with service_<name> 1. No Yes 
udp_server 1
udp_server_port 41122
udp_server_auth_address 10.0.0.20
process_backup_start /usr/local/bin/run_backup.sh
process_backup_stop /usr/local/bin/stop_backup.sh

udp_server 1
udp_server_auth_address 10.0.0.20
service_spooler 1
process_informe_start C:\scripts\informe.bat

Three words on Windows

The Windows EndPoint requires every order to have exactly three words; that is why, to refresh it, the order is REFRESH AGENT *. It is the form used by the alert action "Restart agent" that comes as standard; if a two-word order does nothing on a Windows EndPoint, this is the reason.

From the server, the orders are sent with udp_client.pl (/usr/share/pandora_server/util/udp_client.pl <ip> 41122 "<command>"), which is what the "Remote agent control" alert command and the "Restart agent" action use.

To run arbitrary commands or scripts on the EndPoint from the console, without depending on this UDP server or on predefined actions, there is remote command and script execution: Remote execution of scripts and commands.

docs.title: Other monitoring techniques
docs.text:
Three more mechanisms, for occasional use, complete what an EndPoint can contribute beyond its modules:

  • KeepAlive. A module of type keep_alive that goes to critical when the agent stops sending data. It is created only from the Web console (even if there is no remote configuration) and it leaves no trace in pandora_agent.conf.
  • Command Snapshot. A text-type module that collects the full output of a long command (ps aux, netstat -n) to see it in the console as it is, like a screenshot. It requires enabling the Command line snapshot option in the Web console configuration. With the Go EndPoint it does not work: module_exec only takes the first line of the output.
  • Image monitoring. A text-type module (generic_data_string or async_string) whose datum is an image encoded in base64 (data:image/jpeg;base64,…), which the console shows as an image instead of as text. Normally a plugin generates it.

The EndPoint also takes part in two areas with a chapter of their own: the system inventory, in Inventory, and log collection, in Log collection and monitoring.

docs.title: Watching text files with module_regexp
docs.text:
module_regexp watches a text file looking for the new lines that meet module_pattern (a regular expression); module_pattern_exclude discards those that, meeting it, also match this other one. What it returns depends on the type: with generic_data, how many lines match; with generic_proc, 1 if there is any; with generic_data_string, the lines. All three EndPoints accept it with the same tokens, including module_pattern_exclude: despite what some old documentation says, it is not exclusive to Linux, it also works on the Windows EndPoint. Only Windows adds module_noseekeof: with 1, the module reviews the whole file on every run instead of only what was added since the previous one.

module_begin
module_name Errors in the application log
module_type generic_data_string
module_regexp /var/log/miapp/error.log
module_pattern ERROR
module_pattern_exclude KNOWN_ERROR
module_end

It is the minimum mechanism to watch a single file; for log collection in earnest (centralised, with multiple sources and later search) there is Log collection and monitoring.

docs.title: How it works inside
docs.text:
Everything above (modules, plugins, collections) flows into the same delivery mechanism. It is worth understanding it once, because it explains in one go why the agent appears on its own in the console, what debug 1 really does and why data is not thrown away when the buffer fills up.

The data XML and autocreation. On each cycle, the EndPoint gathers the result of all its modules into a single XML document, wrapped in an <agent_data> tag with the agent attributes (name, alias, group, interval, version…) and one <module> for each module, with its name, type and datum. That file is first written to the temporal folder with the name <agent hash>.<timestamp>.data and it is sent from there; the XML is not generated directly on the fly at delivery time, so a trace always remains on disk while the cycle lasts. It is this same XML that the server processes to create the agent and its modules the first time they appear (autocreate 1, already seen in First steps with a freshly installed EndPoint): there are no two different formats, one for registration and another for day-to-day operation.

Learning, normal and self-disabled modes. Whether a new module from the XML ends up in the console also depends on the mode of the agent, which is chosen when editing it in the Web console:

Mode What it does with the XML Learning mode (default) It creates the new modules and updates the agent data (IP address, interval, operating system and EndPoint version, custom fields) and the configuration of the modules that already exist, except those that come from a policy. Normal mode It only processes data from modules that already exist: the new ones are discarded and the agent data the XML sends does not overwrite the console ones. Self-disabled mode Same as learning, but the server disables the agent when all its modules (not counting the asynchronous ones) go to unknown, and it enables it again as soon as new data arrives. Intended for machines that appear and disappear.

It is the first suspicion when someone adds a module_begin to the EndPoint, checks that the XML comes out well and the module never appears: the agent is in normal mode and the server, obediently, ignores it.

Transfer: Tentacle, SSH, FTP and local. The delivery itself is done by an external program that the EndPoint launches against the .data file, according to transfer_mode: all three EndPoints accept the four modes (tentacle by default, ssh with scp, ftp and local, a file copy for when the EndPoint runs on the same machine as the server) with the same repertoire in Go, Perl and Windows.

Tentacle, the default mode

tentacle is the one the installation templates bring, and its client travels in the EndPoint package itself; ssh and ftp depend on the machine having scp or an FTP client.

With Tentacle, two tokens activate client options: server_ssl 1 adds -c (encryption) to the tentacle_client call, and server_pwd adds -x <key> (password shared with the server). Both translate the same way in the three EndPoints.

The XML buffer. If the delivery of the cycle fails (server down, network cut), by default the EndPoint throws that XML away: the next round generates a new one and the lost datum does not come back. xml_buffer 1 changes that policy: the .data file that could not be sent stays in temporal and the EndPoint tries to send it again, together with the one from the next round, on the following cycle. The policy is applied equally in Go, Perl and Windows, with the same three limits, all with the same default value (1024, in the sense each one indicates):

Token Limit temporal_min_size Minimum free megabytes on the temporal partition; below that, nothing new is stored in the buffer. temporal_max_files Maximum number of .data files accumulated in temporal. temporal_max_size Maximum megabytes occupied by those files altogether.

With xml_buffer 0 (the default value) these three limits are not even checked: the EndPoint accumulates nothing that cannot be sent on the spot.

debug, again. It already came up in Essential parameters of pandora_agent.conf: with debug 1 the delivery does not change (the datum goes out the same, cycle after cycle) but the EndPoint stops checking remote configuration and collections on every round and keeps each .data sent with the sent suffix instead of deleting it, so that it can be reviewed afterwards.

autotime. By default, the EndPoint puts the local time of the machine it runs on in the XML (timestamp). With autotime 1, that attribute disappears from the XML and it is the server that puts its own reception time when processing the datum. It is useful for EndPoints on machines whose clock is not to be trusted (a badly synchronised virtual machine, a device with no NTP) and that, otherwise, would generate data with a shifted timestamp. The behaviour is identical in the three EndPoints.

docs.title: Feature comparison between EndPoints
docs.text:
Before installing a specific EndPoint on a machine, it is worth having at hand what it is capable of doing and what it is not. The table summarises by feature, not token by token; that is in the full EndPoint configuration reference, which details each token one by one with its exact compatibility.

Feature Go Perl Windows Basic native modules (CPU, memory, disk) Yes Yes Yes Unix process modules (module_proc/module_service yes/no, module_cpuproc, module_memproc, module_occupiedpercentdisk) Yes Yes No Windows service and process with asynchronous mode and watchdog No No Yes WMI, performance counters, event viewer, PowerShell No No Yes Native network checks (module_ping, module_tcpcheck, module_snmpget) No (with module_exec) No (with module_exec) Yes module_exec Yes, first line of the output Yes Yes Local plugins (module_plugin) Yes Yes Yes File collections Yes Yes Yes Remote configuration Yes, only tentacle and local Yes, the four transfer modes Yes, the four transfer modes Precondition, condition, intensive, module_crontab, module_absoluteinterval Yes Yes Yes Broker mode Yes Yes Yes, without asynchronous modules on broker agents Proxy mode Yes Yes Yes Secondary server Yes Yes Yes UDP server (remote actions) No Yes Yes module_regexp Yes Yes Yes, also with module_noseekeof Transfer modes of the data XML (tentacle, ssh, ftp, local) All four All four All four XML buffer (xml_buffer) Yes Yes Yes

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Most problems with an EndPoint come down to one of these checks, in the order in which they are best done.

  1. Does the agent appear in the console? If nothing appears, check autocreate on the server (see First steps with a freshly installed EndPoint) and that the EndPoint reaches the server: the Tentacle port (41121 by default) has to be reachable between the two machines.
  2. Is the configuration file the one you think? With remote configuration active, a change made by hand on the machine may end up overwritten by the server on the next cycle if the MD5 does not match (see Remote configuration from the Web console). Compare the local file with the one the console shows before taking a change for lost.
  3. Does the plugin or the module_exec have the right permissions and path? A plugin of your own or a script outside the plugins folder needs the full path, and the file needs the execute permission (chmod 755 on Linux and Unix).

  4. Are the output and the exit code the ones the EndPoint expects? Run the command or the plugin by hand, in the same account the EndPoint runs with, and check two things: that the exit code is 0 (if it is not, the EndPoint discards the datum even if it has written something good) and that the output is exactly what is expected (a single value for module_exec, a complete and valid XML for a plugin). To check the XML of a plugin, xmllint is more reliable than looking at it by eye. Since a plugin writes one or several loose <module> elements, with no root element, they have to be wrapped before validating them:

    (echo "<plugin>"; ./mi_plugin; echo "</plugin>") | xmllint --noout -

  5. Debug mode. With debug 1 (see Essential parameters of pandora_agent.conf), each .data sent is kept with the sent suffix in the temporal folder, so it can be opened to check exactly what each module or plugin generated that cycle, without waiting for it to reach the console.

  6. The EndPoint log. On Linux and Unix, /var/log/pandora/pandora_agent.log by default (logfile in pandora_agent.conf); on Windows, pandora_agent.log in the installation folder, and pandora_debug.log next to it if debug mode is active.
  7. Restart the service after any manual change to the configuration file: systemctl restart pandora_agent_daemon on Linux and Unix, NET STOP / NET START PandoraFMSAgent on Windows (see First steps with a freshly installed EndPoint).
  8. Run the EndPoint by hand, without the service. Each EndPoint has its own way of running outside the service, useful to see the messages as they happen: the Go EndPoint accepts pandora_agent --once /etc/pandora for a single collection and delivery cycle; the Windows EndPoint accepts PandoraAgent.exe --process to run as a user process instead of as a service, and --test-ssh / --test-ftp to test those two transfer modes separately with the current configuration.

EndPoint permissions, not just the plugin's

On Linux, the pandora_agent_daemon service runs as root unless pandora_user is set in the configuration; on Windows, the service runs as SYSTEM. A command that works in an interactive terminal may fail inside the EndPoint if it depends on environment variables or permissions that only the user who opened that terminal has.

For what is not specific to the EndPoint (server, Web console or other component errors) there is the general troubleshooting guide.

docs.title: Bulk operations
docs.text:
Changing the interval of one module takes three clicks. Changing it in the four hundred CPU Load modules of a Linux server farm takes 1,200 clicks, a lost afternoon and, almost certainly, a couple of forgotten modules that someone will find six months from now wondering why that particular server runs at a different pace. Bulk operations exist for this: choose once what changes, choose once who it changes for, and let Pandora FMS do the repetitive work.

The tool has been rebuilt from scratch. Where there used to be one submenu per element type, each with its own form and its own quirks, there is now a single step-by-step wizard that works the same for agents, modules, alerts, policies, users and SNMP alerts. Three ideas hold it up:

  • One wizard. First you choose the operation, then the affected elements and, at the end, the changes or the confirmation.
  • One lock per field. When editing, what is not unlocked is not touched. No more "leave the field blank and cross your fingers".
  • One queue. The operation runs in the background, in batches, while the operator keeps working; when it finishes, it tells you.

A bulk delete cannot be undone

Deleting one hundred agents costs the same as deleting one: a button. There is no bin and no way back. Before confirming a delete, review the list of selected elements with the same care you would give an rm -rf.

docs.title: Access and structure of the wizard
docs.text:
Bulk operations live in Management → Configuration → Bulk operations, with two entries:

  • Execute: the wizard that builds and launches the operation.
  • Queue: the pending or failed operations (see The operation queue).

Every operation follows the same pattern:

  1. Bulk task type. You choose the Task target (agents, modules, alerts, policies, users or SNMP alerts) and the Task type (edit, delete, copy, add…).
  2. Choose elements. You select the agents, modules, policies, users or alerts the operation acts on.
  3. The steps that follow, depending on the operation. An edition ends in Configure & Execute; a delete, in a confirmation with the count of elements; alert and copy operations add intermediate steps (templates, actions, destinations).

The buttons are the same across the wizard: Next, Back, Cancel and, in the last step, Complete, which launches the operation.

These are the available operations:

Task target Task types Agent operations Edit agents · Delete agents Module operations Edit modules · Edit satellite modules · Delete modules · Copy modules between agents Alert operations Add alerts · Edit alerts · Delete alerts · Add alerts actions · Delete alerts actions Policy operations Modules: edit modules, edit satellite modules, copy modules between policies, copy modules from agents · Alerts: add and delete alerts, add and delete alerts actions · External alerts: add and delete external alerts, add and delete their actions User operations Edit users · Add profiles to users · Delete profiles from users SNMP alert operations Edit SNMP alerts · Delete SNMP alerts

In the policies dropdown the task types appear grouped in three blocks (Modules, Alerts and External alerts): there are many of them and, without grouping, finding the one you were after was an exercise in patience.

What appears in this list depends on the user's permissions (see Permissions): a target you have no permission for is simply not offered.

docs.title: The draft: leave and come back without losing your work
docs.text:
Every time you press Next, the wizard saves what you have chosen so far in a draft. If the operator moves to another screen (or is interrupted, which is the usual thing), coming back to Execute resumes the operation where it was left.

There is a single draft per user: choosing a new task type in the first step discards the previous one. Cancel, in any step, discards it too and takes you back to the empty first step. On pressing Complete, the draft moves to the queue and disappears: there is nothing left to resume.

The wizard only complains when there is a reason. If you try to move on without having selected any element, it warns you and does not let you continue; as long as you do not try, it shows no errors.

docs.title: Selecting elements
docs.text:
The second step uses a two-panel selector: on the left, the available elements; on the right, the selected ones. You tick boxes and move them from one side to the other with Add and Remove; the Select all checkbox ticks everything the panel shows at that moment.

For agents, the filters are:

Filter What it does Group Shows the agents of the chosen group Recursion Includes the agents of the subgroups OS Filters by operating system Search Filters by name

The selector includes enabled and disabled agents alike, and only shows those of groups the user can manage.

For modules, you first choose the agents (with the same filters) and then their modules, with these additional filters:

Filter What it does Module type Data modules, network modules, plugin modules, prediction modules, WMI, web or WUX Module data type Boolean, numeric, text, incremental… Common modules Shows only the modules (by name) that every selected agent has Search Filters by module name

The Common modules filter is the one that turns the operation into something genuinely useful: with fifty agents selected, turning it on leaves only the modules that exist in all fifty, which are usually exactly the ones you want to touch.

Two exclusions are worth bearing in mind before you go looking for a module that does not appear:

  • Modules that belong to a policy do not appear in Edit modules or in Delete modules. They are edited from the policy operations (see Policy operations), because any change made by hand on the agent would be overwritten by the policy on its next application.
  • Edit modules leaves out satellite modules, which have an operation of their own (Edit satellite modules) because their configuration is different.

docs.title: The lock: what is changed and what is left alone
docs.text:
The old question of any bulk edition is how to tell "I do not want to change this field" from "I want to leave this field empty". The previous answer was leaving it blank or choosing "No changes" in a dropdown, depending on the screen. The current one is a lock next to each field.

  • Every field appears locked by default (closed lock, grey field).
  • A locked field is not sent: each element keeps the value it had.
  • When you press the lock (Click to unlock), the field is enabled and it is applied as it is. If you unlock it and leave it empty, the value is erased in every selected element.

That last rule is the one that bites. Unlocking a field out of curiosity and pressing Complete amounts to emptying it in every element. If you have unlocked something you did not mean to touch, just lock it again before finishing.

The lock propagates to the dependent blocks: the macros of a plugin and the satellite configuration of a module also start locked and have to be opened explicitly.

Change only the interval

You want to move every CPU Load module of the agents in the Servers-Linux group to 10 minutes, without touching descriptions or thresholds. In step 2 you filter the group with recursion, turn on Common modules and select CPU Load. In step 3 you unlock only the interval, set it to 10 minutes and press Complete. Everything else, locked, stays as it was in each module.

The lock is used in agent, module, satellite module and policy module editions. User and SNMP alert editions do not use it: there each field is applied only if it is filled in. Operations that create something new (adding alerts or actions) do not need it either, because there is no previous value to respect.

docs.title: Edit agents
docs.text:
Steps: Bulk task type → Choose Agents → Configure & Execute.

The third step reuses the same agent edition form, with its tabs (Overview, Advanced and Custom fields) and with every field protected by the lock. Any piece of data you can change in an agent can be changed here in bulk: primary group, description, operating system, assigned server, custom fields…

On execution, Pandora FMS checks again the write permission on the group of each agent. If an agent the user has no permission on has slipped into the selection, that agent is not modified and the attempt is recorded in the audit log.

docs.title: Delete agents
docs.text:
Steps: Bulk task type → Choose Agents → Confirm delete operation.

The last step has no options: it shows how many agents are going to be deleted and warns that the action cannot be undone. If one of them fails, the rest go ahead and the error is recorded in the queue.

On a node whose management is centralised from the Command Center, this operation is not offered: agents are deleted from the Command Center.

Clean up a lab

To delete the test agents of the Lab group: target Agent operations, type Delete agents; in step 2 you filter by the Lab group, Select all and Add; in step 3, you check the count and press Complete.

docs.title: Edit modules
docs.text:
Steps: Bulk task type → Choose Modules → Configure & Execute.

You can mix modules of any kind, but the mix decides which fields you see. The form shows only what makes sense for every selected module at once, according to two things: the module data type (boolean, numeric, text…) and the type of check (data, network, plugin, WMI, web…).

So, with two boolean ICMP modules you can edit the thresholds; with a selection that mixes ICMP, plugins and data modules, the thresholds and the fields specific to each check disappear and the form says so with a notice ("unavailable; modules of different types have been selected"). Only what is common remains (description, interval, enabled or disabled status…), explained in 2.20, Common module configuration.

One rule comes inherited from the individual edition: if a module type does not allow editing a field in its normal form, it does not allow it in the bulk edition either, even if the rest of the modules in the selection could.

Two restrictions affect the parent module:

  • You can only choose a parent if every selected module belongs to the same agent.
  • None of the selected modules can be the parent of the selection; a module cannot be its own parent.

Where the plugin operations went

The old section of plugin operations no longer exists. To enable or disable plugin modules or edit their macros in bulk, you use Edit modules with the Module type filter set to plugin modules. The macros are only editable if every selected module uses the same plugin.

docs.title: Edit satellite modules
docs.text: Same as Edit modules, but limited to the modules a Satellite server collects, with their specific configuration (also under lock).

docs.title: Delete modules
docs.text: Steps: Bulk task type → Choose Modules → Confirm delete operation. As with agents, the last step shows the count and there is no way back. Policy modules do not appear here either.

docs.title: Copy modules between agents
docs.text: Steps: Bulk task type → Choose Modules → Destination agents → Confirm. You choose the source modules, then the agents that will receive them and, in the confirmation, you are shown how many modules will be copied into how many agents.

docs.title: Alert operations
docs.text:
These operations work with alerts associated to agent modules. They all share the starting point: Choose Modules → Choose templates.

Task type Steps after choosing modules and templates Add alerts Choose actions → Confirm Edit alerts Configure alerts Delete alerts Confirm Add alerts actions Choose actions → Confirm Delete alerts actions Choose actions → Confirm

The confirmation tells you how many templates and actions are assigned (or removed) and in how many modules. Templates, actions and how alerts themselves work are explained in their own chapter.

docs.title: Policy operations
docs.text:
Policy operations are divided into three blocks. They all work on the policy definition, not on the agents: after any change you have to apply the policy for it to reach its agents (see Monitoring policies).

Modules:

Task type Steps Edit modules Choose policy modules → Configure & Execute (with lock) Edit satellite modules Same, for the satellite modules of the policy Copy modules between policies Choose policy modules → Destination policies → Confirm Copy modules from agents Choose source agent modules → Destination policies → Confirm

The last one is the convenient way to turn into a policy something you have fine-tuned by hand on one agent: you try it on one, you copy it to the policy and you apply it to the rest.

Alerts (on the modules of the policy): add and delete alerts, add and delete alerts actions. The steps are the same as in Alert operations, but the second step chooses policy modules.

External alerts (defined at policy level, not at module level): add and delete external alerts and their actions. Here the second step chooses policies, not modules.

docs.title: User operations
docs.text:
Task type Steps Edit users Choose users → Configure & Execute Add profiles to users Choose users → Configure profiles Delete profiles from users Choose users → Configure profiles to delete → Confirm

Edit users changes preferences, not identities: language, block size of the lists, home page, default event and log filter, self-refresh time, pages with self-refresh and time zone. Each field is applied only if it is filled in.

Add profiles to users assigns a combination of profile and group to every selected user; Delete profiles from users removes it.

docs.title: SNMP alert operations
docs.text:
Task type Steps Edit SNMP alerts Choose SNMP alerts → Configure alerts Delete SNMP alerts Choose SNMP alerts → Confirm SNMP alert deletion

In the selector, each alert appears with its identifier in front ([ID Alert: 1] - <description>), which is useful when there are several with similar descriptions.

The edition allows changing description, OID, custom OID, source IP of the trap, trap type and subtype, group, unique value and the variable fields of the trap (up to 20). Each field is applied only if it is filled in. How trap alerts work is explained in SNMP trap monitoring.

docs.title: The operation queue
docs.text:
When you press Complete, the wizard does not wait for the operation to finish: it sends it to the queue, goes back to the first step and shows the Operation queued notice. The web server processes it in the background in batches, and the operator can prepare the next one meanwhile.

When it finishes, well or badly, a notification reaches the console with the name of the operation and the number of elements processed.

The Queue page only shows what is pending or has failed; operations completed successfully disappear from the list (the notice that they have finished is the notification). For each entry it shows:

Column Content Operation type The operation launched User Who launched it Status Pending or failed Error Show error button with the detail, if there is one Progress Progress bar, which refreshes by itself every two seconds Created Date and time of launch Op. Delete the entry

The queue does not retry. A failed operation is reviewed with Show error, deleted from the list and, once the problem is fixed, launched again from Execute.

docs.title: Batch size and PHP limits
docs.text:
The operation is not processed in one go, but in batches. Their size is set by Limit for bulk operations, in Settings → System Settings → Behavior (Other block): the number of elements processed in each round, so that a big operation does not run out of memory. It accepts values between 100 and 2000; by default it is half of the PHP max_input_vars. See Complete console configuration reference.

Requirement Detail Enough PHP max_input_vars If the form sends more fields than PHP accepts, the wizard warns you before sending: the leftover elements could be lost. With very large selections, raise the value in php.ini or split the operation Limit for bulk operations Between 100 and 2000 elements per batch; by default, half of max_input_vars

Since the operation is processed in the background, it no longer depends on the PHP max_execution_time or max_input_time.

docs.title: Bulk operations from the Command Center
docs.text:
In the Command Center bulk operations appear as Bulk operations in its management menu, with the same Execute and Queue entries, but with a reduced catalogue:

Task target Available task types Agent operations Edit agents · Delete agents User operations Edit users

Operations on modules, alerts, policies and SNMP alerts are not available in the Command Center; they are done in each node. How the Command Center works and how it relates to the nodes is explained in its own chapter.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Access Required permission Bulk operations → Execute menu Agent write (AW) Queue page Pandora FMS management (PM) Agent and module operations Agent read or write (AR/AW) Delete agents In addition, the node must not be centrally managed from the Command Center Alert and SNMP alert operations Alert write or management (LW/LM; LW for SNMP alerts) Policy operations Agent read or write (AR/AW), on a node without centralised management User operations User management (UM)

Besides the permission to see the operation, running it checks the permission on the group of each element: the selector only offers agents of groups the user can manage, and if one of them does not comply at the moment of execution, it is skipped and recorded in the audit log.

docs.title: Application monitoring
docs.text:
A database that does not respond gives no warning: it simply stops answering, and the users are usually the first to find out. Installing an EndPoint on each database server to watch it is an option, but not the only one, nor the most convenient when the instances are dozens and live on machines that are not always yours. With Discovery, a .disco package from the Marketplace and a task in Discovery → Applications are enough: the server queries the application remotely at every interval and creates, or updates, the corresponding agents and modules. With nothing installed on the monitored host.

How a .disco package is installed and what a task does step by step is explained only once, in section 2.3 (How a .disco package task works). Here only what is specific to applications is left. One warning beforehand: the Applications section shows only what is installed; if the checkbox of an application is missing, its .disco package is missing (The Discovery sections).

This chapter stops at seven applications from the catalog, but what it tells applies to all the others: any .disco package in Applications is installed, configured and run the same way, with the task of a .disco package. What changes from one to another is the fields it asks for and the modules it creates, and that detail (all its fields, the modules it generates, custom queries) lives on the page of each plugin in the integration documentation and in its Marketplace entry, and it is not copied here. For an application that is not in this table, search for it by name on those two sites.

Application Short name in the catalog Detail MySQL pandorafms.mysql Integration documentation and Marketplace Microsoft SQL Server pandorafms.mssql Integration documentation and Marketplace PostgreSQL pandorafms.postgresql Integration documentation and Marketplace MongoDB pandorafms.mongodb Integration documentation and Marketplace Oracle pandorafms.oracle Integration documentation and Marketplace Apache pandorafms.apache Integration documentation and Marketplace NGINX pandorafms.nginx Integration documentation and Marketplace

Virtualization (VMware, Proxmox) and orchestrators (Kubernetes) also appear in the Applications section, but they have a chapter of their own: Virtualized environment monitoring and Container and orchestrator monitoring.

docs.title: Complete example: a MySQL task
docs.text:
MySQL serves as an example because it is the typical case: a list of instances, a user with read permissions and one agent per instance. The generic steps (defining the task, forcing it, reading the summary) are in 2.3; what follows is only what is specific to a database.

  1. What the .disco package asks for. After the first defining step, the .disco package adds two steps. MySQL Base asks for the list of instances (SERVER:PORT, with 3306 by default; one per line or separated by commas), the user and the password.

MySQL Detailed asks for the threads, whether an agent per database is wanted, the prefixes, the metric groups and the custom queries.

The user and the password go in fields of their own, of password type, and not in the Credential manager: MySQL is one of the .disco packages that works that way.

  1. Preparing the user in MySQL. The plugin only reads, and it is advisable that its user does the same:

    Requirement Detail Network Reachability from the Discovery server to each instance (port 3306 by default). Data SELECT permission on the tables of the databases and on those of INFORMATION_SCHEMA. Server status SHOW STATUS and SHOW VARIABLES permissions.

    An example: a pandora_monitor user with those permissions and an instance mysql-prod-01:3306. The permissions are the ones listed on the plugin page in the integration documentation; it is advisable to grant it only what its monitoring policy requires.

  2. Filling in and running. It is saved with Complete setup and the task is forced from the list, as described in The task list.

  3. What it creates. One agent for each reachable instance, with its connection module and the engine modules that have been left enabled. Scan databases adds the per-database metrics, and with Create agent per database each database has its own agent, with the instance agent as its parent. An instance that cannot be reached creates no agent: it is counted in Targets down in the task summary.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
After the MySQL walkthrough, only the particularities change from one database to another. The table collects them; the rest of the mechanics (agent per instance, option of an agent per database, connection module) is the same.

Application What it brings Specific preparation More information Microsoft SQL Server Agent per instance and, if requested, per database; instance and database metrics; custom queries; connection and query timeouts of their own (5 seconds by default). A login with VIEW SERVER STATE, and SELECT for custom queries. ODBC mode is optional and requires the ODBC 17 driver and unixODBC on the machine that runs the plugin. Integration documentation and Marketplace PostgreSQL Agent per target and, with Scan databases, per database; availability, activity, connections, buffer cache, storage, transactions and table statistics. It uses a Custom credential from the Credential manager instead of user and password in the task. The role must be able to connect to the monitored databases and read their statistics views. Integration documentation and Marketplace MongoDB Agent per target; engine and per-database metrics; a step of its own for custom queries. The targets are connection URIs, with the user inside them (port 27017 by default). Roles read or dbAdmin on the databases and clusterMonitor or clusterAdmin for server statistics. Integration documentation and Marketplace Oracle A .disco package present in the Applications catalog. There is no plugin page in the integration documentation: its fields and its permissions are not described here. Integration documentation and Marketplace

With three of them (MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server and MongoDB) the user and the password, or the URI that carries them, are written in the task itself; with PostgreSQL the identifier of a credential is enough. If the password of a monitoring user changes often, the difference matters.

docs.title: Web servers: Apache and Nginx
docs.text:
Web servers are not queried over SQL but over HTTP: each one publishes a status endpoint that the plugin reads and turns into modules. Before creating the task, that endpoint has to be active on the monitored server.

Application Requirement on the server What it creates More information Apache mod_status enabled, with the server-status?auto response machine-readable and restricted to the IP of the system that runs the plugin. Basic authentication is only needed if the endpoint requires it. One agent per distinct network location among the URLs, with an availability module ("Apache Connection") and one module per key/value line of the response. Integration documentation and Marketplace NGINX ngx_http_stub_status_module module compiled and stub_status exposed; basic authentication optional. One agent per URL, with modules for active, accepted and handled connections, requests, and connections in reading, writing and waiting, in addition to availability. Integration documentation and Marketplace

One warning about Apache: server-status counts things on the server that nobody has any reason to read. It must be opened only to the IP of whoever monitors, not to everyone. The Apache plugin, moreover, delivers the data as XML files over Tentacle (the target and the port are fields of the task), instead of answering only with the JSON that 2.3 describes; the result in the console is the same.

docs.title: What you get and how it connects to policies
docs.text:
The result is normal agents, in the group of the task, with their modules, which are updated on every run. To check the first result: force the task, open its summary from the task list ("View summary") and look for the created agents. If something does not appear, the summary usually explains it ("Done" does not guarantee that the plugin has found anything): see When it fails and the troubleshooting table on the plugin page in the integration documentation.

To apply alerts and other configurations homogeneously to the created agents, the place is Monitoring policies.

docs.title: References and links
docs.text:
• Marketplace: https://marketplace.pandorafms.com/. Each .disco package in the catalog has its entry there, with the short name from the table in the introduction.
  • Integration documentation: one page per plugin (MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Apache and NGINX).
  • Reusable credentials: Credential manager.
  • Creating your own .disco packages: Creating discovery plugins.

docs.title: Container and orchestrator monitoring
docs.text:
Docker is monitored through a plugin executed by an EndPoint. Kubernetes and OpenShift are queried by Discovery through the cluster API. The collection method determines where to configure the integration and where to look for its results in the Pandora FMS web console.

Target Collection and results Integration guide Docker The EndPoint executes the plugin and adds modules to its existing agent. Docker Kubernetes Discovery queries the API and generates agents and modules according to the task. Kubernetes OpenShift Discovery queries the API and generates agents and modules according to the task. OpenShift

Installing a .disco package and the shared task lifecycle are covered in How a .disco package task works. The guides in the table provide each integration's specific requirements, permissions, setup, parameters, modules, limitations and troubleshooting.

Before configuration, check target access from the machine that will collect the data and authorize only the necessary queries. Protect credentials. Review the connection and security conditions in the relevant guide: HTTPS alone does not establish that server identity is verified or requests are authenticated.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
The Docker plugin collects container usage and performance statistics, such as CPU, memory, network and block I/O. It is a conventional EndPoint plugin, not a Discovery task. Its modules are included in the EndPoint's existing agent. It does not create a separate agent per container.

Follow the Docker guide to prepare the plugin and integrate it with the EndPoint. Check daemon access under the account and environment running the EndPoint, not only from an administrator's interactive session. Then check in the web console that its agent receives data from the integration.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Discovery queries the Kubernetes API to monitor cluster infrastructure and workloads. The task generates agents and modules according to its scope and the available data, without installing an EndPoint on every node.

Prepare the access and metrics required by the integration, configure the task and check its first run. The Kubernetes guide details that preparation, resource selection, results and limitations. Shared Discovery operation is covered in 2.3. Plugin-specific fields and options belong in its guide.

docs.title: OpenShift
docs.text:
The OpenShift integration also uses Discovery and the cluster API to collect information about infrastructure and workloads. The agents and modules generated depend on the task and the information obtained.

Prepare access and configure the integration according to the OpenShift guide. Do not transfer Kubernetes wizard fields and controls to this integration. Each has its own configuration and limitations. After running the task, review its results and the data received in the web console.

docs.title: Results and first checks
docs.text:
For Docker, check the EndPoint's agent. For Kubernetes and OpenShift, look for the agents and modules generated by the task. The first check should cover both collection and data reception:

  1. Inspect execution errors and confirm that access uses the authorized identity and originates from the machine running the integration.
  2. Find the expected results and check that they receive recent data. A summary reporting generated agents or manual plugin output alone does not prove that the data has reached Pandora FMS.
  3. Compare representative values with the target. A missing module does not prove that the resource is absent, nor does a single indicator establish the health of the entire environment.

For missing information, use the integration's guide for specific troubleshooting. For task lifecycle errors, see When it fails. Perform these checks in the environment that will be monitored.

docs.title: IoT monitoring
docs.text:
A temperature sensor on a factory floor has no room for an EndPoint. Neither does a solar meter or a warehouse door reader. What almost all of them can do is publish what they measure to an MQTT broker: a messaging server that devices write to through named topics (the protocol's channels, such as factory/line-a/temperature). Pandora FMS uses exactly that. It does not talk to the sensor: it listens to the broker, collects what is published on the topics you care about, and turns it into agents and modules like those of any other host.

In practice, anything that can publish an MQTT message can be monitored, with graphs, thresholds and alerts, without installing anything on the device. This chapter explains how that chain works, how to configure it and, above all, which modules come out of which messages, with real examples.

Requirement Detail MQTT broker Reachable from the Pandora FMS server host. Devices publish to it; Pandora FMS only subscribes. Pandora FMS server Includes the IoT service (pandora_iot_server), which collects the messages. IoT .disco package Installed in the console. The task it creates turns messages into agents and modules. Tentacle The task sends the generated data through Tentacle, like any other .disco package. Permissions The IoT service settings are available to administrator users only.

Installing the .disco package and the common life cycle of its tasks are covered in 2.3 (Monitoring and automatic discovery with Discovery) and are not repeated here. What follows is specific to IoT; the integration guide, with the full reference of settings and options, is IoT Discovery.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The chain has four links. Each one fails in a different way, so it helps to keep them straight.

  1. Devices publish messages to the broker, each on its own topic.
  2. The IoT service keeps a single connection to the broker, subscribes to the configured topics and stores every message it receives in a local store on the server.
  3. The Discovery task of the IoT .disco package runs on each interval, reads the messages it has not handled yet and applies the filters you defined.
  4. For each group of messages that matches a filter, the task generates an agent with its modules and sends it to Pandora FMS through Tentacle. From there on it is a regular agent.
flowchart LR
    DEV["Devices<br/>and gateways"]
    BROKER["MQTT broker"]
    SERVICE["IoT service<br/>(Pandora FMS server)"]
    STORE[("Local message<br/>store")]
    TASK["Discovery task<br/>IoT .disco package"]
    TENTACLE["Tentacle"]
    AGENTS["Agents and modules"]

    DEV -->|"publish"| BROKER
    BROKER -->|"subscribed messages"| SERVICE
    SERVICE -->|"stores"| STORE
    STORE -->|"unhandled messages"| TASK
    TASK -->|"filters: agent + modules"| TENTACLE
    TENTACLE --> AGENTS

Three limits explain most of what follows:

  • A single connection. Adding topics does not add connections or processes: the service sends one subscription request carrying all the topic filters.
  • Quality of service 0. Subscriptions are always requested with QoS 0 (delivery at most once, no acknowledgement) and this is not configurable. If the connection drops briefly, messages published in that window are not recovered.
  • Limited retention. Messages are deleted from the store after a set period (24 hours by default), whether the task has handled them or not. A task that does not run within that period loses the messages.

docs.title: Enabling and configuring the IoT server
docs.text:
The service ships with the server but is switched off. Enable it with the Enable IOT Server switch under Setup → System settings → General setup, Features tab. Once enabled, a dedicated page appears, for administrator users only: Setup → System settings → IoT Server.

Labels in the Spanish console

Some labels on this page appear in the Spanish console with text that does not match their function. The table identifies them by their original name and by what they do.

Field What it does Default Server configuration Path of the configuration file the server generates for the service. /etc/pandora/pandora_iot_config.ini Server host Address of the MQTT broker. test.mosquitto.org Server port Broker port. 1883 Server protocol Transport: tcp, websockets or unix. tcp Server user / Server password Broker credentials, if it requires them. empty Server topic Topic or topics to subscribe to (see below). testtopic/# Enable SSL / Trust SSL certificate Connection encryption (see the warning). off / on Database location / Database name Folder and name of the local message store. /opt/pandora/pandora_iot_server/db, pandora_iot.db Data cleaning interval Minimum seconds between two cleanups of expired messages. 300 Data cleaning period Age, in seconds, after which a message is deleted. 86400 (24 hours) Log name / Log location Name and folder of the service log. pandora_iot.log, /var/log/pandora/ Log level Level of detail in the log. info Max log bytes / Log rotation count Maximum size of the active log and number of rotated files kept. 50000000, 3

The default host and topic point to a public test broker: they are good for checking that everything starts, not for production. The first thing to change is the broker.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
The Server topic field accepts two forms:

  • A single filter, such as factory/#.
  • Several filters, as a JSON array on one line: ["factory/+/temperature", "factory/+/status", "alerts/#"].

Wildcards are the MQTT ones: + replaces exactly one level (factory/+/temperature matches factory/line-a/temperature but not factory/line-a/room-1/temperature) and # replaces all remaining levels and must come last (alerts/# matches alerts, alerts/site-a and everything below). A malformed array (trailing comma, single quotes, empty members) stops the service from starting with the error Invalid topic configuration. The field accepts at most 200 characters, brackets and quotes included.
