Only messages from subscribed topics reach the store: a task filter will never see a message whose topic is not on this list. Also remember that the broker decides which filters it accepts according to its own access rules.

docs.title: Connection encryption
docs.text: To encrypt the connection, enable Enable SSL and Trust SSL certificate together. With Trust SSL certificate on, the service does not verify the broker's certificate: traffic is encrypted, but nothing checks that the broker is who it claims to be. With Enable SSL on and Trust SSL certificate off, the service does not set up encryption at all. If your environment requires validating the broker, this version does not offer it; solve it at the network level (restricted access to the broker, for example).

docs.title: When changes take effect
docs.text:
The Pandora FMS server writes the service configuration file and starts the service every time it starts. For that reason, changes made on the IoT Server page do not apply until pandora_server is restarted. After the restart, check the service from the system:

systemctl status pandora_iot_server

The service log (/var/log/pandora/pandora_iot.log by default) should show a line like this for each topic:

MQTT broker accepted subscription to factory/+/temperature with QoS 0

If the broker rejects a filter, the log says so and gives the reason.

docs.title: The Discovery task of the IoT package
docs.text:
The service only collects. The task of the IoT .disco package decides which agents and modules are born, and it is created and managed like any other (see How a .disco package task works). Besides the common first step, its wizard has two steps of its own:

Step Field What it does Iot base DB path Full path of the message store. Defaults to /opt/pandora/pandora_iot_server/db/pandora_iot.db; it must match the service's Database location and Database name. Iot base Time window No effect in this version: leave it empty. Iot base Tentacle IP / Tentacle port Destination of the generated data. Default 127.0.0.1 and 41121. Iot base Tentacle extra options Optional. Not applied to the transfer in this version. Iot detailed Max threads Threads used to process messages (default 1). Iot detailed Filter messages modules Where the filters are written. This is the heart of the package and has its own section below.

Two conditions affect the outcome:

  • The task must be able to read the store. The store is a local file on the server where the IoT service runs, so the task has to run on that same host. If DB path does not match or the file does not exist, the task reports that it cannot find the file and generates nothing.
  • The agents' group comes from the task. Agents are created in the group set in the task's first step, and their interval is the task's interval.

On each run, the task reads the messages it has not handled yet, passes them through the filters, generates the agents and marks the messages as handled: a message is processed only once. The run summary shows two counters, Total agents and Total messages (the agents generated and the modules created).

docs.title: Filters: from message to module
docs.text:
Each filter describes one module: which messages produce it, what value it carries and which agent it belongs to. Filters are written in the Filter messages modules field, one after another, between filter_begin and filter_end:

filter_begin
filter_module_name Temperature
filter_module_type generic_data
filter_topic line-a
filter_message "value"
filter_message_capture_json $.value
filter_module_value __json1__
filter_end
Directive Mandatory What it does filter_module_name Yes Module name. Accepts macros. filter_module_type Yes Module type: generic_data, generic_data_string, generic_proc… filter_module_value Yes Module value. Accepts macros. filter_topic No Text or regular expression that must match the topic. Without it, every topic matches. filter_topic_exact_match No 1: the text must appear as-is in the topic. 0 (default): regular expression. filter_message No Text or regular expression that must match the message content. filter_message_exact_match No Same as the previous one, for the message. filter_message_capture_regex No Regular expression with capture groups; each group feeds a __regexN__ macro. filter_message_capture_json No JSONPath expressions separated by \| (for example, $.soil.moisture); each path feeds a __jsonN__ macro.

Macros usable in filter_module_name and filter_module_value:

Macro Replaced by __topic__ The exact topic of the message. __regexN__ Capture group N of filter_message_capture_regex. __jsonN__ The result of path N of filter_message_capture_json.

Four rules change the result and are worth knowing before writing the first filter:

  1. The agent is named after the text of filter_topic. Not after the message topic: after the filter's text. All filters with the same filter_topic add modules to the same agent; filters with different texts create different agents. A short, clean filter_topic (line-a) gives a well-named agent; one with the full path gives an agent named with the full path.
  2. Modules of the same agent are told apart by the message. Since two filters with the same filter_topic go to the same agent, what separates them is filter_message: the JSON temperature on one side, the literal ONLINE on the other.
  3. One module, one value per run. If several messages in the same run produce a module with the same name in the same agent, only the first is kept. The rest are marked as handled and never reach Pandora FMS. If devices publish faster than the task runs, the task interval sets the resolution of your data.
  4. One message can feed several filters, and a message that matches no filter is marked as handled all the same.

docs.title: Examples and results
docs.text: The following examples were tested with a Mosquitto broker, the IoT service and the package's processor. The tables show what the processor generates for Pandora FMS.

docs.title: A plant with two lines and a greenhouse (JSON)
docs.text:
Devices publish these messages:

Topic Message factory/line-a/temperature {"sensor":"t1","value":21.4,"unit":"C"} factory/line-a/status ONLINE factory/line-b/temperature {"sensor":"t2","value":35.8,"unit":"C"} greenhouse/zone1 {"temp":24.5,"humidity":61,"soil":{"moisture":38}}

The subscribed topics are ["factory/+/temperature", "factory/+/status", "greenhouse/#"] and the task filters are:

filter_begin
filter_module_name Temperature
filter_module_type generic_data
filter_topic line-a
filter_message "value"
filter_message_capture_json $.value
filter_module_value __json1__
filter_end
filter_begin
filter_module_name Line status
filter_module_type generic_proc
filter_topic line-a
filter_message ^ONLINE$
filter_module_value 1
filter_end
filter_begin
filter_module_name Temperature
filter_module_type generic_data
filter_topic line-b
filter_message_capture_json $.value
filter_module_value __json1__
filter_end
filter_begin
filter_module_name Humidity __topic__
filter_module_type generic_data
filter_topic greenhouse/zone
filter_message_capture_json $.humidity
filter_module_value __json1__
filter_end
filter_begin
filter_module_name Soil state
filter_module_type generic_data_string
filter_topic greenhouse/zone
filter_message_capture_json $.soil.moisture
filter_module_value Moisture __json1__ %
filter_end

The task summary reports Total agents: 3 and Total messages: 5, and these agents appear in the console:

Agent Module Type Value line-a Temperature generic_data 21.4 line-a Line status generic_proc 1 line-b Temperature generic_data 35.8 greenhouse/zone Humidity greenhouse/zone1 generic_data 61 greenhouse/zone Soil state generic_data_string Moisture 38 %

Note three things. Line A has two modules because its two filters share filter_topic. The greenhouse/zone agent gathers every zone that matches that text, and the __topic__ macro keeps modules from different zones from overwriting each other: Humidity greenhouse/zone1, Humidity greenhouse/zone2… And the string module (Moisture 38 %) shows that the value does not have to be the bare number: it can be composed from fixed text and macros.

docs.title: Messages that are not JSON: doors and meters
docs.text:
Not every device speaks JSON. With plain-text messages, capture with regular expressions:

Topic Message sensors/door1 OPEN sensors/door2 CLOSED meters/m1 temp=24.5;hum=61 
filter_begin
filter_module_name Door __topic__
filter_module_type generic_data_string
filter_topic sensors/door
filter_message_capture_regex ^(OPEN|CLOSED)$
filter_module_value __regex1__
filter_end
filter_begin
filter_module_name Humidity
filter_module_type generic_data
filter_topic meters/
filter_message_capture_regex temp=([0-9.]+);hum=([0-9]+)
filter_module_value __regex2__
filter_end
Agent Module Value sensors/door Door sensors/door1 OPEN sensors/door Door sensors/door2 CLOSED meters/ Humidity 61

The doors end up in a single agent with one module per door, thanks to __topic__. The meter shows how __regex2__ picks up the second capture group (humidity) and leaves the temperature out; to keep the temperature too, another filter with the same filter_topic and __regex1__ is enough.

docs.title: What to do with the modules once created
docs.text: The generated modules are regular Pandora FMS modules: they show in the agent, can be graphed and used in alerts, reports and dashboards like those of any other agent. Status thresholds are defined on each module once it exists.

docs.title: Checking and troubleshooting
docs.text:
When something does not show up, walk the chain in the order the message travels, left to right.

Symptom Likely cause What to check The service does not start Invalid configuration (Invalid topic configuration), missing folder permissions or unreachable broker. systemctl status pandora_iot_server and the service log. Changes on the IoT Server page have no effect The configuration is written when the server starts. Restart pandora_server. No accepted-subscription lines in the log The broker is unreachable or rejects the credentials. Host, port, protocol, user, password and firewall. The broker rejects a filter Broker access rules or wrong wildcard syntax. The reason logged for each filter. The task reports it cannot find the database file DB path does not match the store, or the task does not run on the service host. That the path is exactly Database location + Database name. The task ends with no agents No filter matches the pending messages, or the messages expired before the run. The summary's Total agents; the subscribed topics; that the task interval is shorter than the retention period. A published value is missing Several messages produced the same module in the same run and only the first is kept. Shorten the task interval or publish less often. The agent has an unexpected name The name comes from the text of filter_topic. Adjust filter_topic (see rule 1). Values are not extracted The JSONPath does not match the message, or the regular expression lacks the expected groups. Test the path or expression against a real message; JSON paths use the $.field.subfield syntax.

The service log records messages and inserts only with Log level set to debug. At that level the log also includes the parameters loaded at startup, password included, so it should not be left on debug in production.

docs.title: API monitoring
docs.text:
A web server that answers is not the same as a service that works. ping replies, port 443 is open, the process is in the list... and the API returns a 200 whose body says "status": "degraded", or a queue with 128 unprocessed orders, or a 503 nobody has seen because the monitoring dashboard is still green. Almost everything that matters to a business is now queried over HTTP and answered in JSON, and a check that only asks "is the port open?" is often not enough.

Pandora FMS handles this with API modules: the server sends an HTTP(S) request to the address you give it, reads the response and turns it into a module. No plugin, no script, and nothing installed on the system that exposes the API. There are two questions you can ask an API, and each has its own module:

  • "What value does it return?" A number, a text or a true/false extracted from the response. This is the API retrieve module.
  • "Is it healthy?" A status, normal or critical, that comes from comparing the HTTP code and several response fields against what you expect. This is the API custom module.
Requirement Detail Network server API modules are executed by the Pandora FMS network server. If none is active, the console does not offer these types when you create a module. Connectivity The server host must be able to reach the API URL (name resolution, port and firewall included). Response JSON. If the API answers anything else, the module processes nothing. Creation Only as agent modules, policy modules and in bulk operations. They are not available as network components.

This chapter covers what is specific to API modules: the request, data extraction and condition evaluation. The fields common to all modules (interval, group, thresholds) work as in any other module; alerts are covered in 5.5, Alerts and notifications and spreading modules across many agents in 2.10, Monitoring policies.

docs.title: API module types
docs.text:
When you create an agent module, the type selector offers two new entries, next to the web and prediction modules:

Selector entry Data type What it is for API retrieve module Numeric, boolean or alphanumeric, your choice Store the value found at a specific point of the response: a queue, a latency, a version, a flag. API custom module Boolean Decide whether the API is fine: 1 if all conditions are met, 0 if not.

Internally there are four module types, because the retrieve module splits according to the data it stores:

Type Data What it stores API retrieve numeric data Numeric The number found at the path. API retrieve boolean data Boolean 1 if the value found is true; 0 in any other case. API retrieve alphanumeric data Alphanumeric The text found. If the path points to an object or a list, its content is stored as JSON text. API custom retrieve Boolean 1 or 0 depending on the conditions.

The rule for choosing fits on one line. If you want the value (to graph it, to set thresholds on it), use retrieve. If you want a verdict on the health of the API, use custom. If you need both, create two modules on the same URL: they do not interfere with each other.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The module does not go through any EndPoint. The network server runs it, just like a network or web module:

  1. When the module is due (according to its interval), the network server builds the request from the URL, method, headers and, if applicable, the body.
  2. It sends the request with the configured timeout. If it fails, it retries: three attempts by default, which you change with the Retries field of the Data tab. Responses of up to 20 MB are accepted.
  3. It checks that the response is JSON.
  4. Depending on the type, it extracts the value from a path (retrieve) or evaluates the HTTP code and the conditions (custom).
  5. It processes the result like that of any other module: the data is stored, the status is calculated with the thresholds and the alerts fire.
flowchart LR
    SRV["Network server"]
    API["API (HTTP/HTTPS)"]
    JSON{"Valid JSON<br/>response?"}
    REC["Retrieve:<br/>value at the path"]
    CUS["Custom:<br/>codes + conditions"]
    MOD["Module:<br/>data and status"]
    ERR["No data<br/>(the query failed)"]

    SRV -->|"request"| API
    API -->|"response"| JSON
    JSON -->|"yes"| REC
    JSON -->|"yes"| CUS
    JSON -->|"no"| ERR
    REC --> MOD
    CUS --> MOD

One detail worth keeping in mind: when the query fails (the API does not answer, the response is not JSON or the URL is empty), the module does not receive any data. It does not turn critical for that reason: it simply gets no new value and, if the failure persists, ends up in unknown status when its interval expires. That is why the custom module has its own error codes (see below): they are the way to turn a specific API failure into a critical.

docs.title: Configuring the request
docs.text:
Both modules share the request block, in the Basic tab of the module creation or edit form (the other tabs, common to all modules, are in 2.20):

Field What it does Default Timeout Seconds to wait for the response before considering it failed. It is the one in this tab: the Timeout field of the Data tab plays no part in these modules. 10 URL Full address of the endpoint, including the scheme (http:// or https://). Required: without a URL the module does not run. empty Method GET, POST, PUT or DELETE. GET Ignore certificate When enabled, the API certificate is not validated. Use it only for tests or for internal certificates you cannot fix: it turns off the check that you are talking to who you think you are. disabled Edit Headers HTTP request headers, as key-value pairs. Content-Type: application/json Edit body Request content. Makes sense with POST, PUT and DELETE. {}

Three rules explain most of the modules that "do not do what they should":

  • The body is only sent if the method is not GET and the Content-Type header is exactly application/json. If you change that header, the body is silently ignored.
  • Authentication goes in the headers. There are no user and password fields: a token-based API is queried with a header such as Authorization: Bearer <token>, and an API key is sent in whichever header that API requires. Keep in mind that the header is part of the module configuration, so anyone who can view or edit the module can see the token.
  • Headers arrive as configured on GET. The server also identifies itself with the user agent Pandora-API-Client/1.0, in case the API filters on it.
  • The server queries, not the console. The request leaves the Pandora FMS server host. The API being reachable from your browser does not prove it is reachable from the server.

Content-Type on POST and PUT

In tests with version 8.0NG.805, the target API received POST and PUT requests with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded even though the module header was application/json; the body did arrive intact. If your API requires exactly application/json, check it with a real request before trusting the module.

docs.title: Extracting a value from the response
docs.text:
The retrieve module stores what it finds at the JSON path query (JSON path Query). The path is written as field names separated by dots, and list elements are numbered from zero:

API response Path Value {"queue": {"name": "orders", "pending": 128}} queue.pending 128 {"queue": {"name": "orders", "pending": 128}} queue.name orders {"items": [{"id": 7}, {"id": 9}]} items.1.id 9

This is not full JSONPath

The console talks about "JSONPath" in its messages, but the actual syntax is the dot syntax in the table. A path such as $.queue.pending, queue['pending'] or items[?(@.id==9)] finds nothing. Field names that contain a dot cannot be used either.

Retrieve modules have their warning and critical thresholds in the same Basic tab, like any module with data; how they work is in 2.20.

You do not need to type the path by hand. With the URL already filled in, the magnifier button next to JSON path Query makes a preliminary request and shows the response as a tree; click a value and confirm, and the path is filled in for you. That button makes the request from the console, not from the server, so it may work even if the server cannot reach the API (and the other way round). The Test button does the same and shows the result of the path before you save.

The module type decides what is done with the value:

Type Value found Module data Numeric 128 128 Alphanumeric "2.4.1" 2.4.1 Alphanumeric an object, such as queue in the first table Its content as JSON text; field order may change ({"pending":128,"name":"orders","consumers":4}) Boolean true 1 Boolean "true" (text) 1 Boolean false, "ok", 1 or anything else 0

If the path is empty, the response is not JSON or the path does not exist in the response, the module stores nothing in that run.

docs.title: Checking the status of an API
docs.text:
The custom module does not extract a value: it gives a verdict. Its data is 1 (normal) when everything is fine and 0 (critical) when something does not add up. It has no thresholds of its own: the status is decided by the error codes and the conditions.

Evaluation follows a fixed order:

  1. Error codes. The Error Codes field is a comma-separated list of HTTP codes. The default for a new module is 500, 404, 403. If the response carries one of them, the module becomes 0 and nothing else is evaluated.

    Write the codes without spaces

    In tests with version 8.0NG.805, with spaces after the commas (500, 503, 404, 403, which is also the format of the default value) only the first code is recognized: a 503 or a 404 does not turn the module into 0. Without spaces (500,503,404,403) they all work. Until this is fixed, write the list without spaces.

    1. Conditions. If the code is not in the list, each condition is evaluated. All of them must be met for the module to be 1; if one fails, it is 0. A module without conditions is 1 as long as the code is not in the list.

Each condition has four parts:

Part What it is JSON path Query The path of the field to evaluate, with the same dot syntax as the previous section. Filled in with the magnifier. Type The expected data type: Null, String, Number or Boolean. Condition The comparison operator (depends on the type; next table). Value The value to compare against. Not used by operators that do not need one.

The available operators depend on the type you choose:

Type Operators Met if Boolean Is true / Is false The field is true / false. They do not use Value. Null Equals / Not equals The field is / is not null. Number Equals / Not equals The number is equal to / different from the expected one. Number Greater than / Less than It is greater / smaller than the expected one. String Equals / Not equals The text is equal to / different from the expected one. String Contains / Not contains The text contains / does not contain the expected one. String Is empty / Is not empty The field is empty / not empty. They do not use Value. String Regex match The value matches the regular expression, case-insensitive.

Some rules that change the result:

  • A path that does not exist counts as an unmet condition. If the API changes format and the field disappears, the module becomes 0, which is exactly what you want.
  • The type must match the data. With type Number, a non-numeric field fails the condition.
  • Error codes are evaluated on a JSON response. If the API answers an error with a body that is not JSON (an HTML error page, for example) or with no body, the query is considered failed and the module is left without data instead of becoming 0 (checked with a 500 and an HTML body). If you want to catch that case, also watch for the module staying in unknown status.

The console includes a Test button below the conditions. It sends the request and shows which conditions are met, how many were evaluated (Total conditions), how many pass (Passed) and how many do not (Failed).

Always use it before saving: it is much cheaper than finding out about a badly written condition at three in the morning.

docs.title: Examples and results
docs.text:
The three examples use a fictional API at api.example.com. They were reproduced on an 8.0NG.805 console against a local test API, and the results are what the module returned.

Pending orders queue (numeric retrieve)

You want to graph how many orders are waiting in the queue and alert if it goes above 500.

Configuration: API retrieve module, numeric data; URL https://api.example.com/v1/queues/orders; method GET; path queue.pending; critical threshold from 500.

API response:

{"queue": {"name": "orders", "pending": 128, "consumers": 4}}

Result: the module is 128 and is graphed like any numeric module. When the API returns "pending": 612, the threshold turns it critical and the associated alerts fire.

Deployed version (alphanumeric retrieve)

You want to know which version runs in production, to see in the history when it changed.

Configuration: alphanumeric data; URL https://api.example.com/v1/info; path build.version.

Response: {"build": {"version": "2.4.1", "commit": "9f3c2ab"}}

Result: the module is 2.4.1. Each deployment shows up as a value change.

API health with an authentication header (custom)

You want a single module that turns the API critical if it is not healthy, if the database is slow or if it answers with an error.

Configuration: API custom module; URL https://api.example.com/v1/health; method GET; headers Content-Type: application/json and Authorization: Bearer <token>; error codes 500,503,404,403 (no spaces); two conditions:

JSON path Query Type Condition Value status String Equals ok checks.database.latency_ms Number Less than 500

Result depending on what the API answers:

Response Module Why 200 with {"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": {"latency_ms": 120}}} 1 Code not in the list and both conditions are met. 200 with {"status": "degraded", "checks": {"database": {"latency_ms": 120}}} 0 The first condition fails. 200 with {"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": {"latency_ms": 900}}} 0 The second condition fails: 900 is not less than 500. 200 with {"status": "ok"} 0 checks.database.latency_ms does not exist. 503 with {"error": "unavailable"} 0 Code in the error list (and status is missing as well). 200 with an HTML page no data The response is not JSON.

docs.title: Use with policies and bulk operations
docs.text:
API modules can be created in the same ways as the rest of network modules:

  • On an agent, from its modules form.
  • In a policy, to spread the same module across many agents (see 2.10, Monitoring policies). This is the typical case for an API with the same contract in several environments.
  • With bulk operations, to change a field (a timeout, a header) in many modules at once (see 2.11, Bulk operations).

Secrets in headers

A policy that carries a token in a header distributes it to every module it generates. If the token expires or rotates, change it in the policy (or with a bulk operation), not agent by agent.

docs.title: Checking and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause Check The console does not offer the API types when creating a module. No active network server, or a network component is being created. Check the server list for a running network server; create the module on an agent. The module has no new data. The API does not answer, the response is not JSON or the URL is empty. Repeat the request from the server host (curl -i <url>) with the same headers and check that the response is JSON. The retrieve module stores nothing. The path does not exist in the response or is badly written (for example, with $. in front). Use the magnifier to pick the path on the real response. The boolean module is always 0. The value at the path is not true. A 1 or an "ok" gives 0. Switch to a numeric module or to a custom module with conditions. A code in the error list (for example 503 or 404) does not turn the module into 0. The list is written with spaces after the commas and only the first code is recognized. Rewrite the list without spaces: 500,503,404,403. The custom module is 0 and the API answers fine. A condition is not met: nonexistent path, type mismatch or wrong operator. Press Test: it shows how many conditions fail. The custom module is 1 even though the API is broken (for example, it answers 401). The code is not in the error list and no condition detects it: without conditions, anything not in the list gives 1. Add the code to Error Codes (401 if authentication fails) and define at least one condition on the body. The body does not reach the API. Method GET, or the Content-Type header is not exactly application/json. Check the method and the header. Certificate error (HTTPS). Expired or self-signed certificate, or a name mismatch. Fix it on the API; as a last resort only, enable Ignore certificate. The magnifier works, but the module does not. The console reaches the API and the server does not (or the other way round). Test the request from each host separately.

To see what the server does with each request, check its log (/var/log/pandora/pandora_server.log). Query failures (empty URL, failed request) appear with the module identifier; the detail of successful runs and of non-JSON responses is only visible by raising the server verbosity.

docs.title: Log collection and monitoring
docs.text:
Logs are that file nobody looks at until something catches fire at three in the morning and it is time to work out what happened. Pandora FMS collects them from every origin you name: the Windows event log, text files from any Unix flavour, the syslog of any machine. It leaves them in a single console, ordered by the moment they arrived. This chapter explains how that collection is enabled, how logs are requested from each EndPoint and what can be done with them afterwards.

Pandora FMS does not store logs in its monitoring database. It keeps them in OpenSearch, a search engine built for text, and that is why the first requirement, before touching anything in the console, is to have that engine available and reachable. The rest of the chapter assumes it already is; the installation and configuration of the engine have a technical appendix of their own.

What this is not

Unstructured log monitoring is not a SIEM. Pandora FMS keeps the text as it comes, without analysing it, and puts it at your disposal so that you can search it. If what you want is to correlate events and launch rules, that is Pandora SIEM, which builds on these same data.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The chain has four links and it is worth keeping them clear, because each one can fail on its own.

  1. The EndPoint reads the event log or the text file and puts the raw logs, in RAW format, inside the XML report it already sends as usual. No separate channel is needed.
  2. The Pandora FMS Data Server receives that XML, which carries monitoring and logs at the same time. When it processes it, it separates one from the other.
  3. The references of the EndPoint that has reported and of the log origin are stored in the main database. The log text is not: the text goes to OpenSearch.
  4. OpenSearch indexes it. Pandora FMS creates a new index every day for each instance, with a name such as pandorafms-<identifier>-<year.month.day>, plus an auxiliary index of origins that ends in -sources.

Logs travel over the network encoded, to prevent a strange format from breaking the transport. If you also want them to travel encrypted, encrypted Tentacle is used; nothing special has to be done for logs, it is the same secure transport that applies to the rest of the XML.

A server maintenance task deletes the old information after the interval you set (30 days by default). It is not a blunt deletion: the server removes the documents by date and, when an index is left empty, it removes that too.

The Syslog Server is the shortcut. Instead of waiting for an EndPoint to read a file and send it, this component reads the syslog of the machine where the server lives and processes it on the spot. For high volumes of syslog it is quite a bit faster, and it allows spreading the load: several EndPoints on one side and several remote syslog servers on the other.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Requirement Detail OpenSearch Installed, started and reachable from the Pandora FMS server. Without it there is nowhere to store the logs. Log collector Enabled in the web console (next section). If it is disabled, modules of type log are discarded without further ado. rsyslog Only if you are going to use the Syslog Server; it is installed on the server and, if needed, on the clients that send. Ports The one of the search engine (9200 by default) for the collector, and 514 (TCP and UDP) for syslog collection.

docs.title: Log collector configuration
docs.text:
Menu Management → Settings → System Settings → Log collector. It is enabled with Activate Log Collector and confirmed with Update. Until you enable it, that screen only shows the switch.

Once activated, the OpenSearch options appear, which are the ones that connect the console with the engine:

Option What it is for OpenSearch IP Address or name of the OpenSearch server. Use https Enable it if the engine listens over HTTPS. OpenSearch Port TCP port; 9200 by default. Number of logs viewed How many records the log viewer shows; 50 by default. Days to purge old information Days before deleting what has been collected; 30 by default. Basic authentication User (User) and password (Password) if the engine asks for them. Having them set is strongly recommended.

The screen itself tells you whether the connection works: OpenSearch is running. when everything lines up, Unauthorized when the credentials are not correct and There is no OpenSearch defined. Empty ip or port. when the address or the port is missing. That indicator is the fastest way to know whether the problem is configuration or network.

Index configuration: touch it only if you know what you are doing

The Index configuration block changes how OpenSearch builds the index. A wrong configuration can destabilise the system, so do not move it out of curiosity. On top of that, template changes apply from the following index on: they do not rewrite what is already indexed.

The options in the Index configuration block are the following:

  • Indexing size: maximum length, in characters, that OpenSearch indexes from each line as a full value (keyword). Lines that exceed it are still stored and can be searched by words, but they are left out of regular expression searches (REGEX mode). 2000 by default.
  • Number of shards: primary shards of the index; 1 by default. It is only set when the index is created: it cannot be changed on an index that is already closed.
  • Number of replicas: replicas of each shard; 0 by default. Setting 0 saves disk, but a restart of the node leaves the information temporarily unavailable and a corruption becomes permanent loss.
  • Auto expand replicas: adjusts the replicas only according to the number of nodes, with a range such as 0-1 or all as a cap. If the allocation rules prevent placing all the replicas, the cluster can be left in YELLOW state.

docs.title: Collecting logs with EndPoints
docs.text: The real collection is done by the EndPoints, both on Windows and on Unix (Linux, macOS, Solaris, HPUX, AIX, BSD…). To register the modules from the Module log collection wizard the collector has to be configured already, and if you are going to add modules of type Windows event channel, the EndPoint has to be a Windows one. The rest of the modules and their general tokens are in Monitoring with EndPoints and in the full EndPoint configuration reference.

docs.title: Plain text logs
docs.text:
To watch a text file, a module of type log is used with the module_regexp token, which points to the path of the file. An example module on Linux:

module_begin
module_name Syslog
module_description Collection of the system messages file
module_type log
module_regexp /var/log/messages
module_pattern .*
module_pattern_exclude DEBUG
module_end

On Windows the syntax is the same, only the path changes:

module_begin
module_name Apache_log
module_description Collection of the Apache log
module_type log
module_regexp C:\server\logs\apache.log
module_source_type apache
module_pattern .*
module_end

module_pattern filters the lines you are interested in and module_pattern_exclude excludes the ones you are not. Other examples of our own:

module_begin
module_name apache_access
module_type log
module_regexp /var/log/httpd/access_log
module_pattern .*
module_pattern_exclude \s200\s|\s301\s
module_source_type web-log
module_end

module_begin
module_name Audit denied
module_type log
module_regexp /var/log/audit/audit.log
module_pattern denied
module_end

module_begin
module_name Secure
module_type log
module_regexp /var/log/secure
module_pattern Failed|failure|invalid|denied|accepted|root
module_end

module_type log does not store in the database

A module with module_type log is not stored as a normal module: it is sent to the log collector. If the collector is disabled, the information is discarded. It is the number one cause of "I have put the module in and I see nothing".

Log collection on Linux used to be done with plugins. Since version 781 this is the recommended method; the plugins were left as legacy.

docs.title: MS Windows events with module_logchannel
docs.text:
On Windows, besides files, the event log can be read. For that there is module_logchannel, which displaces the old module_logevent. The latter still works for compatibility, but it is not supported since LTS version 2025 and it only makes sense on old Microsoft systems (Windows 7, Windows 2003 or earlier). On a modern Windows, module_logchannel.

The general format is this one:

module_begin
module_name MyEvent
module_type log
module_logchannel
module_source <logName>
module_eventtype <event level (optional)>
module_eventcode <event id (optional)>
module_application <origin (optional)>
module_pattern <substring to search for (optional)>
module_source_type <log type for the SIEM (optional)>
module_end

There are two warnings worth reading before fighting with the filters. The first: only events later than the last EndPoint run are taken into account. On the first run not everything that already existed in the log is collected; sending starts from that point on. The second: parameter names are case-sensitive, so copy them exactly as they are.

docs.title: module_source
docs.text:
It is the source that originates the event: the old Windows NT classification (System, Application, Security…). Do not confuse it with module_application, which identifies the application. You can use one or the other, but one of the two is needed.

Even if the event viewer shows it to you in your language, here they are written in English: System, Application, Security. Long names are copied exactly as they are, without translating:

Microsoft-Windows-DeviceManagement-Enterprise-Diagnostics-Provider/Administration

docs.title: module_source_type
docs.text:
It is the type of log that the SIEM decoders and rules consume. If you omit it, syslog is used by default. The types the tool usually handles are syslog, ids, web-log, squid, host-information and ossec.

Not all types are active from the factory

The decoder engine does not bring all those types ready to use. In the default installation ossec (Windows events), web-log, ids, firewall and syslog are active; squid and windows come in the folder of disabled decoders, and host-information does not exist as such. Before choosing a type, check which decoders you have active in the SIEM chapter.

For the SIEM, Windows events are processed with ossec. This example collects all the security events:

module_begin
module_logchannel
module_name Security_Events
module_type log
module_source Security
module_source_type ossec
module_end

docs.title: module_eventtype
docs.text:
Optional filter by event level. The values are those of the event viewer:

Code Event type 0 Success audit 1 Critical 2 Error 3 Warning 4 Information

To keep only the security warnings:

module_begin
module_logchannel
module_name Security_Events_Warning
module_type log
module_source Security
module_eventtype 3
module_source_type ossec
module_end

docs.title: module_eventcode
docs.text:
Optional filter by event identifier, the eventID you see in the viewer. It is the most precise filter of all. This example takes only the events with identifier 4798:

module_begin
module_logchannel
module_name Security_Events_4798
module_type log
module_source Security
module_eventcode 4798
module_source_type ossec
module_end

docs.title: module_application
docs.text:
Origin of the event, optional. To get the exact name of the provider, select an event in the Windows viewer, open Properties and copy the Full name field. If the name has spaces in it, do not put it in quotes. For example:

module_begin
module_name Pandora_Events_Windows
module_type log
module_logchannel
module_application Pandora FMS
module_source Application
module_end

As a reference, the providers that appear most are the operating system's own (Microsoft-Windows-Winlogon, Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing, Microsoft-Windows-WindowsUpdateClient, Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler…), those of applications and services (MSSQLSERVER, Windows Defender, Windows Firewall, VSS…), the useful ones for advanced diagnosis (Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-General, Microsoft-Windows-DistributedCOM, Microsoft-Windows-Ntfs…) and third-party ones (VMware Tools, Oracle Database, Symantec Endpoint Protection, TeamViewer, Apache Service…). Each application uses its own and there are hundreds of them.

docs.title: Windows events and Sysmon
docs.text:
Sysmon (System Monitor) is a free utility from Microsoft, inside the Sysinternals package, that records in detail activities that the normal event viewer lets through: process creation and execution, incoming and outgoing network connections, changes in the Windows registry, DLL loading, file access, code injection into legitimate processes. It is common material in intrusion attempts and lateral movement, and that is why it matters so much in cybersecurity.

It works by installing a driver in kernel mode that keeps writing to the Event Viewer. Pandora FMS collects it as one more channel of the Windows EndPoint and sends it to the server. The combination Sysmon + Pandora FMS + Pandora SIEM gives visibility far above that of the traditional log: early detection of advanced attacks, automatic alerts on the events you define and a correlatable history for forensics or auditing.

Sysmon comes in the Sysinternals Suite package and its configuration file is long: monitoring "everything" punishes the performance of the machine and of the system that receives the data. For Sysmon events this module has to be used, with the exact name and type:

module_begin
module_name WinEvtLog
module_type log
module_logchannel
module_source Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational
module_source_type windows
module_end

Here module_source_type windows replaces ossec, and the name WinEvtLog is the one the Pandora SIEM rules expect.

Sysmon does not come ready from the factory

The Sysmon channel has to be enabled and its decoders and rules fine-tuned; in a freshly installed system, the decoders and rules of windows/sysmon are disabled and the active Windows channel is the ossec one. Do not take for granted that adding the module is enough to see the events processed by the SIEM: check decoders and rules in Pandora SIEM.

docs.title: Pandora FMS Syslog Server
docs.text:
The Syslog Server allows Pandora FMS to analyse the syslog of the machine where the server resides and store it in OpenSearch. Its advantage is that it unifies origins without depending on every machine having an EndPoint: any machine that knows how to export syslog can send its messages to it. And for convenience: every host from which logs arrive generates its agent automatically if it did not exist.

The installation of rsyslog is for both the server and the clients:

dnf install rsyslog

On the server, edit /etc/rsyslog.conf and enable listening over TCP and UDP:

# Syslog reception over UDP
module(load="imudp")
input(type="imudp" port="514")

# Syslog reception over TCP
module(load="imtcp")
input(type="imtcp" port="514")

Restart the service and check that port 514 is listening:

systemctl restart rsyslog
netstat -ltnp

On the client, in its /etc/rsyslog.conf, enable forwarding to the server (replace remote-host with the real address):

action(type="omfwd" Target="remote-host" Port="514" Protocol="tcp")

The 8 KB limit and phantom origins

By default, rsyslog cuts messages at 8 KB. A longer log is split into several entries and the following ones lose the host name, which creates new origins, and agents, that do not exist. To avoid it, raise the maximum size:

$MaxMessageSize 512k

And, if you can, create the agents with alias as name equal to the hostname of the client: that way they are not duplicated.

To enable the feature on the Pandora FMS server, edit pandora_server.conf:

# Enable (1) or disable (0) the Pandora FMS Syslog Server
syslogserver 1

# Absolute path of the input file that the Syslog Server reads
syslog_file /var/log/messages

# Number of threads of the Syslog Server
syslog_threads 2

# Maximum number of lines queued by the Syslog Server
syslog_max 65535

And, of course, the device or the client has to be told to send its logs to the server. Without that, the server listens to nothing.

docs.title: Filters at the Pandora FMS server level
docs.text:
The server can sift what comes in with two tokens of pandora_server.conf. syslog_whitelist admits only what matches the regular expression and discards the rest. syslog_blacklist discards what matches and lets the rest in. Both come disabled.

The white list is applied first, which reduces the work of the black one, and the black one at the end. The expression is case-sensitive: windows is not Windows. And there are two traps:

  • If you enable syslog_whitelist without an expression, nothing gets in. With the .* expression of the example everything does.
  • If you enable syslog_blacklist without an expression, nothing is blocked.

docs.title: OpenSearch interface: the Log Viewer
docs.text:
With the collector running and data inside, everything is looked at from Operation → Logs → Log viewer. The screen shows the occurrences per unit of time and allows filtering by date, group, agent, origin and keyword.

The Search field is the most useful part. It combines with the search mode (Search mode), which has four options:

  • Exact match: the log contains the exact string.
  • All words: it contains all the words, in any order. It is the default mode.
  • Any word: it contains some of the words, in any order.
  • REGEX: it treats the text as a regular expression.

If you tick the option to see the context, the viewer also shows you the neighbouring lines of the result, which often explain more than the line itself.

With the Search field empty there is no filtering by content: the viewer lists every entry in the period, with the date, agent and origin filters you have set. Write a term (the name of the agent, a word from the message) only to narrow the results.

docs.title: Advanced display and search
docs.text:
In the Advanced options tab the view can be changed and the logs turned into charts. The Display mode decides whether text entries or a chart are shown. For the chart a capture model has to be chosen (Use capture model): a set of regular expressions and identifiers that extract values from each line.

The default model is Apache log model, which understands the access_log of Apache in standard format and draws response times grouped by page and response code. A few more models come from the factory and you can create your own with the edit and create buttons.

docs.title: Frequent filters
docs.text:
If you repeat the same combination of filters, save it: Save filter, you give it a name and Save. Later you bring it back with Load filter, choosing it from the list. A saved filter can be overwritten with the current changes.

In Operation → Logs → Filters those filters are managed: edit them, delete them one by one or in bulk, and create new ones.

docs.title: Saved filters as pinned elements
docs.text: The pinning system of Pandora FMS allows leaving the Log viewer at hand in the menu, with the filters already set. It is done with the drawing pin icon next to the title of the section. When the filter is loaded again, the pin appears disabled, and if you click it the pinning is removed. Pinned elements are independent of frequent filters; they do not get in each other's way.

docs.title: Log source in the agent view
docs.text:
Every agent that sends logs says so on its own page. In the agent view a Logs box appears with one row per origin, where you see the date of the last update and a Review button (the magnifying glass) that opens the Log Viewer already filtered by that agent and that origin. It is the most convenient way to jump from "this agent stopped sending logs" to "here are its last messages".

By default, both the box and the viewer work with the last 24 hours; it is changed when needed.

docs.title: Monitoring the log engine itself
docs.text:
And what if the one that goes quiet is the engine itself? When the collector is enabled, the Pandora FMS server watches itself: it generates a battery of modules on OpenSearch and adds them to its self-monitoring agent (pandora.internals by default). They appear like any other module, in Resources → Manage agents, inside that agent.

There are fourteen of them, on top of the usual internal modules of the server:

Module What it measures Values Log server connection Connection with the engine 1 connected; 0 not connected Total sources Distinct origins with logs Whole number (0 or more) Total documents Stored documents (lines) Whole number (0 or more) Opensearch nodes online Nodes that answer in the cluster Whole number (0 or more) Opensearch CPU % Cluster CPU 0–100 % Opensearch available memory Free memory of the system 0–100 % Opensearch JVM heap usage Usage of the JVM heap 0–100 % Opensearch Disk usage Used disk 0–100 % Opensearch Total shards Occupancy of the shard capacity per node 0–100 % (it can go over 100 if there are more shards than capacity) Opensearch Index Health Health of the most recent index green, yellow or red Opensearch Index Status Status of the most recent index open or close Opensearch daily index The most recent index is today's 0 yes; 1 no Opensearch index deletion Purge of old indexes 0 normally; 1 it is not being purged Longest data archived Date of the oldest data Date YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS

With this, what really hurts is detected: that the engine stopped ingesting logs. To find out without looking by hand, set up an alert on any of these modules, as with any other (Alerts and notifications).

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: The viewer follows the usual permissions on agents. To open it, agent read permission (AR) is needed. Without it, the screen is not shown. Searches also respect the groups on which the user has read permission, just like the rest of the web console.

docs.title: Credential manager
docs.text: Any task that has to connect to something with a username and password (a cloud resource, a network device, a Windows machine) ends up asking for those credentials in some form. Typing them every time is the most effective way to end up with the same password copied in twenty places and forgotten in nineteen. The credential manager avoids that spread: credentials are stored once in the Web console, under an identifier, and from there whoever needs them uses them.

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text:
The manager centralises the username and the password (and, depending on the credential type, some additional field) so that they are not repeated in every Discovery wizard, every NCM task or every Deployment Center deployment. Those tasks do not store the values, but the identifier of the credential, and they retrieve it when they run: when the password changes, it is updated once in the manager and all of them use the new one on their next run. Modules and policies work in a different way, as explained in Where they are used.

In the Web console it is in Setup → Credential store.

docs.title: Access and permissions
docs.text: Entering the credential manager requires holding the PM and UM permissions at the same time; with only one of the two, the Web console denies access and that denial is audited. Scope also depends on the group: each credential belongs to one, and if that group has propagation to child groups enabled, the visibility filter includes them. The All group is a separate case: its credentials are available to any user, with no need to belong to it, but creating or editing a credential in the All group additionally requires the administrator permission of that group ("ALL group manager"). A console administrator sees and filters by any group without any of these restrictions.

docs.title: Creating, editing and deleting credentials
docs.text: A credential identifier only accepts valid ASCII characters, and any space becomes a hyphen when saving. Both the identifier and the credential type are fixed at the moment of creation: when editing it later, the Web console shows both fields but disabled, so there is no way to reuse an existing credential for another type or to rename it; a new one has to be created. Deleting a credential repeats the same visibility check as accessing it: if the user has no permission over that credential by group or by ACL, the deletion is rejected even if they know its identifier.

docs.title: Credential types
docs.text:
The form changes its fields depending on the credential type chosen:

Type Form fields Custom Account ID, password AWS Access key ID, secret access key Azure Account ID, application secret, tenant or domain name, subscription ID Google Full service account JSON (pasted whole) SAP Account ID, password WMI Username, password, namespace SNMP Version; community (v1/v2); in v3 also: security level, user, authentication method and password, privacy method and password

Google is a special case: the form does not ask for a username or a password, but for the whole JSON of the service account to be pasted. On saving, the Web console extracts the service email and the key identifier from that JSON, only to show them in the listing; when the credential is used, the full JSON is reused, not those two loose values.

docs.title: Where they are used
docs.text:
The credential manager has no equivalent through the API or the command line: every credential is created, edited and consumed from the Web console. The points where a stored credential is used are:

  • The Discovery wizards (Automatic monitoring and discovery with Discovery), both Host & Devices and Cloud: the task stores the identifier and retrieves the credential when it runs.
  • NCM (Network configuration management (NCM)), for access to the managed network devices.
  • The Deployment Center (Automatic agent distribution and installation), when deploying EndPoints.
  • The module editor and the SNMP or WMI modules of a monitoring policy: the credential selector only fills in the form of the module or the policy with the stored values; it is not linked live to the credential. If the credential changes later, the module does not find out, and it has to be applied again by hand.
  • The AWS reports.

docs.title: Credentials and encryption
docs.text: If the database does not have encryption enabled, the credential manager screen itself warns that whatever is stored there will be kept unencrypted, with a link to the encryption documentation. It is worth heeding that warning: a password store in the clear is, above all, a gift for anyone who gets a copy of the database. Encryption is an Enterprise feature. Enabling, changing or removing the encryption passphrase is explained in Database encryption.

docs.title: Common module configuration
docs.text:
A module is a specific measurement of an agent: "how much CPU it uses", "does port 443 answer", "how many orders are waiting in the queue". What changes from one module to another is how the data is obtained (a command on the EndPoint, a ping from the server, an SNMP query, an API request), and that is explained in the chapter of each technology. What does not change, or changes little, is everything else: how often it is measured, which values count as normal, what happens when the data does not arrive, how much is stored and how it is organized. That "everything else" is a single form, the same for almost every type, and this chapter explains it once so it is not repeated in the nineteen previous ones.

You reach it from Manage agents, with the agent's Modules button and Create module, or by editing an existing module. A policy (see 2.10, Monitoring policies) uses the same form to define modules that it then spreads across agents.

The form is split into eight tabs:

Tab What it contains Basic Name, type, warning and critical thresholds, and the fields specific to the module type (a URL, an OID, a command…). Information Description and per-state instructions. Thresholds Dynamic thresholds, unknown, quiet mode and flip-flop protection. Intervals Execution interval and cron-style scheduling. Data Timeout, retries, minimum and maximum values, historical data, unit and post process. Categorization Module group, parent, identifier, category and tags. Macros The module's custom macros. Relationships Direct or failover relationships with modules of other agents.

Not every field always appears

The form adapts to the module type. An EndPoint module has no timeout or retries, because the server does not run it; an API custom module has no thresholds, because its status comes from its conditions; and the FlipFlop timeout field only exists in asynchronous modules. If a field in this chapter is not in your form, the module type does not use it.

docs.title: Basic data
docs.text: Field What it does Name Module name, unique within its agent. It appears in views, reports and alerts, so it should be understandable without seeing the agent: "CPU usage", not "mod3". Disabled The module stops running and receiving data, but keeps its configuration and history. It is the way to switch it off without losing it. Module type The kind of data it returns: numeric, boolean (proc: 1 normal, 0 critical), alphanumeric or incremental, plus the asynchronous ones. The type decides which thresholds make sense. Type names and their EndPoint usage are in 2.1. Description, in Information Free text. It is the first thing whoever receives an alert sees, so it deserves a sentence.

docs.title: Thresholds and statuses
docs.text:
A module can be in one of four statuses: normal, warning, critical and unknown. The first three come from comparing the data with the thresholds; the last one, from the data not arriving.

The warning and critical thresholds are in the Basic tab. Each has a minimum and a maximum value, and three modes:

Mode When the status changes Normal The value is inside the range. If you set no maximum, any value above the minimum counts; in numeric modules, a maximum of 0 means infinity. Inverse interval The value is outside the range. It also works with alphanumeric modules. Percentage The new value is compared with the previous one, and the status changes if the variation, as a percentage, exceeds the increase (maximum) or decrease (minimum) given.

If a value meets the warning and the critical threshold at the same time, critical wins.

CPU with warning from 70 and critical from 90

Warning threshold with minimum 70 and maximum 95; critical threshold with minimum 90 and maximum 0 (no upper limit). The two ranges overlap between 90 and 95.

Value received Status Why 40 Normal Outside both ranges. 75 Warning Inside the warning range. 92 Critical Meets both and critical prevails. 99 Critical Above the critical minimum, no upper limit.

Below the warning threshold, Change to critical status after N intervals in warning status promotes to critical a module that has been in warning for N runs in a row. With 2, the sequence warning → warning → warning goes to critical. If a module stays "in warning" forever because nobody looks at it, this field keeps it from becoming decoration.

docs.title: When the data does not arrive: unknown
docs.text:
If a module goes more than two intervals without receiving data, it enters unknown status. Three settings in the Thresholds tab govern that behavior:

Field What it does Ignore unknown The module never goes to unknown: it keeps its last known status. Useful for data that arrives sporadically; dangerous if you enable it to "clean" a red screen, because it stops telling you the module is dead. Discard unknown events The module does go to unknown, but does not generate the event. Quiet The module keeps receiving and storing data, but generates no events and fires no alerts. Used while testing a new module or during an intervention.

docs.title: Dynamic thresholds
docs.text:
Instead of setting the values by hand, the module can calculate its thresholds from its own history. It is enabled by choosing a Dynamic threshold interval in the Thresholds tab: the system takes the data of that period, calculates the mean and the standard deviation and sets the thresholds from them.

Field What it does Dynamic upper limit / Dynamic lower limit Adjust the calculated limit, as a percentage. If the mean is around 60 and the upper critical threshold is 80, a dynamic upper limit of 10 raises it to 88. Dynamic two tailed Adds a lower threshold to the upper one, so both very high and very low values change the status.

docs.title: Flip-flop protection
docs.text:
A value that oscillates between good and bad on every cycle is an interpretation problem: the module changes color constantly and the alerts never stop. The FF threshold requires the new status to repeat several times in a row before the change is accepted. With 0 (the default) the module changes status as soon as it receives an out-of-range value; with 2, two more consecutive critical values are needed before it goes critical.

  • All state changing / Each state changing: use the same tolerance for any change, or a different one for the change to normal, to warning and to critical.
  • FF interval: shorter interval for the next check when the protection is triggered, so the confirmation arrives sooner than usual.
  • FlipFlop timeout: only in asynchronous modules; the identical data that confirm the change must arrive within that time.
  • Keep counters: advanced option that counts per status instead of per value.

The EndPoint equivalents (module_ff_interval, module_min_ff_event…) are in 2.1.

It is a tool for unstable environments

With flip-flop, the console takes longer to reflect a real failure: it has to repeat. Use it where noise is the problem, not by default.

docs.title: When it runs
docs.text:
In the Intervals tab, the Interval is the period in which the module must return data. In EndPoint modules it is expressed as a multiple of the agent interval: the console shows it as "Agent interval ×N". In modules run by the server it is the period at which the check is launched. It is also the reference for the unknown status: two intervals without data.

The Cron from and Cron to fields restrict when the module runs, with five fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month and day of the week. Three cases:

Configuration When it runs All fields on "Any" (default) Always, no restriction. Only Cron from, with specific values (15 20 * * *) When it matches those values: every day at 20:15. Cron from and Cron to (5 * * * * and 10 * * * *) During the interval: every hour, between minutes 5 and 10.

The EndPoint equivalent is module_crontab, explained in 2.1.

In the Data tab are the Timeout and the Retries: the seconds to wait for the response of a remote check and how many times it is repeated if it fails. They make no sense in local EndPoint modules. With 0 the server default is applied.

docs.title: Data: what is stored and how it is shown
docs.text:
All in the Data tab:

Field What it does Min. Value / Max. Value Range the module may return. The server discards data outside it. Historical data With it disabled only the last known value is stored: there are no graphs, but database space is saved. It is only justified when the system needs to run faster. Unit Text shown next to the value (%, MB, ms). Post process Multiplier applied to the value before storing it. Accepts decimals. Data translation Applies a translation or formula when displaying the data; if you choose one, the unit field is disabled. Export target Export server the module is sent to, if you have one configured. MADE Numeric modules only: the data is processed by the MADE engine (if active) and generates events automatically.

From bytes to megabytes

A module returns bytes and you want to see megabytes: post process 0.00000095367 (1 / 1,048,576) and unit MB. A value of 5242880 is stored as 5.

Changing post process with data already stored

The data is stored already transformed. If you change the multiplier on a module with history, old and new data end up on different scales and the graphs become inconsistent. Set the scale when you create the module, not afterwards.

docs.title: Organizing modules
docs.text:
In the Categorization tab:

Field What it does Module group Functional group of the module (network, system, database…), different from the agent group. Used to filter and group views. Module parent Module this one depends on, for the hierarchy of cascade protection. Custom ID Your own identifier, for example from your inventory. Category No effect in the regular interface; it is meant to be used with the Command Center. Module tags Tags that propagate to the module's events, serve as a filter in reports and views, and can restrict a user's access to certain modules. Policy tags Tags the module receives from its policy.

Other settings that organize or document the module:

  • Cascade Protection Services, in Thresholds: if the module is part of a service, alerts only fire at the highest level of the tree where the conditions are met, not at all levels at once.
  • Critical, warning and unknown instructions, in Information: what the person receiving the alert should do. This is the place for "restart service X, and if that fails, call Y".
  • Macros: variables of the module itself, with names like _name_, that can be used in alerts.
  • Module relations (direct or failover): allow one module to replace another in the SLA calculation.
  • Import from credential store: in the types that support it, fills the fields from a stored credential (see 2.2, Credential manager). It only copies the data into the form; the module is not linked to the credential.

docs.title: In a policy and in bulk operations
docs.text:
The form is the same, but it behaves differently:

  • In a policy, the fields the policy controls appear locked in the agent's module. They are changed in the policy, not agent by agent. Some fields, such as module tags, are not available in a policy module. See 2.10.
  • In a bulk operation each field has a lock: only the fields whose lock you open are changed, and the rest are respected. See The lock: what is changed and what is left alone in 2.11.

docs.title: Checking and troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Check The module is in unknown status. It has gone more than two intervals without data: the agent or the check does not respond. Look at the time of the last data; check the agent or the server running the module. A module with old data looks normal and never goes unknown. Ignore unknown is enabled: it keeps the last status. Review the Thresholds tab. The data exceeds the threshold and the status does not change. FF threshold above 0, or the wrong threshold mode (normal versus inverse). Review the FF threshold and the mode of each threshold. The module changes status and there is no alert. Quiet mode, or cascade protection delegates it to the parent service. Review Quiet and Cascade Protection Services. The module has data but no graph. Historical data disabled. Review the Data tab. Data that does arrive is missing. Outside Min. Value and Max. Value: the server discards it. Review the range in the Data tab. Graphs show a scale jump. Post process was changed with data already stored. Review the change history and reapply the scale from a clean date. The module does not run at the expected time. Restrictive cron schedule, or a long interval. Review Cron from, Cron to and the interval.

docs.title: 3. Automatic monitoring and discovery with Discovery
Automatic monitoring and discovery with Discovery
docs.text: Registering an agent by hand (creating it, giving it an IP address, deciding which modules it needs) is reasonable for ten machines. For the five hundred behind a corporate network, or for the instances a cloud creates and destroys on its own, it is a curse. Discovery is the set of wizards in the Pandora FMS Web console that avoids that curse: instead of creating every agent one by one, it finds what is there (devices on a network, instances of a cloud, a hypervisor, an application) and registers the agents and their initial modules without anyone typing a registration per device. And, depending on the type of task, it either steps aside once the registration is done or stays in charge of the monitoring; the difference matters, and it is explained right below.

docs.title: What Discovery is
docs.text:
Discovery works with tasks. A task is a job left scheduled: what has to be explored (a network range, a cloud account, a database, a hypervisor), which credentials to get in with, in which group to leave whatever appears and how often to repeat the search, or whether it is only launched by hand. It is created with a wizard, it stays in the task list and, from there on, it runs on its own.

There are two families of tasks, and it is worth not confusing them, because after the registration they behave very differently:

Host & Devices Applications, Cloud and Custom What they explore Networks (see Network discovery with Host & Devices): the devices that answer in a range, the ones that arrive in a CSV or the ones a script of your own finds A specific service: an AWS account, a vCenter, a database, a Kubernetes cluster… What they leave Agents with their modules and, in the network scan, relationships between devices and a network map Agents with their modules Who monitors afterwards The usual servers (network, WMI, plugins…): Discovery steps aside Discovery itself, which on every run queries the service again and brings the data; the task interval is the monitoring interval Where they come from They come with the console .disco packages installed separately (see Extending Discovery)

In both cases, the one doing the work is the Discovery server, one more of the Pandora FMS servers: without it running, tasks are created but nobody runs them. It is started and sized like any other, with the tokens described in Full server configuration reference.

docs.title: Where it is in the console
docs.text:
Discovery has its own entry in the management menu, Management → Discovery, visible with any of the agent access permissions over the All group (AR, AW, RR, RW or PM). Creating tasks inside Host & Devices requires write permission, AW; managing the custom scan scripts, in Manage scan scripts, requires PM; and uploading or removing .disco packages in Manage disco packages is reserved for a console administrator.

The start page of the menu, Start, is only its cover: it has no content of its own, just one shortcut to each section. When Applications or Cloud do not have any .disco package installed yet, the Web console replaces the listing with an empty notice with a button that takes you straight to installing one.

docs.title: The Discovery sections
docs.text:
Section What it does Where it is documented Task list All the tasks, by tabs (console, Host & Devices, applications, Cloud, custom) This chapter; console tasks, in Console tasks Host & Devices Network scan, CSV import, EndPoint deployment, custom scans Network discovery with Host & Devices Applications Application wizards installed as a .disco package Application monitoring (and containers or virtualization, depending on the .disco package) Cloud Cloud provider wizards installed as a .disco package Cloud environment monitoring Custom Own .disco packages or third-party ones with no category Creating discovery plugins Manage disco packages Uploading, updating and uninstalling .disco packages This chapter

Applications, Cloud and Custom are not fixed lists: each one only appears in the menu when there is at least one .disco package installed in that section. Without .disco packages, the whole section disappears from the menu instead of showing up empty. Each installed .disco package appears as a tile of its own inside its section (here, Applications with VMware, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle and the vulnerability scanner), and creating a task means going into the tile of the corresponding wizard:

The creation form changes from one .disco package to another (the VMware one is not the Oracle one), but all of them share the same frame: name and group are mandatory and, from there on, as many steps as the wizard asks for, with a progress indicator at the top and the Next button to move from one to the next:

Like any Discovery task, these can also notify when they fail, from their Actions tab (see Discovery task alerts).

Saving without finishing all the steps leaves the task created but incomplete, and the task list warns about it: an Applications, Cloud or Custom task that has not gone through its final step (the Complete setup button) appears with a warning icon in the operations column instead of the usual force-run button, and it has to be edited to finish defining it; the server will not run it until then.

docs.title: Extending Discovery: .disco packages and Marketplace
docs.text:
What turns a Discovery wizard into something installable is the .disco package .disco: a file that packages the definition of the wizard form together with the executables the server launches to carry it out. Without a .disco package there is no wizard; the network scan of Host & Devices is the exception, because it comes built in from the factory.

The catalogue gathers close to forty .disco packages: clouds (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Digital Ocean, OVH), virtualization (VMware, Proxmox, XenServer), orchestration (Kubernetes, OpenShift), databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, DB2, Microsoft SQL Server, MongoDB) and other tools, such as a vulnerability scanner or user experience monitoring with Selenium. All of them come from the Marketplace, which the Web console carries integrated in its own menu, Management → Marketplace. Each entry of the Discovery catalogue links to its page: to that menu if the console has a connection to the Marketplace, or directly to the Marketplace website if it does not.

docs.title: Installing, updating and uninstalling a .disco package
docs.text:
There are two ways, and which one applies depends on a single question: does the Web console have Internet access?

With a connection: from the console Marketplace. It is the convenient way, and the usual one in any installation that sees the Internet:

  1. In Management → Marketplace, search for the .disco package (in Search, or from the link in its entry in the Discovery catalogue) and open its page.
  2. Click Install and confirm. The console downloads the .disco package, installs it and shows the progress on the page itself; when it finishes, the button gives way to Installed.
  3. The wizard appears in its section (Applications, Cloud or Custom, depending on what the .disco package declares).

Installations done this way are recorded in Marketplace → Downloads (visible to administrators), from where a .disco package can be Reinstalled without searching for it again. Without an Internet connection, the console Marketplace itself warns that it needs one to work.

Without a connection: manual installation, for isolated environments. When the console lives on a network with no way out (the usual thing in industrial, defence or simply paranoid environments), the .disco package is carried by hand:

  1. Download the .disco package from the Marketplace website on a machine that does have Internet (a Marketplace .zip has to be renamed first with that extension) and carry it to the isolated network.
  2. Upload it in Discovery → Manage disco packages. The console validates its content, installs it and copies it to every active Discovery server, so that they know how to run its tasks.
  3. The wizard appears immediately in its corresponding section.

Whichever of the two ways is used, updating a .disco package means installing the new version on top. Uninstalling it, from Manage disco packages, removes it from the console and from the servers alike; tasks already created with that .disco package can no longer run. Creating a .disco package of your own, including the fields its form can ask for, is covered in Creating discovery plugins; broadly speaking, each field is declared with its label, a help text and a type (text, number, selector, checkbox or password), and the ones of type password can be stored encrypted in the database, besides always being shown hidden in the form like any field of that type.

Manage disco packages lists, for each installed .disco package, its name and icon, the short name, the section where it appears (Applications, Cloud or Custom) and the version loaded. In the actions column, besides deleting it, there is a button to force the synchronisation of its files with the active Discovery servers (the console already synchronises on its own when a .disco package is uploaded, so it only has to be pressed if something was left half done). That synchronisation copies the folder of the .disco package to the remote configuration directory (remote_config/discovery/, by default), from where it then reaches every Discovery server. If a .disco package is missing its directory or its .ini file in the console, that button disappears and an error icon is shown in its place: its .disco package has to be uploaded again to fix it.

docs.title: How a .disco package task works
docs.text: So far, a .disco package is something that gets installed. What matters is what it does when someone uses it: the .disco package task is the wizard installed, filled in and scheduled. It works the same for Applications, Cloud and Custom, and that is why it is told once, here, instead of repeating it in every chapter that hangs from them. Its result is agents and modules in the console, created by the Discovery server with whatever the .disco package plugin returns. What it does not do is install anything on the monitored machine: neither EndPoint nor files. Every run repeats the query and updates those agents.

docs.title: The first step: defining the task
docs.text:
All .disco package wizards start with the same form, before the .disco package says anything of its own:

Field What it does Task name Mandatory. Description Free text. Discovery server Active Discovery server that will run the task. Mandatory. Group Group of the task and of the agents it creates. Mandatory. Interval Defined (300 seconds by default) or Manual. A manual task only runs when it is forced from the task list. Mandatory. Use execution cron Optional. The task is still queued on every interval, but it only runs if it matches the five-field cron expression; that expression replaces the interval selector in the form.

If the name, the server, the group or the interval is missing, the form does not save. The Actions tab of that same step carries the Timeout and the notification options in case of error, which already have their section further down: Discovery task alerts.

docs.title: The steps the .disco package defines
docs.text:
Afterwards, each .disco package declares the configuration steps it needs and, in each one, the fields that have to be filled in.
