The MySQL .disco package, for example, adds two: "MySQL Base" and "MySQL Detailed". Next saves the step and moves on to the next one; Complete setup closes the task. Until it is pressed, the server does not run it, and the task list marks it with a warning icon. A step can also be built on the fly: the console runs a script from the .disco package that returns the form in JSON, and if that script fails, the step shows "The discovery script failed:" and the error, instead of the fields.

A .disco package can ask for these types of field:

Type What the user sees String, number and text area Free field; it can be mandatory and carry help text and placeholder. Password Masked field. It is only saved if it changes, and the .disco package can ask for it to be encrypted when saving it. Checkbox Yes/no switch; it can show or hide other fields. Selector and multiple selector List of options of the .disco package itself, or Pandora data: agent or module groups, agents, modules, module types, statuses, templates and alert actions, intervals, tags and operating systems. Tree Browser of a structure, for example a bucket or a resource tree. Credential Selector of the credentials of the Credential manager of type Custom, AWS, Azure, SAP, SNMP, Google or WMI.

With credentials, the field only shows identifiers; the username and the password are not copied into the task definition. When running it, the server looks the identifier up in the credential manager and hands the plugin the data as a JSON encoded in base64. The field names depend on the type:

Credential type Data the plugin receives Custom and SAP user, password AWS access_key_id, secret_access_key Azure client_id, application_secret, tenant_domain, subscription_id WMI user, password, namespace Google and SNMP The document stored in the credential, as it is

Nothing forces the use of the selector: a .disco package can ask for the username and the password in fields of its own, as the MySQL one does. The PostgreSQL one, on the other hand, uses a Custom credential.

docs.title: What happens on each run
docs.text:
1. The assigned Discovery server takes the task when its interval turn comes, or when someone forces it (with cron, only if the expression matches). In the .disco package command it replaces the values of the fields and adds data from the task: group, interval, temporary path and access to the console API.
  2. It launches every command the .disco package declares, with the timeout of the task applied to each one.
  3. The plugin answers with a JSON on standard output. If it brings monitoring data, the server creates or updates the agents and their modules with them. The rest (counts, notices, plugin errors) is saved as the task summary, with one entry per command, and it is read with the summary icon of the task list.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
• A command that ends with a non-zero exit code leaves the task in Failed and triggers the error options of the Actions tab: event and alert actions.
  • If a command exceeds the timeout, the summary says "The execution timed out." and the task is also left in Failed.
  • With a zero exit code, an empty response or one that is not JSON does not change the status: the task ends in Done, and whatever came out (or whatever is in the standard error) stays in the summary. It is worth looking at it: "Done" says that the plugin did not break, not that it found anything.
  • A JSON without monitoring data does not create agents either; it is saved in the summary and nothing else.
  • In the SAP .disco package, if the licence does not allow it, the server does not run the command and notes it in the summary.

docs.title: The task list
docs.text:
The task list, in its Host & Devices, applications, Cloud or custom tab, shows the task name, the assigned Discovery server, interval, network, status, task type, progress and date of the last update, and it can be filtered by task name, group, Discovery server, network and status. On each task its immediate execution can be forced, its progress seen, its pending results reviewed, and it can be edited, disabled or deleted; seeing the network map it has generated only makes sense (and is only available) for network discovery tasks, not for the applications or Cloud ones, which do not draw a topology.

Any task, whatever its type, also has a summary icon that opens its run summary: in the Applications, Cloud and Custom ones it details what the .disco package has been finding or the errors it has found along the way, with the detail the .disco package itself decides to show.

Status When it appears Not started The task exists but the server has not run it yet. Pending Queued, waiting for its turn or for its next run. Searching / Processing Under way: searching for devices or processing what has been found. Review It finished and there are results waiting for the user to decide which ones to turn into an agent. Done It finished with no errors. Failed It finished with at least one error. Cancelled The server restarted while the task was running; it has to be launched again.

Console tasks (database backups, PHP functions, scheduled report generation and the like) share the same list, in their own tab, but they have a chapter of their own: Console tasks.

docs.title: Discovery task alerts
docs.text:
A Discovery task works on its own and, for that very reason, it can fail on its own: an expired credential, a cloud API that changes, a network range that no longer exists. Without a notice, the failure is only discovered the day someone misses an agent. In order not to depend on that coincidence, all tasks (network scan, custom scan, Applications, Cloud and Custom) can notify when a run ends in error, with two options that can be used together or separately:

Option What it does Generate event on error It creates a critical event, "[Discovery] Task error: task name", in the group of the task, visible in the event console like any other one. Execute alert action on error It launches one or several of the alert actions already defined in the console (an email, a message, a command…).

Where they are configured depends on the family: in Host & Devices they are in the first step of the network scan and custom scan form; in Applications, Cloud and Custom, in the Actions tab of the wizard.

In those same Applications, Cloud and Custom tasks, the Actions tab also brings the Timeout field: the maximum time, in seconds, that each run is allowed to go on before it is considered failed; 60 seconds by default.

The alert action receives "Discovery task error: task name" as its main text, and the _discovery_task_ macro, with the task name, is available to compose messages of your own in the action.

The notices only fire when the run fails, that is, when the task ends in Failed status. A correct run that finds nothing is not an error: if the network is empty, Discovery does not consider it a reason for alarm.

docs.title: Inside the Discovery server
docs.text:
The server schedules its tasks according to the interval of each one: the automatic ones reschedule themselves; the manual ones are only launched when someone asks for it. Each task runs in its own thread, and the server opens in parallel as many threads as the higher of its two thread tokens sets (one meant for Host & Devices and applications tasks, another for the legacy network scan), so raising the one in use is enough for more tasks to run at the same time. If the server restarts with a manual task half done, that task is marked as cancelled in the list, waiting to be launched again; automatic tasks, on the other hand, are simply rescheduled for their next round.

What the server does at the end of each round depends on the family. In Host & Devices, the devices found are turned into agents, right away or after the user's review (see Reviewing the results before creating agents). In applications, Cloud and Custom, on every round, the server runs the .disco package, collects the monitoring data it returns and with them creates the agents that are missing and updates the values of their modules. For these tasks, Discovery is not only the one that registers: it is also the one that monitors, and if the task is disabled or deleted, its modules stop receiving data.

The server tokens related to Discovery (the switch and the server threads, and the paths that some application .disco packages use to connect to Java, SAP or Microsoft SQL Server) are described, with their default values, in Full server configuration reference.

docs.title: Network discovery with Host & Devices
docs.text:
Host & Devices is the Discovery section that explores networks: it walks a range of addresses, asks every machine that answers what it is and what it is called, and registers it as an agent, with its modules, its relationships with the rest of the network and, if wanted, a map. It is the shortest path between "I have a network" and "I have a monitored network", and the only part of Discovery that comes built in from the factory, with no packages to install.

Once the agents are created, Host & Devices steps aside: day-to-day monitoring is left in the hands of the network, WMI or plugin servers. What Discovery is in general, what a task is, where the task list is or what the Discovery server does is told in Automatic monitoring and discovery with Discovery; here it is taken as read.

docs.title: What Host & Devices offers
docs.text:
It is in Management → Discovery → Host & Devices, and creating tasks in it requires write permission (AW) over the group. It gathers five options:

Option What it is for Network scan The main option: explore one or several networks and register whatever answers. Import CSV Register agents from an inventory that already exists in a spreadsheet. EndPoint deployment Install EndPoints on machines that have already been located. Custom network scan Launch a discovery script of your own instead of the standard scan. Manage scan scripts Register those scripts of your own (requires PM).

docs.title: Network scan: first steps
docs.text:
The usual case. When creating the task:

  • Task name and an optional description.
  • Discovery server that will run it and group it will belong to.
  • Networks: one or several, in CIDR format (192.168.10.0/24) or by fully qualified domain name, separated by commas, or loaded from a file with one network per line.
  • Interval: defined (with a time selector; 300 seconds by default) or manual, for tasks that are only launched by hand.
  • SNMP credentials to try, from the credential manager (see Credential manager): with none configured, the scan tries SNMP v1 and the public community by default; with credentials of your own, it tries with them (see Device discovery).

Once the task is saved, it appears in the task list and runs according to its interval: it will create the agents it has to and their initial modules, unless results review is active.

A whole /24 network

Network: 192.168.10.0/24. With the default detection options (see below), the task scans the 254 possible addresses, tries SNMP with the public community and with the additional credentials given, and registers one agent per machine that answers.

The agents a network scan creates are remote agents, with no configuration file behind them: they are good for SNMP or WMI monitoring from the server, but they do not accept local monitoring policies or mass configuration changes until an EndPoint is installed on top of them (see Deploying EndPoints from Discovery).

Repeating the scan of a network that is already known does not duplicate what already exists. Discovery looks every machine up by its agent name and, if it finds it, updates its data —interval, operating system version and last contact, among others— instead of creating a new agent; if its IP address has changed, it adds it as an additional address without touching the one it already had. Modules follow the same logic: only the ones the agent is still missing are created (for example, a new network interface), never the ones it already has.

docs.title: Reviewing the results before creating agents
docs.text:
With Review results on, the machines the scan finds do not become agents right away: they stay pending in a list and the user chooses which ones to register. It is worth turning it on in the first scan of an unknown network, or in large networks where nobody wants two hundred new agents showing up unattended.

The option turns itself on —and can no longer be turned off— when the number of agents the task would create, calculated from the size of the configured networks, exceeds what the licence covers: in that case, reviewing the results stops being an option and becomes the only way not to run into the limit.

The machines a scan finds go through an intermediate result status before becoming an agent: without results review on, the server itself registers them as soon as the task finishes; with it on, they stay pending until someone accepts them from the Web console.

The review screen presents a tree with one node per discovered agent and, hanging from it, its detected modules; each one is checked separately, with buttons for "Select all", "Deselect all", "Expand all" and "Collapse all". The agents and modules that already existed before the scan appear disabled in the tree —they are already checked, but they cannot be unchecked— to make it clear that they are not going to be duplicated. The same screen also decides whether the task must generate the network map ("Create network map").

Accepting the review creates nothing on the spot: the task goes back to the queue with the selection saved, and it is the Discovery server that, on its next run, registers the checked agents and modules.

docs.title: What the scan detects
docs.text:
All these options are extras: whatever has been checked, every machine that answers the scan always receives a Host Alive module —an ICMP ping—, the minimum that guarantees the new agent says whether it is alive or not. SNMP, WMI and the rest of the options in this table add modules on top of that minimum; they do not replace it.

Option What it adds By default Scan SNMP network interfaces Network interface modules and data for the topology scan of network maps Enabled Scan SNMP known hardware SNMP modules according to the device manufacturer, identified by its Private Enterprise Number Enabled Scan WMI devices WMI modules on MS Windows machines Disabled Resolve hosts names Name resolution of the machines found Enabled Guess hosts OS Operating system detection (it can make the scan quite a lot longer) Disabled Scan additional information Additional information, visible later in the agent description (it can also make the scan longer) Disabled

SNMP credentials (v1, v2c or v3) and WMI credentials are typed in the form itself or chosen from the credential manager.

docs.title: Topology and network map
docs.text: With Create network map —on by default—, Discovery works out which machine hangs from which, assigns them a parent agent and generates a network map with the result (see Network topology maps). Parent detection, on by default, follows the network routes up to five hops before giving up.

docs.title: Importing agents from CSV
docs.text:
For when the inventory already exists in a spreadsheet, Import CSV registers agents from a file, without going through a scan. The form lets you choose the server that will be assigned to the created agents, the field separator (comma by default), whether the agent alias must also be used as its name and whether the default basic monitoring is added to it (enabled by default).

The file carries one row per agent with these columns, in this order:

Column Content 1 Agent name or alias 2 IP address 3 Operating system identifier 4 Interval, in seconds 5 Group identifier 6 Comments (optional) 7th onwards Identifiers of the network components to apply

The operating system and group identifiers are the ones the Web console already uses in its own management listings; the network component ones are those of the component library. The import rejects a row if the agent name already exists, if the group given does not exist or if the row is missing mandatory columns.

An example with four machines: a Linux web server and a Linux database, a Windows domain controller and a switch. Comma separator, no header row:

web01,192.168.10.21,1,300,13,Main web server,37,39
db01,192.168.10.30,1,300,8,MySQL in production,39
dc01,192.168.10.5,9,300,2,Domain controller
sw-core,192.168.10.1,18,300,9,,3,53

Read column by column, the first line creates the agent web01, with IP 192.168.10.21, Linux operating system (1), interval of 300 seconds, in the Web group (13), with the comment "Main web server" and two modules created from the network components Check HTTP (80) (37) and Check SSH (22) (39). The switch leaves the comment empty —the comma is kept so the columns do not shift— and receives the SNMP components Sysname (3) and System Uptime (53). The identifiers in the example are the ones a new installation brings (operating systems Linux 1, Windows 9, Switch 18; groups Servers 2, Databases 8, Network 9, Web 13); in an installation with history they may have changed, so it is worth checking them in the console before preparing the file.

Three details that save trouble

  • No header. All lines are processed as agents; a row of titles would end up in the report as a failed line (its "group" does not exist).
  • Default monitoring already adds availability and latency. With Add default monitoring on, there is no need to list the Host Alive and Host Latency components: they would be duplicated.
  • Report lines are counted from zero. If the result says "Line 2", it is the third line of the file.

docs.title: Deploying EndPoints from Discovery
docs.text: After discovering machines, EndPoint deployment lets you install an EndPoint on them directly: over SSH on Unix systems (Linux, BSD, Solaris, AIX, HP-UX) and over WinRM —or its encrypted variant, Secure WinRM— on MS Windows. The full detail, including installer and credential registration, is in Automatic agent distribution and installation.

docs.title: Custom network scan
docs.text:
When the standard scan is not enough, Custom network scan launches a script of your own in its place. The script is registered beforehand in Manage scan scripts (PM only), giving its name, the full path of the executable on the server, a description and the fields it needs —each one with its own help text, a default value and the option of hiding it if it is a credential—.

When creating the task, the data common to any Host & Devices task are asked for —name, comment, Discovery server, group, interval (600 seconds by default), event and alert action in case of failure— and, in a second step, the script already registered that is to be run, with its fields filled in.

A freshly made installation already brings two registered scripts, with nobody having to register them by hand:

  • IPMI Recon explores a network looking for IPMI management controllers with the credentials given, for the cards that are managed through that channel instead of through the normal network (see Advanced automatic discovery (IPMI, etc.)).
  • IPAM Recon checks which addresses of a network managed by IPAM are available and gives them a name, and associates the result with that IPAM network (see IP address management (IPAM)).

What the script has to do by itself

The Discovery server runs the script handing it the task identifier, the group one and the value of each configured field, but it does not interpret what the script writes on its output: it neither creates agents nor modules from it. That output is only kept, for diagnosis, when the server works with verbosity 10: it goes to the server log and to a copy per task in the discovery/ directory, next to the logs. A custom scan has, therefore, to register its own findings —through the API or by sending its own data XML— inside the script itself; Discovery only launches it and marks the task as failed or finished according to the exit code it ends with.

docs.title: How it discovers the network: the heuristic
docs.text: Finding the machines that answer on a network is only the first step; Discovery also tries to work out how they are connected to each other, in order to raise the complete network map. It does so with a heuristic of several steps, each one built on the previous one.

docs.title: Routes to the targets
docs.text: For every target network, Discovery launches a traceroute and adds, as additional networks to explore, the ones of the intermediate hops it keeps finding along the way. In the simple scan, that traceroute points at the address 8.8.8.8 —to try to "go out" to the Internet—, and all the networks the Discovery server itself is connected to directly are added too. The mask of a network discovered this way is fixed at /24 unless it can be determined more precisely, in which case it may stay as wide as the real data indicates.

docs.title: Device discovery
docs.text: With the networks already gathered —plus the ones given by hand in an advanced configuration—, Discovery uses nmap to locate the machines that answer on each one and to test whether they have the SNMP port open. The credentials chosen for the task are tried on the ones that do (see What the scan detects): with no credential of your own configured, the scan tries SNMP v1 and the public community by default; with credentials of your own, it tries with them. The ones that work stay in cache, so as not to repeat the test on every round. WMI, on the other hand, is not detected by nmap: if Scan WMI devices is on, it is queried directly with the WMI credentials of the task.

docs.title: Gateway discovery
docs.text: For every network, Discovery tries to work out its gateway by querying the route table of the devices that answered over SNMP: the IP address that appears most often as a hop in that table, among all the SNMP devices of the network, is taken as its gateway. If no device reveals it over SNMP, Discovery falls back on an order of likely addresses within the network: first .1, then .254, .100 and last .10. That network gateway does not prevent the specific devices whose real gateway can be determined from being assigned their own.

docs.title: Additional IP addresses, MAC and switches
docs.text: On every device with SNMP, Discovery queries its additional IP addresses and crosses them with the interface and IP-MAC resolution tables to know which MAC address corresponds to which IP and to which interface. With the table of MAC addresses learned by the switches it gathers more addresses and, on the way, marks as a switch any device that has data in that table. Those same tables —the IP-MAC resolution one and the switches one— also serve to work out through which interface each neighbouring device has been reached, data that is needed later to trace the map connections. When the device supports it, Discovery also adds whatever it finds through CDP and through LLDP, two protocols meant precisely for a machine to announce to its neighbours who it is.

docs.title: Name resolution and operating system detection
docs.text: With Resolve hosts names on —it is by default—, Discovery tries to give every machine a name by reverse DNS; if it does not manage it, it tries over SNMP and, as a last resort, by what CDP or LLDP may have told. That order is not entirely strict: when it finishes scanning the whole network, Discovery reviews again the names seen by CDP and LLDP and, if any of them matches a device already named by DNS or SNMP, it overwrites it without asking —a deliberate simplification of the mechanism itself: a name from a more trusted source is worth more even if it arrives late—. With Guess hosts OS on —off by default, because it makes the scan quite a lot longer—, operating system detection is down to nmap.

docs.title: Additional information
docs.text: With Scan additional information on —off by default, for the same reason as operating system detection—, Discovery looks for a description of the device: first over SNMP; if there is none, it falls back on nmap probing some usual ports in search of a title or a service identification; and here too whatever CDP and LLDP contribute is added, with the same caveat as before: they can overwrite data already obtained from another source.

docs.title: Building the network map
docs.text:
With all that information gathered, Discovery rebuilds the connections between devices in several steps:

  1. If a device has several network interfaces and in some of them there appear IP addresses that are not from its own network, it looks that address up in the network it belongs to, to replicate the information of that interface there.
  2. It marks as trunk interfaces the interfaces of the routers and switches through which more than one device has been reached.
  3. It counts, for every non-trunk interface of every device, how many devices have been discovered through it.
  4. If the count gives exactly one, and that other device sees in turn a single connection that matches the origin, it traces a direct connection between the two.
  5. If the count gives more than one and any of the candidates on the other side turns out to be a trunk interface, it creates an aggregation node —a "bridge"— that gathers that interface and all the ones on the other side, except the trunk ones.
  6. The interfaces left with no connection in the count are reviewed in case any of their candidates is already connected to a bridge: if so, they are linked to the same point.
  7. The trunk interfaces still to be connected are linked to an existing bridge or to a new one, depending on whether or not there is some device on that side already connected to one.
  8. A device that, after all this, still has no connection is not left orphaned: a bridge connected to its gateway is created and the device joins it directly, without going through any specific network interface.

The result is the network map that Host & Devices shows (see Topology and network map): it may not match other maps already saved in the Web console if these have been edited by hand or have gone a long time without being updated.

Deep-scan intermediate transit networks and Scan secondary networks attached to hosts, the two in the advanced options of the scan (see just below), widen which networks enter the first two steps of this heuristic —device and gateway discovery— and whether the neighbours that appear outside the current network are added as new networks to explore.

docs.title: Advanced scan options
docs.text: Option What it does By default Advanced mode Replaces the automatic network scan with the ones the user indicates; it requires traceroute and route installed on the Discovery server Simple mode Blacklist of IPs and networks Addresses or networks excluded from the scan, in the same format as the networks to scan (or a file) Empty Deep-scan intermediate transit networks Widens discovery to the intermediate networks the path to the targets goes through Disabled Scan secondary networks attached to hosts Widens discovery to other networks connected to the machines already found Disabled Apply autoconfiguration rules Applies the self-provisioning rules to the created agents (see Self-provisioning mechanisms) Disabled Event and alert action on failure Generates a critical event or launches alert actions if the task ends with an error (see Discovery task alerts) Disabled

docs.title: Console tasks
docs.text: Taking a backup by hand every night, or logging in every Monday to send the same report by email, is the kind of task an administrator forgets exactly the week it is needed most. Console tasks solve that oversight: they are periodic jobs of the Web console itself —they do not go through any monitoring server— that are scheduled once and run on their own, with the date and the interval they are given.

docs.title: What console tasks are
docs.text: They are in Discovery → Task list, on the Console tasks tab. They share a screen with the rest of the Discovery tasks, but they have nothing to do with them: they do not scan networks or inventory anything, so it is worth not confusing them just because they sit one tab apart.

docs.title: Console task types
docs.text:
Every console task is, at bottom, a call to a specific function, with its own parameters. This is what the Task selector offers when creating a new task:

Type (the "Task" selector) What it does Its own parameters Backup Pandora database Generates a full backup of the installation Path where to save it; enable or disable it Send custom report by email Generates an already saved custom report and sends it by email Report, email addresses, subject, message, format (PDF/CSV/JSON) Send custom report (from template) by email The same, but from a report template (per agent or combined) Template, agents, "Report per agent", addresses, subject, message, format Save custom report to disk Generates a custom report and saves it to disk instead of sending it Path, file prefix, format (XML/PDF/JSON/CSV) Execute custom script Runs a system script on the console server Script path Call PHP function (untranslated; it appears in English) Calls an internal PHP function by name; internal use of the console itself —for example, starting the remote console service GoTTY—, not meant to be created by hand Function name

It does not appear in the creation selector, although it shares the same internal table of types: Send csv log (sending a log of events in CSV, deliberately removed from the creation form). Like "Call PHP function", it has no translation either, so in a Spanish Web console it would show in English if it ever appeared in a listing.

Creating and designing the report or the template these types send or save — what it contains, in what format— is the business of Reports; here only how to schedule its sending or its periodic saving is covered. What the backup contains and how to restore it is explained in Backup and restore; here only how to schedule it is covered.

docs.title: Creating and scheduling a task
docs.text:
From Task list → Console tasks, a new task asks for a name, a type (previous table), a schedule —once or periodic: hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly or custom, with a calendar of days for weekly recurrence—, the date and time of the next run, a group and the parameters of the chosen type. Saving creates the task, which stays in the listing waiting for its turn.

Scheduling a backup, a script of your own or the saving of a report to disk requires write or administration permission (see Required permissions below); without that permission, those three types do not even appear in the selector.

docs.title: Editing, enabling/disabling, forcing a run and deleting
docs.text: The listing shows user, task (name and type), schedule, next run, last run, Console ID —see The "Console ID" column—, group and operations, and it can be filtered by task, schedule, console and group, and narrowed by date and time of the last run. Each row offers forcing the immediate run, editing, enabling or disabling, and deleting, although not all actions are always visible: editing and deleting require administration —or, if the task is one of the three report types, reports management is enough too—, and enable/disable is hidden for the backup, the script, "Call PHP function" and the sending of internal feedback.

docs.title: Required permissions
docs.text: Action Permission Viewing the "Console tasks" tab and forcing a task to run Read, write, reports management or administration (any of the four) Creating or editing a task (form) Reports management or administration Editing a task, your own or one created by another user Reports management or administration; write alone is not enough, not even for the user who created it Creating a "sensitive" type (backup, script of your own, saving to disk, function call) Write or administration; otherwise the type does not even appear in the selector

docs.title: How and where they actually run
docs.text:
No Pandora FMS server runs console tasks: the Web console itself does. For that, the operating system crontab has to call a console page, enterprise/extensions/cron/cron.php, over HTTP every minute; on every call, the console records that cron has been there, checks which tasks have reached their date and time and runs them. The typical line, with the console URL and the system user that applies:

* * * * * <user> wget -q -O - --no-check-certificate --load-cookies /tmp/cron-session-cookies --save-cookies /tmp/cron-session-cookies --keep-session-cookies https://<console>/pandora_console/enterprise/extensions/cron/cron.php >> /var/www/html/pandora_console/log/cron.log

There is no need to copy it from here: the console itself shows it, already with its URL and its installation path, in the notice described below. That same cron pass takes care, on the way, of other internal maintenance of the console —status checks, licence token renewal, sending reports by other means—; they are not part of this screen and are not documented here.

A task with a "once" schedule deletes itself when it finishes running; with a periodic schedule, it waits for the next round.

Console tasks also exist in the Command Center: the same Console tasks tab, with the same types, is available in the centralised console, and it needs its own crontab line, on the Command Center machine itself, pointing at its cron.php. When a task needs to choose agents as a parameter —for example, a report per agent—, the form groups them by the node they come from, since the Command Center gathers agents from several managed consoles.

docs.title: The "Console ID" column
docs.text: Meant for architectures with more than one console: each task can be anchored to a specific console so that only that one runs it, or left open ("Any") so that the first console whose cron passes runs it. It is not that the different consoles "do not talk" to each other, as a quick reading might suggest: it is that each task decides, by configuration, whether it is exclusive to one console or open to all, and that distribution prevents the same task —a report sending, for example— from firing twice when several consoles have their own active crontab. In the listing, the column shows the identifier of the assigned console, "Any" if there is no restriction, or "None" if the assigned console no longer exists.

docs.title: Requirements for them to run and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Requirement Detail System crontab entry A line that calls enterprise/extensions/cron/cron.php of the console with wget every minute and saves the output in log/cron.log of the installation (see the example line above) HTTP access to the console The machine where the crontab runs has to be able to open the console URL; with certificates of your own, --no-check-certificate keeps wget from stopping Warning if it does not run The console checks when it last ran and warns if it has been more than ten minutes without doing so, or if it has never run

If the Web console detects that this cron has gone more than ten minutes without running, or that it has never run, it shows a notice of its own —"not running properly" or "not configured"— with the exact crontab line to add, and it links back to this same screen. That notification is the first stop when debugging why a scheduled task has not run on its date.

docs.title: Network monitoring
docs.text: Remote monitoring is the other half of the trade: everything an EndPoint cannot tell you because it does not live inside the machine, but is checked from outside —a router, a switch, a printer, a UPS— or that is worth checking from outside even when the device has an agent of its own, such as the real availability of a service as seen from the network. This chapter covers ICMP, TCP, SNMP, WMI, remote commands and the use of remote server plugins: everything a Pandora FMS server does on the other side of the network, with nothing installed at the destination. The notices devices send on their own, SNMP traps, have a chapter of their own: SNMP trap monitoring.

docs.title: Remote monitoring: what it is and when to use it
docs.text:
Checking a device from outside does not require touching it: it is enough that it answers a network request —a ping, a TCP connection, an SNMP or WMI query, a command over SSH— and that some Pandora FMS server has network visibility all the way to it. It is the only possible path for a device that does not accept software of its own (a router, a switch, a printer, a UPS) and a reasonable alternative for a server that does, when what matters is what the network sees and not what the operating system itself sees.

No EndPoint is needed to have an agent. A logical agent can be registered straight from the Web console, with no configuration file behind it, and have network modules attached to it: it is what, for example, Discovery does when it scans a network. If a module leaves its target address field empty, it uses the IP address of the agent itself; that way an agent with no EndPoint can carry all its modules without repeating the IP in each one.

Check Server that runs it Token that enables it ICMP (availability and latency) Network High Performance Server, in bulk with fping networkhpserver SNMP Network High Performance Server, in bulk with pandorafsnmp (v1, v2c and v3) networkhpserver TCP Network Server networkserver Remote commands Network Server networkserver WMI Network Server, with the pandorawmic client networkserver Remote plugins Heavy Server heavyserver

All three come enabled from the factory and share out the work on their own: with the Network High Performance Server running, the Network Server leaves ICMP and SNMP in its hands and keeps the rest. If the high-performance one is disabled, the Network Server takes charge of ICMP again (with the system ping) and of SNMP (with snmpget, query by query). The details of that split are in Performance, fine tuning and troubleshooting.

When the network to be checked is not visible from any central server —a site with no direct route, an isolated network—, a satellite server does exactly the same work from inside that network and delivers the data as if it were one more server.

A router with no EndPoint

An agent "router-core" is registered with address 192.168.10.1, with nothing installed on it. From there, network modules are added to it —ICMP to know whether it answers, SNMP to read its interfaces— exactly as with any other agent.

docs.title: First steps: creating a network module
docs.text:
A network module is created from the agent view, on the Modules tab, with the Create button → Create network module. The form asks for the type first:

Family What it is for Section ICMP Availability and latency of the network Availability and latency with ICMP TCP Network ports and services Services with TCP SNMP Devices with an SNMP agent (routers, switches, UPS…) SNMP monitoring Remote command Commands over SSH or Windows remote Remote commands: SSH and Windows WMI Windows devices with no EndPoint Windows without an agent: WMI Plugin Checks packaged in a script Remote server plugins

The complete table of internal types, with what each one returns and how its status is interpreted, is in Module type reference; each section of this chapter links to its row.

All network modules share these fields, with their default value:

Field Default value What it does Target IP empty (auto) If left empty, it uses the agent IP. It accepts the _agentname_ and _agentalias_ macros when the agent name or alias resolves to a valid IP. Port empty (161 in SNMP, 22 in remote commands over SSH) Destination port, when the check needs it. Interval 300 s How often the check is repeated. Warning threshold (min/max) 0 / 0 Range that sets the module to warning status. Critical threshold (min/max) 0 / 0 Range that sets the module to critical status. Timeout 0 (uses the server one) Maximum time before the check is taken as failed. Retries 0 Additional attempts before discarding the data. FF threshold (flapping) 0 (disabled) Number of state changes in a row that have to be seen before taking them as real; see the example below. Unknown instructions empty Text the operator sees when the module falls into unknown status. Minimum / maximum 0 / 0 Any data outside this range is discarded as invalid.

Ping and latency to the router, with thresholds

On the "router-core" agent (192.168.10.1), two network modules:

  • Available (remote_icmp_proc): with no configuration beyond the target IP, it is enough to know whether the router answers.
  • Latency (remote_icmp): same target, with a warning from 100 ms and critical from 300 ms.

As soon as the Network Server runs the module, the agent status goes from "No data" to normal and the first value appears in its view; it is the sign that the module is well configured.

docs.title: Common advanced properties
docs.text:
These editor tabs appear in all network modules, whatever the type. The whole form, with thresholds, unknown status, intervals and data, is explained in 2.20, Common module configuration:

  • Custom ID (Categorization tab): a free identifier to relate the module to an external system, such as a CMDB.
  • Post process (Data tab): multiplies the data received by the given factor, before storing it. It is useful, for example, to convert octets into bits: a module that reads octets per second with a post process of 8 already stores the data in bits per second.
  • Export target (Data tab): also sends the data to an export server.
  • Category (Categorization tab): grouping used by the Command Center.
  • Cron (Intervals tab): if Cron from is enabled, the module stops running by interval and runs only when the current date and time match the configured expression.

Running a module only at night

A module with Cron from set to 0 2 * * * runs once a day, at two in the morning, instead of every 300 seconds.

The FF threshold (from flapping) keeps an alert from firing because of an isolated state change: it requires seeing the same number of state changes in a row before taking them as real.

Avoiding a false spike from flapping

An unstable WAN link goes from normal to critical and back to normal several times in a few minutes. With an FF threshold of 3, the module does not change status —and does not fire alerts— until it sees three readings in a row with the same sign; the flickering stops generating noise.

docs.title: Network components: do not start from scratch
docs.text:
A network component is a prefabricated module: the same configuration of a network module, saved as a template so that it does not have to be filled in every time. In the editor of a new module, the Using network component field lets you choose one instead of filling in the form by hand; the manual option (--Manual configuration--) is still available to use none.

The installation brings components grouped by manufacturer and technology: Cisco MIBs, UNIX systems, Microsoft Windows, WMI, databases, and so on with the rest of the groups included from the factory.

Applying Host Alive and Host Latency from components

When creating a new module, selecting the Host Alive component (Network Management group) registers the same boolean ICMP module that would be configured by hand; Host Latency, from the same group, does the same with latency. It is the fastest way to leave an agent with no EndPoint with the minimum covered. In fact, the agent registration form itself brings a checkbox, checked by default, that creates these two modules (Host Alive and Host Latency) automatically as soon as the agent is registered, without going through the module editor.

Creating a component of your own is as simple as configuring any network module and saving it as a component instead of applying it directly to an agent, from Management → Modules → Network components. From there it can be applied to any agent, included in a monitoring policy or left for Discovery to apply it in bulk during a scan.

docs.title: Macros in the module fields
docs.text:
Some fields of remote modules accept macros that the server replaces with agent data every time it runs the module. That saves typing the same value by hand on every agent, and it is what allows a network component or a policy module to work the same for agents with different data. The typical case is the SNMP community: if every device has its own, it is stored in an agent custom field and the module uses the macro instead of the community.

The fields that accept macros are these:

Field Modules Target IP ICMP, TCP and SNMP SNMP community SNMP v1 and v2c User, authentication password and privacy password SNMP v3 User and password WMI and remote WMI inventory

These macros can be used in those fields:

Macro Replaced by Where _agentcustomfield_N_ Value of the agent custom field whose identifier is N All the fields in the previous table _addressn_N_ IP address number N of the agent, with its addresses sorted All the fields in the previous table _agent_, _agentalias_ Agent alias Target IP _agentname_ Agent name Target IP

The macro is only replaced if the field value starts with it: a value such as _agentcustomfield_3_ works; comunidad_agentcustomfield_3_ is sent as it comes. Custom fields are created in Management → Resources → Custom fields. The identifier that appears in that listing is the N of the macro. The value is filled in on each agent.

A different SNMP community per device

The "SNMP community" custom field is created, which receives the identifier 4, and it is filled in on each agent with its community (sw-core-ro, sw-planta2-ro…). An SNMP network component with SNMP community _agentcustomfield_4_ is then applied to all the switches, directly or through a policy: each module queries with the community of its own agent.

Watching the second IP of a device

On a server with two interfaces registered in the agent, an ICMP module with Target IP _addressn_2_ checks the second address. The order is the one of the sorted addresses, not the order in which they were added.

The remote plugins have a macro set of their own, a wider one; it is explained in Plugin macros.

docs.title: Availability and latency with ICMP
docs.text:
ICMP is the most basic check and it has two types: Available (remote_icmp_proc), which returns whether the IP answers or not, and Latency (remote_icmp), which returns the response time in milliseconds (see Module type reference). The Network High Performance Server measures with fping, grouping all the pending destinations in a single call (if it is disabled, the Network Server does it with the system ping): it sends as many packets per attempt and as many retries as the icmp_packets and icmp_checks tokens indicate, with the timeout of network_timeout. If there is no answer within those limits, the availability module marks critical status and the latency one is left with no data.

Availability of a printer

An Available module on 192.168.10.50: with no adjustment beyond the target IP, it warns as soon as the printer stops answering ping, with no need to install anything on it.

Latency of a WAN link

A Latency module on the IP of the remote router, with a warning at 100 ms and critical at 300 ms: a link that starts to degrade can be seen coming before it goes down completely.

For something finer than latency —for example, the percentage of lost packets instead of only the round-trip time— there is the packet loss plugin the installation brings (see Remote server plugins).

docs.title: Services with TCP
docs.text:
TCP checks a service by its port, with four types: open port (remote_tcp_proc, boolean), numeric (remote_tcp), text (remote_tcp_string) and incremental (remote_tcp_inc); what each one returns, in Module type reference. Two fields do the work:

  • TCP send: what is sent to the port. Several steps of a conversation are separated with |; the ^M sequence is replaced by a real carriage return.
  • TCP receive: what is expected back, compared case-insensitively. It is mandatory in the text and incremental types; in the open port one, only if it is filled in.

Open port

A module of the open port type on port 443, with no TCP send or TCP receive: it is enough for the port to accept the connection to mark normal status.

Header of a web server

TCP send: GET / HTTP/1.0^M^M. TCP receive: 200 OK. The module goes to normal as soon as the response contains that string, no matter whether the server returns it in upper or lower case.

Three-step SMTP conversation

TCP send: HELO midominio.com^M|MAIL FROM: <a@midominio.com>^M|RCPT TO: <b@destino.com>^M. TCP receive: 250|250|250. Every step is sent and checked before moving on to the next one.

SSH banner

Port 22, with no TCP send, and TCP receive with the text SSH-2.0 to confirm the protocol version the server announces when connecting.

Retries and timeout are adjusted as in any network module, with the server defaults in tcp_checks and tcp_timeout.

docs.title: SNMP in five minutes
docs.text:
To monitor a device over SNMP, it needs the SNMP agent enabled and Pandora FMS needs to know how to talk to it: which protocol version (v1, v2c with a read community; v3 with user, authentication and privacy) and which OID to read. An OID (Object IDentifier) is the address of a specific piece of data inside the device —temperature, CPU, the status of an interface—; it can be written in its numeric form (.1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0) or, if the server has the MIB that describes it loaded, in its textual form (sysName.0). Every OID that is monitored is a different network module.

OID What it is .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0 (sysUpTime) Time the device has been up .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0 (sysName) Configured name of the device .1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8 (ifOperStatus) Operational status of an interface .1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10 (ifInOctets) Input octets per interface (32-bit counter) .1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6 (ifHCInOctets) The same, in its 64-bit version for fast links

When the OID is textual, the server translates it to numeric with the MIBs it has loaded (see MIB manager); without the right MIB, the browser and the modules can only work with the number.

The recommended way to register SNMP modules is one of the two wizards in the agent view: they explore the device over SNMP and propose the modules already configured, without looking up a single OID by hand. Creating the SNMP modules one by one, later in this section, is left for the cases a wizard does not cover: a loose OID that appears in no template, a MIB of the manufacturer's own, or the fine tuning of a module already created.

docs.title: SNMP interfaces wizard
docs.text:
In the agent view, the SNMP Interfaces Wizard tab. It is the shortcut for switches and routers: instead of creating one module per interface and magnitude by hand, it walks the IF-MIB::interfaces branch of the device and proposes all the modules at once.

The first step asks for the SNMP connection —the same form the SNMP wizard of the next section uses—:

Field Default value What it does Target IP empty Address of the device to explore. It is a free-text field: it does not accept the agent macros _agentname_ or _agentalias_; a real IP has to be typed even if the agent already has one associated. Port 161 SNMP port of the device. Server to run the command Local console Which Pandora FMS server makes the real SNMP query. It only needs changing when the console has no direct path to the device: see Running wizards and tests from a remote server (Exec Server). Import from credential store — If there is any SNMP set saved in the credential manager visible to the user, it appears here; choosing it fills in the rest of the fields by itself. SNMP version 2c 1, 2c or 3. Choosing 3 shows the authentication form below. SNMP community public Read community, for v1 and v2c.

With version 3, the form adds the usual SNMPv3 fields: security level (no authentication or privacy, with authentication and no privacy, or with both), user, authentication method and password (MD5, SHA, SHA256 or SHA512) and privacy method and password (DES, AES, AES192 or AES256) — the same as in SNMP modules.

Once the query is done, the wizard decides once, for the whole device, whether it works with 32- or 64-bit traffic counters: if the device answers on the high-capacity counter branch (meant for fast links), it uses that one for all its interfaces; if not, it stays with the classic 32-bit counters. The result is presented as a collapsible block per interface, with a switch that includes or excludes it whole; only the interfaces that are operationally and administratively up come already enabled, so as not to fill the agent with dead modules for ports with nothing connected. Above the blocks there is a filter bar with free-text search by interface name or description, two switches to keep only the ones that are operationally or administratively up, and a switch to select at once all the interfaces that pass the filter. Inside each block, another switch marks or unmarks all its modules at the same time, and each module can be enabled or disabled separately and brought with its warning and critical thresholds already edited before creating anything. A special block, at the beginning of the listing, applies the same set of modules to all the selected interfaces at once, without repeating the selection interface by interface.

For every interface that stays checked, the wizard proposes:

Module What it measures Threshold Operational status Whether the interface is up, down, in testing… It depends on the administrative status of the interface: if it is administratively up, the critical threshold expects it to be operationally up too (it warns or fails if not); if it is administratively down, the threshold is inverted so as not to warn about something expected; if it is in testing, it uses a third set of ranges. Input / output octets Traffic in bytes per second Incremental, with no threshold by default Input / output unicast packets Packets per second Incremental, with no threshold by default Input / output multicast and broadcast packets (only with 64-bit counters) Packets per second Incremental, with no threshold by default CRC errors Frames discarded because of a frame error Incremental, with no threshold by default Bandwidth, input usage, output usage Percentage of the link capacity in use, calculated from the traffic and the interface speed The aggregated bandwidth module brings an 85% as default critical threshold; the input and output usage ones, separately, with no threshold

The three usage percentage modules do not read an OID directly: an internal plugin calculates them from the traffic and the nominal speed of the interface, so they count as plugin-type modules in the agent, even though the wizard presents them just like the rest. On Cisco devices recognised by their PEN, the wizard also adds a duplex mismatch module per interface, when the device exposes that data.

Which modules of this table come already checked by default, without touching anything, is decided in Setup → System settings → Performance, on the Interfaces wizard tab (see 9.2 · Full console configuration reference): it is one switch per module, valid for all agents.

Before creating, the wizard goes over the list and marks in grey, with a warning, the modules that already exist in the agent (or in the policy, if a policy is being edited) with the same name; it does not prevent going on, but it warns so as not to duplicate without noticing. The modules created behave afterwards like any SNMP module: they are edited, their threshold is changed or an alert is added in the same way as to one made by hand.

A 24-port switch, only active interfaces and their traffic

Target IP 192.168.10.2, version 2c, community public. After the SNMP walk, only the interfaces with operational status up are left checked (the OperStatus UP filter helps to check it at a glance) and, of the modules each one proposes, only Operational status and the input and output octets: the availability and the traffic of each port in use, without errors or packets that an access switch rarely needs watching.

A router with SNMPv3 from the credential store

Target IP, the one of the router; version 3. Instead of typing user and passwords by hand, the set already saved in the credential manager is chosen, with security level authPriv, authentication SHA and privacy AES: the wizard fills in the rest of the form by itself and makes the exploration with those credentials.

docs.title: SNMP wizard
docs.text:
In the agent view, the SNMP Wizard tab. Unlike the previous one, this wizard monitors the device as a whole, not only its interfaces, and shares the same connection form of the previous section (target IP with no agent macros, port, server to run the command, import from the credential store, version and community or v3 credentials).

With the connection made, the wizard identifies the manufacturer of the device by its PEN (Private Enterprise Number, the identifier every manufacturer registers with IANA inside the identification branch of the device). If the PEN is not registered in Pandora FMS, the wizard says so and proposes nothing: it has to be registered or, if it is of no interest, the modules have to be created by hand from SNMP modules. If it recognises it, it offers the library of modules already prepared for that manufacturer —plus the ones that are good for any device— grouped in blocks according to what they measure: CPU, memory, disks, storage, and so on with the rest. Each block is enabled or disabled at once with its own switch, and each module inside a block can be checked or unchecked separately, with its warning and critical thresholds already editable before creating anything; an indicator next to each block warns how many of its modules are selected.

This wizard creates two kinds of modules:

  • Fixed OID: they read an OID of the manufacturer MIB directly —CPU, memory, sensors…—, just like an SNMP module created by hand.
  • Calculated by plugin: for data that do not come out of a single OID —a percentage of disk used, free memory expressed as a percentage…—, the wizard relies on a remote plugin called snmp_remote.pl. If that plugin is not registered in the installation (see Remote server plugins), these modules stay disabled in the wizard even if the manufacturer is recognised.

As in the interfaces wizard, before creating, the modules that already exist in the agent or that repeat with the same name inside the selection itself are marked in grey, without that preventing going on.

The catalogue of manufacturers and components this wizard uses is not closed: it can be extended with new manufacturers and with components of your own, of fixed or dynamic OID, read directly or calculated by a plugin —see Extending the SNMP and WMI wizards with components of your own.

A Linux server with net-snmp

On a server with the net-snmp agent installed, the wizard recognises the Net-SNMP/UCD PEN and proposes CPU, memory and disk space modules ready to check and create, without looking up a single OID by hand.

A Windows server with the SNMP service

On a Windows server with the SNMP service enabled and a read community configured, the same connection is repeated (version 2c, the community of the device): if the wizard recognises the PEN the service declares, it offers the blocks of modules already prepared just as in Linux; if it does not recognise it, it warns that the PEN is not registered and what corresponds is to document the device with SNMP modules or to register it by hand.

docs.title: SNMP browser
docs.text:
For when it is not known which OID is needed: the SNMP browser walks the whole tree of the device, or only a specific branch if the exploration is to be shortened, and allows searching for a text string with highlighting of matches. On any OID found there are direct actions: create a network component, an agent module or a policy module, without leaving the browser.

Looking up the temperature of a switch

"temperature" is searched in the already explored tree of the switch, the OID corresponding to the sensor is located and the agent module is created directly from the result, with Create agent module.

docs.title: SNMP modules
docs.text:
For what no wizard covers: a loose OID with no template, a MIB of the manufacturer's own or the fine tuning of a module already created. Four types: numeric (remote_snmp), status (remote_snmp_proc), text (remote_snmp_string) and incremental (remote_snmp_inc, for counters: see Module type reference). Fields of their own, with their default value:

Field Default value Port 161 OID — Version 2c Community (v1/v2c) empty; public in the wizards Security level (v3) noAuthNoPriv User (v3) — Authentication method (v3) MD5, SHA, SHA256 or SHA512; MD5 by default (the console asks for a minimum of 8 characters in the password) Privacy method (v3) DES, AES, AES192 or AES256; DES by default

The Credentials field allows choosing a set saved in the credential manager instead of typing community or user by hand. Next to the OID field, the SNMP Walk button opens the same browser of the previous section without leaving the module editor.

Uptime over v2c

OID .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0, version 2c, community public: numeric module with the uptime of the device, in hundredths of a second.

CPU of a device with a manufacturer OID

A switch exposes its CPU load in an OID of its own, outside MIB-II (for example, .1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.109.1.1.1.1.7.1 on Cisco devices). Numeric module with that OID, version 2c and the community of the device.

v3 authPriv module with SHA and AES

Version 3, security level authPriv, user pandora_ro, authentication SHA with its password, privacy AES with its own: the highest level of SNMP security the form offers.

Traffic of an interface as incremental

OID .1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6.1 (ifHCInOctets of interface 1), type incremental. The SNMP counter grows without stopping while the device is up; Pandora FMS stores the difference between two readings divided by the elapsed time, that is, a rate (octets per second), not the raw value of the counter.

docs.title: MIB manager
docs.text:
MIBs describe what every OID of a manufacturer means; without the corresponding MIB loaded, an OID is only seen in its numeric form. The MIB uploader allows uploading the ones of the manufacturer, in .mib or .zip format, and leaves them available to translate OID in the browser, in the modules and in the traps.

Loading the MIB of a UPS

The .mib file the UPS manufacturer delivers is uploaded; from there on, its OIDs appear translated in the browser and traps of that same manufacturer can be used, already identified by their name.

docs.title: SNMP from an EndPoint
docs.text:
It makes sense when the SNMP device is only reachable from inside a network that only an EndPoint reaches, not the central server. The Windows EndPoint has a native directive for it:

module_snmpget
module_snmp_version 2c
module_snmp_community public
module_snmp_agent 192.168.10.1
module_snmp_oid .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0

(SNMPv3 credentials are given inside the advanced options of the module itself, with no dedicated sub-token per field).

The Go and Perl EndPoints do not have an SNMP directive of their own: they rely on module_exec to call the system snmpget, just as for any other external command.

The same OID, from each EndPoint

Windows: 

module_snmpget
module_snmp_version 2c
module_snmp_community public
module_snmp_agent 192.168.10.1
module_snmp_oid .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0
Go or Perl: 
module_exec snmpget -v 2c -c public 192.168.10.1 .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0

See 2.1 · Monitoring with EndPoints for the rest of the directives of the local configuration file.

All of the above is polling: Pandora FMS asks and the device answers. For the opposite —the device warns at the moment something happens— there are the traps, which are received, filtered, translated and turned into alerts as explained in SNMP trap monitoring.

docs.title: Windows without an agent: WMI
docs.text:
WMI allows reading information from a Windows device without installing an EndPoint on it, provided remote access to WMI is enabled at the destination. The WMI module relies on the pandorawmic client, which the Network Server launches with the given credentials —stored in the credential manager or typed by hand— against the target device. Its five types (numeric, status, text and incremental) are in Module type reference.

Fields of the module:

Field What it is IP Target Windows device WMI credential From the credential manager, or a user and password typed separately Namespace WMI namespace where the queried class lives; empty by default WMI query The query in WQL, the WMI dialect similar to SQL Field number Which column of the response to use, if the query returns several Key string Optional: if filled in, the module returns 1 or 0 depending on whether the response contains that string, instead of the string itself

Free space on C:

Namespace root\cimv2, query SELECT FreeSpace FROM Win32_LogicalDisk WHERE DeviceID='C:', field number 0: it returns the free space of the disk in bytes.

Spooler service running

Query SELECT State FROM Win32_Service WHERE Name='Spooler', key string Running: the module returns 1 while the service is active and 0 as soon as it stops.

A WQL query of your own

Any WMI class of the device can be queried the same way, adjusting the field number to the column of interest in the response —for example, SELECT Name, Status FROM Win32_PnPEntity with field number 1 to keep only the status.

The WMI Wizard, in the agent view, groups the most usual queries in templates ready to check: services (boolean, running or stopped), processes, disk space and registered WMI components —the same component mechanism as in SNMP, but for WMI—, without writing a single WQL query by hand. That catalogue of WMI components can also be extended with queries of your own, just like the one of the SNMP wizard: see Extending the SNMP and WMI wizards with components of your own.

For the target Windows device to answer WMI, its firewall has to let the corresponding incoming connections through (see Windows firewall requirements for agentless monitoring).

docs.title: Remote commands: SSH and Windows
docs.text:
A remote command module runs a command on the target device and collects its output (numeric, status, text and incremental types: see Module type reference), with three connection methods: Inherited (uses the operating system configured in the agent itself), SSH for Linux and Windows remote (WinRM) for Windows. In all three cases, the command connects with a credential from the credential manager —of the generic credential type— and the Command field, in single quotes when needed (double quotes are escaped with \").

The wizard in the agent view brings three ready templates: disk usage, status of a process and status of a service.

Disk usage over SSH

SSH method, credential of the Linux device, command: 

df -h / | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | tr -d '%'
it returns the usage percentage of the root disk as a numeric value.

nginx process running

SSH method, command: 

pgrep -c nginx
A boolean module that returns 0 if there is no nginx process running, and a higher number if there is.

Windows remote (WinRM) needs, just like WMI, the firewall of the target device to let the corresponding incoming connections through (see Windows firewall requirements for agentless monitoring below).

docs.title: Windows firewall requirements for agentless monitoring
docs.text:
Both WMI and Windows remote need the firewall of the target device to have these inbound rules enabled:

Requirement Detail File and Printer Sharing (SMB) File and Printer Sharing (SMB-In) rule RPC (endpoint mapper) File and Printer Sharing (Spooler Service - RPC-EPMAP) rule WMI Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI-In) rule

Without these three rules active, the device rejects the connection even if the credentials and the query or the command are right.

docs.title: Remote server plugins
docs.text:
A remote plugin is a script or executable that the Heavy Server launches with parameters and from which it collects a single value —numeric, boolean or text—; the type of data is decided by the module (see Module type reference). There are two classes: standard, which only returns the value, and Nagios, which besides an error code can return a descriptive string. The installation brings several registered from the factory and the administrator can register the ones needed from Management → Servers → Plugins.

When a plugin is registered, its type is given, the maximum time of execution —15 s to start with— and the field macros (_field1_, _field2_…) that whoever applies it to a module will use, each one with its description, help text, default value and whether it must be hidden in the form (for passwords and sensitive data). The effective timeout of a specific plugin is the shortest between the one configured in the server and the plugin's own; if neither of the two turns out valid, 15 s are used as a last resort.

As soon as a plugin is used by some module or component, the editor blocks its Plug-in parameters and its field macros: they can no longer be added, removed or edited, so as not to break the modules that already depend on them. To change the parameters, the plugin has to stop being used in all its modules and components first.

docs.title: Plugin macros
docs.text:
Macros are what makes a plugin reusable: the command is registered once with gaps, and every module that uses it fills those gaps with its own values. There are three families: the field macros, which are defined by whoever registers the plugin; the agent and module ones, which the server provides; and the ones left available for the module alerts.

Field macros. In Plug-in parameters the parameter line is written as the script expects it, with _field1_, _field2_… in the place of each value. In Parameters macros each one is described:

Field What it is for Description Label of the field in the module form Default value Value with which the field appears filled in when creating the module Help Help text shown next to the field Hide value The field is shown as a password (dots) and the value is stored encrypted

The Command preview shows the complete line with the default values replaced, useful to check the registration before saving. When creating a module of the plugin type and choosing that plugin, the form shows one field per macro, with its description, its help and its default value. Hidden values are decrypted only at the moment of launching the plugin.

Plugin of your own with user and password

A script that queries the status of an application is registered with these Plug-in parameters: 

-H _field1_ -u _field2_ -p _field3_
and three macros: _field1_ with description "Server", _field2_ with description "User" and default value monitor, and _field3_ with description "Password" and Hide value checked. In the module, 192.168.10.20, monitor and the password are filled in, which is shown with dots; the server runs the script with -H 192.168.10.20 -u monitor -p <password>.

Agent and module macros. Besides the field ones, the parameter line accepts these macros (more than the fields of the other remote modules, see Macros in the module fields), which the server replaces every time it runs the plugin:

Macro Replaced by _agent_, _agentalias_ Agent alias _agentname_ Agent name _agentdescription_ Agent description _agentgroup_ Name of the agent group _agentstatus_ Agent status _address_ Main IP address of the agent _addressn_N_ IP address number N of the agent, with the addresses sorted (_addressn_2_ is the second one) _agentcustomfield_N_ Value of the agent custom field whose identifier is N _module_ Module name _moduledescription_ Module description _modulegroup_ Module group _modulestatus_ Module status _moduletags_, _name_tag_ Module tags _email_tag_, _phone_tag_ Emails and phone numbers associated with the module tags _interval_ Module interval, or the agent one if the module has none of its own _target_ip_, _target_port_ IP and port of destination configured in the module _policy_ Name of the policy the module comes from, if it comes from one _id_agent_, _id_module_, _id_group_ Numeric identifiers of the agent, the module and the group

The server replaces the field macros first and then these, so the value of a field macro can in turn be one of them. It is the way for the same module to serve many agents: with _address_ as value, each agent checks its own IP.

A plugin module for all the agents of a policy

In the DNS Plugin plugin, the DNS Server to check field is filled in with _address_ instead of a fixed IP. Applied through a monitoring policy to the agents of all the DNS servers of the company, each module asks the IP of its own agent, without touching a single module by hand.

Custom field as parameter

If the agents have a custom field with the administration port of each device (identifier 3), the parameter -p _agentcustomfield_3_ passes the port of each agent to the plugin.

Macros for alerts. In the alerts of a plugin module, _plugin_param1_, _plugin_param2_… stay available with the value of each field macro, and _plugin_param1_desc_, _plugin_param2_desc_… with its description. They serve so that the notice says what the check was run against without repeating the data in the alert text. A macro with Hide value is also replaced here, and in the clear: it is not advisable to use the macro of a password in the text of an alert.

Alert that says which server failed

With the plugin of the first example, the alert text Failure at _plugin_param1_desc_ _plugin_param1_ (_module_) arrives as "Failure at Server 192.168.10.20 (Application status)".

docs.title: Factory plugins
docs.text:
Factory plugin What it is for DNS Plugin Resolves a domain name against a given DNS server UDP port check Checks whether a UDP port answers SMTP Check Verifies an outgoing mail server MySQL Plugin Runs a query against a MySQL server Packet Loss Percentage of packets lost towards a destination Check certificate validity Validity and expiry of a certificate SSL Verification SSL/TLS connection check IPMI Plugin Reading of IPMI sensors (see 9.12 · Advanced automatic discovery, IPMI, etc.) SNMP remote Used internally by the SNMP wizard for the calculated modules

DNS resolution against 8.8.8.8

DNS Plugin with its fields filled in like this: Target IP 192.168.10.30 (the IP the domain must return), Domain to check midominio.com and DNS Server to check 8.8.8.8. The module checks that midominio.com resolves to that IP when that DNS server is asked.

Checking an SMTP server

SMTP Check plugin pointing at port 25 of the mail server: boolean module that fails if the server stops accepting SMTP connections.

Open UDP port

UDP port check plugin with the IP and UDP port of the service to check (for example, an NTP server on 123/udp).

Creating a plugin of your own, instead of using the factory ones, is told in 9.9 · Creating remote plugins.

docs.title: Route monitoring
docs.text:
The route analyzer traces the network path to a destination and warns if it changes, something neither ICMP nor TCP do by themselves: it is not enough to know that the destination answers; what matters is where the traffic goes through to reach it. It relies on the route_parser plugin of the source EndPoint, which combines ping and traceroute:

route_parser -t <destination_address>

It requires an EndPoint at the source point of the route and ICMP reachability to the destination. It is registered from the plugins tab of the agent view, just like any other local plugin, and once enabled it generates a visualisation with every hop of the route and the time to it.

Route to a remote site

On the EndPoint of the head office, route_parser -t 172.16.0.2 (the IP of a device at the remote site) shows, hop by hop, which routers the traffic goes through between both sites and warns if that route changes.

docs.title: Running wizards and tests from a remote server (Exec Server)
docs.text: When the console has no direct path to a network, because it is behind a firewall or on another segment, the SNMP wizards and the SNMP browser can be run from another server that does reach it, for example the satellite server of a remote site. It is chosen in the Server to run the command field of the wizard. How to prepare that server and what requirements it has is explained in Satellite servers.

docs.title: Module type reference
docs.text:
Internal type Family Returns What it is used for remote_icmp_proc ICMP Boolean Availability over ping remote_icmp ICMP Numeric Latency in milliseconds remote_tcp TCP Numeric Connection time to the port remote_tcp_proc TCP Boolean Port open or closed remote_tcp_string TCP Text Textual response of a service remote_tcp_inc TCP Incremental Counter read over TCP remote_snmp SNMP Numeric Value of an OID remote_snmp_inc SNMP Incremental SNMP counter (traffic, packets…) remote_snmp_string SNMP Text OID of string type remote_snmp_proc SNMP Boolean Status derived from an OID remote_cmd Remote command Numeric Numeric output of a command remote_cmd_proc Remote command Boolean Success or failure of a command remote_cmd_string Remote command Text Textual output of a command remote_cmd_inc Remote command Incremental Counter read over command wmi_generic_data WMI Numeric Numeric value of a WQL query wmi_generic_proc WMI Boolean Boolean result of a WQL query wmi_generic_data_string WMI Text String returned by a WQL query wmi_generic_data_inc WMI Incremental Counter read over WMI wmi_generic_data_inc_abs WMI Absolute incremental Difference between two readings of a WMI counter generic_data Plugin Numeric Numeric value returned by the plugin generic_proc Plugin Boolean Correct or failed result of the plugin generic_data_string Plugin Text String returned by the plugin generic_data_inc Plugin Incremental Counter returned by the plugin, as a rate generic_data_inc_abs Plugin Absolute incremental Counter returned by the plugin, as a difference

A plugin module has no family of types of its own: it uses the generic types of the table and it is whoever creates the module who chooses the one that corresponds to what the plugin returns.

The boolean types (with the _proc suffix) are interpreted with the same rule in all cases: 1 is correct (normal) status and 0 is critical status. The incremental ones store a rate per second: the difference between two readings divided by the time elapsed between them, not the raw value of the counter. The absolute incremental ones (suffix _inc_abs) store the difference between two readings, without dividing by the time. In both cases the first reading only serves as a reference: the server discards it and the module shows no data until the second one.

docs.title: Performance, fine tuning and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Remote monitoring is shared out by three servers, enabled from the factory: the Network High Performance Server (ICMP and SNMP in bulk), the Network Server (TCP, remote commands and WMI, and the SNMP modules that fail repeatedly) and the Heavy Server (remote plugins). What each one does and how they share out the work is explained in Compatibility and migration to the new server architecture. Each one has its own number of threads, which is the first thing worth raising when a type of check starts arriving late. The threads, retries, timeouts and binary paths are in 9.3 · Full server configuration reference.

Ports that have to be open from the Pandora FMS server to the monitored devices:
