docs.title: Planned downtime
docs.text: A system patch, a backup that starts at two in the morning or a scheduled reboot of the hypervisor are windows in which the infrastructure behaves oddly on purpose. Monitoring, which does not know that, fires alerts by the dozen. A planned downtime is how you tell the web console, in advance, which stretch of time it should not take seriously.

docs.title: What a planned downtime is
docs.text:
The web console lets you create planned downtimes from Management → Alerts → Scheduled downtime. The idea is simple: a window of time is defined, along with what happens inside it, and the Pandora FMS server applies that state while the window is open.

Depending on the Type chosen, the downtime does one of four things: disable the selected EndPoints, disable their modules, disable only the alerts of those modules or mark them as quiet. In all four cases, when the downtime starts and when it ends, the server generates an informational system event, one of those that appear in blue in the events console. That trace is the practical difference from disabling an EndPoint by hand: the downtime is temporary, scheduled and reversible, and the event records that it ran and when.

Do not confuse the two gestures. Disabling an EndPoint by hand and forgetting to enable it again is a classic of the trade, and it stays in the reports as a gap with no explanation. A planned downtime, on the other hand, switches itself off when the time comes, and the periods it covers are marked as valid in the availability and SLA reports, as explained further down.

docs.title: Creating a planned downtime
docs.text:
The creation form asks for little and brings the most convenient values already filled in:

Field Default value Detail Name empty Mandatory and unique; two downtimes cannot have the same name Group All Group the downtime will belong to Description empty Free text to document the window Type Quiet The four options are detailed in their own section Execution Once With an initial slot from the current time to the current time plus one hour

Before saving, the console checks that the dates are coherent: the start before the end, the start time before the end time and the correct day range in the periodicities that use one. A repeated name or an inverted slot does not pass the filter.

One option changes the meaning of "creating in the past". It is Allow create scheduled downtimes in the past, and it lives in the general settings, in the behavior section. It is enabled by default. With it enabled, a downtime whose window has already passed can be registered: the downtime does not run, because the server does not see it start, but its existence is reflected in the availability reports and in the SLA calculations. It is useful to document a maintenance that was done without having created the downtime on time. Anyone who reads that downtime in the list should not expect to see it move to "Running".

docs.title: Execution modes: once, periodically and cron
docs.text:
The Execution field accepts three modes, and each one hides a different form.

Once. The most direct one: start date and time and end date and time. The downtime starts when the start arrives, applies during the slot and ends on the end date. It is the option that solves a one-off maintenance.

Periodically. It repeats the window over time. The Type Periodicity can be Weekly or Monthly. In the weekly one the days of the week are chosen; in the monthly one, a range of days of the month (for example, from day 20 to day 10 of the next month). In both cases a time slot is set with From hour and To hour, and the slot is allowed to cross midnight. Here the Expiration Date also appears, with a Never switch: if it is disabled, the downtime stops running past that date. It is the only mode that offers expiration; Once and Cron from/to do not show it.

Cron from/to. The most flexible mode and the least friendly one. Two conditions are defined, one for the start (Cron from) and one for the stop (Cron to), and each one is made of five fields: Hour, Minute, Month day, Month and Week day. Each field is set as Any or Custom. Watch the order: in the form the fields go Hour, Minute, Month day, Month, Week day, but the expression the console stores —and that you will see in the Configuration column of the list— starts with the minute (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week). The server checks every minute whether the expression matches the current minute: it requires an exact match, not an approximate one.

Two examples to fix the format:

  • 0 2 * * 1 starts on Monday at 02:00.
  • */15 9-17 * * 1-5 starts every fifteen minutes between 09:00 and 17:00, from Monday to Friday.

The expression is stored as is and the server evaluates it on every cycle. It is worth reviewing the condition after creating it, because it is the piece that decides when the downtime starts and when it stops.

docs.title: The four types of downtime
docs.text:
The Type drop-down offers exactly four options. It is worth reading them calmly, because two of them are similar in name and do different things.

Type What it does When it ends Disabled Agents Disables the selected EndPoints and, with them, all their modules Re-enables only those that were not already disabled by hand Disable Modules Disables the selected modules, including those already disabled before the downtime Re-enables the modules the downtime covered Disabled only Alerts Disables the alerts of the selected modules, without disabling the module Reactivates the alerts Quiet Marks the EndPoint or the modules as quiet: they keep collecting data, but generate no events and fire no alerts If it quieted the EndPoint, it goes back to its previous state; if it quieted modules, they are reactivated even if they were already quiet

The first row deserves a nuance. Disabled Agents acts on the EndPoints and drags all their modules with it. The other three act on the modules, not on the whole EndPoint. And Disabled only Alerts disables no module: what it switches off are the alerts of those modules.

The detail that generates the most questions is the preservation of the manual state. If an EndPoint was already disabled (or quiet) by hand before the downtime started, when the automatic end comes it respects it: it stays as it was. With modules there is a nuance worth having clear: the automatic end of the server re-enables everything the downtime covered, including what was already switched off by hand. The difference is in who ends it: if you stop it by hand from the console, only what the downtime itself switched off is reverted, in agents as well as in modules.

docs.title: Adding agents and modules
docs.text:
The creation form already includes the element selector: the EndPoints and the modules affected are chosen in the same creation step, with no need to create an empty downtime and add them afterwards. The selector is a dual panel: on the left the Available agents, on the right the Selected agents, with the Add and Remove buttons to move them from one side to the other. If there are no agents selected yet, the modules are not filled in and the console warns with a Select agents first.

The panel filters do most of the work:

  • Group limits the list of available agents to the chosen group.
  • Recursion decides whether the agents of the subgroups are also included: recursion is respected. The "All" group resolves to the user's groups and only adds subgroups when recursion is enabled.
  • Module data type filters the modules by their data type, with All types by default.
  • Common modules shows only the modules that are present in all the selected agents. It is the quick way to apply the downtime to a shared module without going agent by agent.

A practical rule that saves trouble: in Quiet, if no specific module is selected, the whole EndPoint is quieted; in Disabled Agents and Disabled only Alerts, leaving the module list empty applies the downtime to the agent as a whole. In Disable Modules, on the other hand, at least one module has to be chosen: with no modules selected the downtime starts but does nothing. And in that type the selector does not filter by status: disabled modules appear too.

Elements are saved as they are added and can be removed one by one from the same screen.

docs.title: Managing the list: filter, stop, copy, delete and export
docs.text:
The downtime list shows one row per downtime with these columns: Name (Ag.) (the name and, in brackets, how many agents are affected), Description, Group, Type, Execution, Configuration, Running, Affected, Stop downtime, Copy, Edit and Delete. At the top are the filters Search, Group, Between dates, Execution type, Agent, Module and the Do not display previous or stopped downtimes checkbox, plus the Export to CSV button.

The Between dates filter only makes sense with Once downtimes; the periodic ones and the cron ones are not searched by slot. And the order of the list is not the creation date: it is sorted by execution type and by start date, so the creation date is a fact of the record, not the criterion of the table.

The Configuration column sums up the window in the format that applies:

Mode How it is shown Once 2026-10-01 13:57 to 2026-10-01 14:57 Periodically, weekly Weekly: Thu (00:00:00-23:59:59) Periodically, monthly Monthly: From day 20 to day 10 (08:00:00-09:00:00) Cron from/to Start condition: * * * * * - Stop condition: * * * * *

You can act on every row. While a downtime is Running it cannot be edited and the Delete button shows as N/A; what is available is Stop downtime, which cuts the execution on the spot and answers with a "Downtime has been stopped successfully". Copy duplicates the downtime to reuse its configuration, and Export to CSV dumps the list with the filters applied.

One notice is left, the one that appears when the console detects downtimes created with old, malformed formats: "WARNING: There are malformed scheduled downtimes" and the question "Do you want to migrate automatically the malformed items?". On accepting, the console splits each malformed downtime into two halves, labelled [1/2] and [2/2], so that the window that crossed from one period to another is expressed in a valid way.

docs.title: How it runs inside
docs.text:
The execution is not done by the console: it is done by the Pandora FMS server. In an installation with several servers, only the master applies the downtimes, so that they do not step on each other.

Every 60 seconds, the server goes through the downtimes and checks whether it is time to start or stop any of them. The check depends on the execution type: a Once downtime compares the current time with its slot; a Periodically one looks at the day and the time; a Cron from/to one evaluates its two expressions against the current minute. When a downtime starts, the server applies the state and writes the system event "Server \<server> started planned downtime: \<name>"; when it ends, it writes the corresponding "stopped".

Requirement Detail Pandora FMS server running Without a server there are no downtimes; the console only defines them Master server In installations with several servers, only the master applies the downtimes One cycle every 60 seconds The server checks every minute whether it is time to start or stop one Server clock Cron conditions are compared by the minute with the server time Downtime not entirely past A downtime whose window has already passed does not start; the permission to create it in the past is read by the console, not by the server

docs.title: What changes in reports and SLA
docs.text:
Here is the reason for everything above. The periods covered by a planned downtime are considered valid: they do not penalise the SLA and do not muddy the availability, because the system knows the infrastructure was down on purpose. Without that mark, a one-hour maintenance would read as a one-hour outage.

The reports sum up a period with several states according to the Priority mode, which decides whether the OK state or the unknown one prevails when they coincide. That setting is not from this screen and it is explained in detail in Reports; here it is enough to know that a well-created downtime protects the calculation.

If the past option is enabled, the downtime is recalculated backwards in time, so that a window already closed keeps counting in the reports that cover it. In service reports, a downtime that affects any element of the service is considered to affect the whole service, and malformed downtimes stay out of the calculation. The detail of services is in Business and service monitoring.

docs.title: The Scheduled Downtime dashboard widget
docs.text:
Planned downtimes also have their place in dashboards. The widget is called Scheduled Downtime in the catalogue and shows the name of each downtime, its configuration, whether it is running and the elements affected. It accepts a filter by group, pagination and export to CSV and JSON.

How a widget is added to a dashboard, which sizes it accepts and how it is placed is explained in Dashboards; here it is only noted that it exists and what it shows.

docs.title: Outside the console: API and CLI
docs.text:
The console is the convenient path, but not the only one. The API allows creating, editing and deleting downtimes, besides adding agents, adding modules and removing agents from a downtime that already exists, with operations such as planned_downtimes_edit, planned_downtimes_deleted, planned_downtimes_add_agents and planned_downtimes_delete_agents. The general operation of the REST API and the webhooks is covered in Integration and automation.

From the server command line, the command appendix offers --create_downtime to create it, --add_item_downtime to add elements, --get_all_planned_downtimes and --get_planned_downtimes_items to list, --stop_downtime to stop it and --set_planned_downtimes_deleted to delete it. There is a nuance worth keeping in mind: stopping a periodic downtime in execution does work from the web console, but the CLI rejects it. The command answers with an "[ERROR] … cannot be stopped" and an "[INFO] Periodical and running planned downtime cannot be stopped". If a periodic one that is running has to be cut, it has to be done from the interface, not from the CLI. The command catalogue is in Quick command cheat sheet.

A broad-brush alternative is left for whoever does not want to create one downtime per case: the CLI allows enabling or disabling whole groups of EndPoints with --enable_group and --disable_group. It serves for a quick, global deactivation, but it does not schedule the return and does not leave the downtime mark in the reports. That is what the planned downtime is for.

docs.title: Groups, users, profiles and tags
docs.text:
Pandora's web console is designed so that several users can work on the same installation without seeing each other. That is possible because the permission system is multitenant: one server, one database, and each user seeing and touching only what belongs to them.

There is no mystery to it, but there are two pieces you need to understand before creating the first user: groups and profiles.

A group decides what a user sees. A profile decides what they can do with it. The combination of the two, assigned to a user, is the permission. And since the same user can have different profiles in different groups, you can set up anything from the technician who only looks at their department to the administrator who sees everything.

docs.title: The permission model
docs.text:
Groups are sets of elements with their own rules, and they exist to control access to agents and everything that hangs off them. The rule to be clear about from the start: an agent belongs to a single group, but a user can have access to several groups.

There is an exception worth knowing from the start: an agent can also be in several secondary groups at the same time, and then users from all of them see it. We cover it in detail below.

Profiles define which operations a user can perform. They are a set of access bits (view, write, manage alerts, administer...) assigned per group. Thus, the same user can be read-only in the "Production" group and administrator in the "Laboratory" group, which is exactly what a well-built multitenant environment requires.

Hence the warning that has caused more than one scare: a user with no profile and no group cannot log in. It is not a bug, it is by design. Before creating users, it is better to have the groups and profiles decided, not the other way around.

Requirement Detail Groups defined The user needs at least one group to access Profiles defined The user needs at least one profile assigned in that group Administrator user A user marked as administrator (superadmin) bypasses the ACL and has access to everything

docs.title: Agent groups
docs.text:
Groups work as containers for agents: a department, a company, a site, a customer. They are the basis of multitenancy, because they allow differentiated visibility over the same inventory. The menu is in Management → Resources → Manage groups.

When creating a group (Create group), these are the fields that matter:

  • Name. If you are going to use the group in automatic EndPoint provisioning, leave it without spaces or strange characters. They are supported, but you save yourself trouble.
  • Parent. A group can hang off another. Permissions can propagate to children (see Propagate ACL below).
  • Password. Optional. It restricts agent self-creation: only those that bring that same password are created. Useful so that nobody invents agents in a group that is not theirs. Do not use spaces or symbols.
  • Alerts. If checked, the group's agents can send alerts. It is the quick switch to cut the alerts of an entire group.
  • Propagate ACL. If active, child groups inherit the parent's permissions. The All group has it enabled by default.
  • Custom ID. Your own identifier to integrate it with an external system (a CMDB, for example).
  • Contact and Other. Contact information and notes, available in the _groupcontact_ and _group_other_ macros.
  • Max agents allowed. Agent limit for the group. Default 0, which means no limit.

Each group can have its own visual theme in Group settings → Style configuration. If a user belongs to several groups with their own theme, the console applies the one from the first group other than All that has it configured. And the theme the user chooses in their preferences overrides the group's.

docs.title: Secondary groups
docs.text:
An agent belongs to a group, yes, but Pandora FMS allows it to belong as well to other groups: these are the secondary groups. The agent keeps its main group and the necessary secondary ones are added.

What it is for, with the case that explains itself: an agent lives in "Applications", but the "Networks" team also needs to see it. Instead of duplicating the agent or putting everything in a common group, "Networks" is marked as a secondary group and users with permission in "Networks" start seeing that agent just like the "Applications" users. It is the clean way for two users with different permissions to access the same agent without sharing a group.

They are assigned on the agent record, in the Secondary groups field, under Resources → Manage agents. They can also be changed from bulk agent operations. A detail that avoids confusion: the main group cannot be repeated as a secondary one; the form itself prevents it.

What changes when an agent has secondary groups:

  • Visibility. The agent is visible to anyone with permission in its main group or in any of its secondary groups. The relationship applies to everything that hangs off the agent: modules, events, alerts, SNMP traps, inventory and reports.
  • Filters. In the event and alert views there is a Search in secondary groups checkbox, so that the search takes secondary groups into account. If a user is only related to the agent through a secondary group and that checkbox is off, they may not see its information. Enabling it has a cost: it forces the server to cross-reference more data.

Three warnings that save support calls:

  • The Tree view can show the agent repeated. If an agent is in several groups, it appears once per group. That is normal, not an error.
  • Deleting a group deletes its links as a secondary group. If that group was marked as secondary on an agent, those agents stop belonging to it.
  • It has a performance cost. It is an optional feature: if no agent uses secondary groups, the console skips the additional cross-references. As soon as it is used, many lists and counters add work. Use it with judgement, not as a substitute for good group organization.

docs.title: The All group
docs.text: The All group does not exist as such in the database: it is a code-controlled group with the reserved identifier 0. Depending on the context, it means all groups or any of them, and it saves you from ticking groups one by one. It is the piece that makes "this user administers everything" easy to say.

docs.title: Deleting a group is irreversible
docs.text:
Here it is worth reading twice before clicking. Deleting a group cannot be undone. And what is worse: the agents it contained still exist and keep working, but they stop appearing anywhere in the web console. They are left orphaned.

To recover them, you have to reassign them to a new group from the CLI, with a command like:

pandora_manage /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf \
  --update_agent "pandora.internals" "group_name" "New_group" "use_alias"

The destination group must not have spaces or symbols. Before deleting a group, check how many agents it has.

docs.title: Importing groups from CSV
docs.text:
If you need to create many groups at once, they can be imported from a file in Management → Admin tools → Extension manager → CSV import group. The file has the fields in this order, separated by the character you choose (comma by default):

Group name, icon, parent id, propagation (1 or 0)

Choose the file with Select a file, adjust the Separator and click Go.

docs.title: Group recursion in the views
docs.text:
Propagate ACL and group recursion sound the same and are not. Propagate ACL decides whether permissions go down the group tree. Recursion is something else: it is a checkbox that appears in the filters of many views (events, reports, policies...) and makes the view also include the subgroups when you choose a group.

It is convenient when you filter by a parent group and want to see everything that hangs off it, but it is not free: the console itself warns that it can affect performance. Enable it when you need it, not out of habit.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Users are managed in Management → Profiles → Manage users. When creating or editing one, these are the fields worth knowing:

  • Administrator user. A superadmin is not governed by the internal ACL: they have access to everything. A standard user is governed by the permissions assigned to them.
  • Login Error. If checked, the user can only log in through the API, not interactively through the web console.
  • Local user. Forces authentication against Pandora FMS's own database. Other authentication methods exist (see Part 04 · External authentication).
  • Session timeout based on. Enabled by default. It closes the session if there is no activity for the configured time.
  • Session timeout (mins). The default value is 0; in that case the value from the general authentication configuration is used. To make the session never expire, set -1. Note: a screen left open with auto-refresh does not count as inactivity.
  • Language. The language in which that user will see the console. By default, the system's.
  • Block size for pagination. How many rows per page that user sees.
  • Timezone. The time zone used to show data to them.
  • Login allowed IP list. If enabled, it limits login to a list of addresses or ranges separated by commas. The * wildcard allows any address.
  • Homescreen. The user's start screen on login: by default, a visual console, the event list, the group view, the tactical view, the alert detail or an external link. Be careful about setting a dashboard from a group that is not theirs as the start screen: they will only see the dashboards of the groups they belong to.
  • Profiles/Groups assigned to this user. Here the user's profiles and groups are assigned; this is what really gives them permissions.

Each user can adjust part of their own record in Operation → Workspace → Edit my user, but not their group permissions. There is also the API Token to authenticate through an HTTP header with a bearer token.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Pandora FMS has a notification system for users, with group management so you do not go crazy administering them. It is configured in Management → Settings → System Settings → Notifications, and there are six categories:

  • System status. Generated by the Pandora FMS server itself.
  • Message. Messages between users.
  • Pending task. Pending tasks from features such as Discovery.
  • Advertisement. Notices and proposals from Pandora FMS.
  • Official communication. Official communications for extraordinary matters.
  • Suggestions. Suggestions and tips.

The ENABLE USER CONFIGURATION switch decides, for each category, whether users can turn those notifications on or off in Operation → Workspace → User notifications, both in the console and by email.

Two rules that explain almost every surprise:

  • For them to arrive by email, the user must have their email address configured and the server must know how to send email.
  • If a whole group is subscribed to a category, its users receive those console notifications and cannot turn them off, even if the user configuration switch is active. Group membership weighs more than personal preference.

A superadmin ends up in all categories, whether they want to or not, when created or edited from the web console. A superadmin created or modified by CLI is not added to the notification system: if someone "does not receive anything", start by checking where the account was created.

docs.title: Browser push notifications
docs.text:
In addition to console and email notifications, Pandora FMS can launch pop-up notifications to the operating system through the browser used to access the console. They are enabled in Management → Settings → System Settings → Notifications → Web Push notifications.

The requirement that breaks more than half the attempts: HTTPS is needed. If the console runs over HTTP, the browser itself rejects the notifications. And even with HTTPS, they do not work in incognito mode or in Chromium or Chrome's guest mode, nor if the browser profile has them blocked. Pandora FMS only notifies in the browser profile used to log in to the console, not in the others.

When you enable the Enable Web Push Notifications switch, the browser asks the user whether to allow them. The Send test notification button checks that it works, but use it sparingly: the message reaches all registered subscriptions, not just yours. Each stored subscription does not identify its owner.

If a user wants to remove them, there are several ways: clear the browsing data of that profile, block notifications in the profile, delete the profile (carefully, it takes the other sites with it) or create a new profile and say No when asked.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Profiles define what a user can do. They are managed in Management → Profiles → Manage profiles. Five come out of the box and you can create as many as you need:

Profile What it is for Operator (Read) The read-only one: view without touching Operator (Write) The daily operation one: view and write Chief Operator Extended operation Group coordinator Group coordination, with group and user management Pandora Administrator Full platform administration

Exactly which bit each one carries is the table below: a profile is nothing more than a combination of those bits.

A profile is a collection of access bits. These are the ones the product ships with and what each one enables:

Bit What it allows AR View agent data (all views), tactical view, group view, view users, SNMP console, Tree view, extension groups and search bar AW Agent management view, agent and .conf editing, bulk operations, create agent, duplicate remote configuration, view and manage policies, manage filters AD Manage service downtimes and disable an agent, module or alert LW Assign already-created alerts and manage alerts LM Define and modify alert templates and actions LF Force alerts and force module checks UM User management DM Database maintenance ER View events EW Validate and comment on events, manage filters and run responses EM Delete events, change owner and reopen events RR View reports and graphs, apply report templates and view Cronjobs RW Create visual consoles, reports and combined graphs; view, edit, run and create Cronjobs RM Create report templates; view, edit, run, create and delete Cronjobs MR View network maps MW Edit network maps and delete your own MM Delete any network map VR View visual consoles VW Edit visual consoles and delete your own or any VM Manage visual consoles NR View NCM data NW Operate NCM NM Administer NCM PM Pandora administration: manage responses, event columns, update manager, inventory modules, modules, SNMP console, profiles, servers, audit, setup, extensions and all kinds of Cronjobs GW Group management: a non-superadmin user can only edit the group of their profile, and the children if the group has Propagate ACL

There are also combinations that enable specific functions: EW + IW allows creating an incident from an event, and LM + AR or AW + LW allow validating alerts.

A warning that saves arguments: superadmins are exempt from the ACL, even if they have the administrator profile assigned. The ACL only binds everyone else.

docs.title: Assigning permissions
docs.text:
Permissions are granted from the user edition, assigning groups and profiles on the record. And here it is worth keeping in mind the coexistence rules between administrators and user managers (UM permission), because they are the source of half the questions:

  • A manager with UM on the All group can manage any user, whatever group they belong to.
  • A manager only sees and edits the profiles and groups of the users they can see, that is, of the groups they manage with UM.
  • A manager without UM on a group cannot even see which users belong to that group.
  • A manager cannot remove UM from another user who has the same permissions on the same group. Only an administrator can touch that.
  • An administrator can create other administrators and manage anyone.

When the last profile/group relationship of a user who is also going to be deleted is about to be removed, the console warns first. It is worth reading the warning.

docs.title: Hierarchy
docs.text:
Permission propagation to child groups is controlled with Propagate ACL in the parent group. If you want to cut it for a specific user, when assigning the permission check No hierarchy and the ACL does not go down the tree.

The group hierarchy is independent of secondary groups, which are something else and are explained in "Secondary groups".

docs.title: Tags and extended per-tag permissions
docs.text: Groups and profiles give permissions "in bulk": a whole group, a complete profile. To fine-tune further there are module tags. With them you can decide that a user sees some modules and not others within the same group, which is exactly what group permissions cannot reach.

docs.title: What a tag is and where it applies
docs.text:
A tag is a named mark that is defined once and reused. They are created in Management → Resources → Module tags, and the screen asks for:

  • Name. The tag identifier. It does not accept commas.
  • Description.
  • URL. A help link that must exist before you set it.
  • Email and Phone. Contact data used later in the alerts associated with the tag (see below).

The tag list shows, for each one, how many modules and how many policy modules carry it. Managing them requires an administration profile; in a Command Center with centralized mode, the information is read-only and is managed from the Command Center itself.

And a nuance that saves useless searches: tags are assigned to modules, not to agents or groups. They are set (and removed) on the module record, in the categorization section, Tags field. Since a policy module can also carry them, tags travel with the policy and apply to all agents that receive it. There is also a bulk operation to tag modules and policy modules at once. A module can carry several tags.

docs.title: Per-tag permissions (ACL)
docs.text:
Here is the trick. In the user's profile and group assignment there is a Tags selector, next to the group and the profile. The rule is simple:

  • If left empty, the user sees all modules in that group.
  • If one or more tags are filled in, the user sees only the modules that carry those tags within that group.

The restriction is per combination of profile, group and tags: the same user can see some modules in one group and different ones in another. Tags complement group access, they do not replace it: the group and the profile are still required.

Two warnings worth their weight in gold:

  • A profile without tags opens everything. If the user has several profiles on the same group and any of them does not restrict by tags, the user sees all modules. The most permissive restriction wins.
  • Tags propagate with the group. If the group has Propagate ACL enabled, the tag restriction also goes down to child groups.

docs.title: Limits, cost and viewer
docs.text:
The tag-based security mode has a performance cost: it forces modules to be cross-referenced with tags on every query. It is designed to give access to small portions of information, so it is not advisable to go beyond two or three tags per combination of user, profile and group. For serious segmentation, groups are the reasonable choice; tags are a scalpel, not a sledgehammer.

And a nuance that prevents misunderstandings: in some global views (tactical view, group view, tree counts) the totals show all modules, not only those the user sees through their tags.

To explore monitoring by tag there is the Tag view, available in Enterprise installations, in Monitoring → Views.

docs.title: Tags in alerts
docs.text:
Since a tag stores an email and a phone number, alerts can use that data from the module that carries it. They are useful when the notification has to reach whoever actually looks after that system, not always the same inbox:

  • _moduletags_ and _name_tag_ replace the names of the module's tags.
  • _email_tag_ replaces the emails of the module's tags.
  • _phone_tag_ replaces the phones of the module's tags.

In other words: tagging a module not only fine-tunes permissions, it can also say who to notify when that module goes wrong.

For fine-grained control by pages and menus, beyond groups, profiles and tags, there is the advanced ACL system, covered in Part 04 · Advanced security and visibility.

docs.title: External authentication and centralized access
docs.text:
Pandora FMS ships with its own authentication, but almost nobody uses it in production: the normal thing is to delegate it to the company directory. This chapter covers the available methods, field by field, and what changes when there is a Command Center above.

Everything is configured in Management → Settings → System Settings → Authentication. There are four methods, and one rule that repeats across all of them: administrators (superadmin) always authenticate against the local database. It is the safety net that keeps you from being locked out if the directory goes down.

docs.title: Local and external authentication
docs.text:
The Authentication method is chosen from a drop-down:

Method What it is Local Pandora FMS The default authentication, against the internal database LDAP Delegated to an LDAP server Active Directory Delegated to Active Directory. Enterprise SAML Delegated to a SAML identity provider. Enterprise

Two fields apply to almost all external methods:

  • Fallback to local authentication. If enabled, when the external system does not validate the user, local authentication is attempted. Administrators always have it enabled, whether they want to or not.
  • Autocreate remote users. If enabled, Pandora FMS registers the user the first time they log in against the directory, without creating them by hand.

docs.title: Local authentication
docs.text: It is the factory one: username and password against Pandora FMS's internal database. There is nothing to configure except choosing it as the method. It is the one administrators use and the one that serves as a fallback when the directory does not respond.

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text:
First of all, the dependency: the OpenLDAP utilities are needed on the server, installed with the distribution package (ldap-utils on Debian/Ubuntu, openldap* on RHEL).

The connection fields:

Field What it is for LDAP server and Secondary LDAP server Server address, direct (x.x.x.x) or as a URL (ldap://…, ldaps://…) LDAP port Server port (389 by default) LDAP version Protocol version Start TLS Encrypts communication between client and server Base DN Starting point for searches Login attribute Attribute used to identify the user. It is case-sensitive LDAP administrator login and LDAP administrator password Credentials of an account with permission to query the directory LDAP search timeout (seconds) How long the search waits before giving up Enable secondary LDAP Enables a second server, with its own server, port, version, Start TLS, base DN, login attribute and administrator credentials

Two decisions that change the behavior:

  • LDAP function. Choose how searches are made: Local command, which uses the system's ldapsearch command, or PHP function, the console's own engine. For directories with many entries, the console recommends the local command.
  • Login user attribute. Which directory attribute is taken as the user identifier (for example, the email).

And for automatic user creation:

  • Save password. Stores the directory password in the local database. If the local fallback was enabled, this is enabled too.
  • Force automatic user profile creation and, below it, Profile autocreation, Group autocreation and Tag autocreation, to decide with which permissions the newly created user is born, and Automatically assigned no hierarchy.
  • Autocreate blacklist. A comma-separated list of users that will not be created automatically.
  • Recursive group search.

If Advanced Config LDAP is enabled, Advanced LDAP permissions appear, where rules with profile, groups and tags tied to an attribute filter are added. Attributes are written in the format Attribute_name = Attribute_value: if the user matches any of them, they are created with that profile.

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
It is the LDAP variant for Active Directory, and it is Enterprise. It shares the concept, but with its own fields:

  • Active Directory server, Active Directory port (389 by default), Start TLS and Domain. If you use the advanced configuration, the domain must contain the full LDAP path, like ldap://addc.mydomain.
  • Enable secondary Active Directory, with its server, port, Start TLS, domain and AD search timeout (seconds) (5 by default).
  • Save password, Advanced AD configuration and Advanced AD permissions, with the same idea of attribute rules as in LDAP.
  • Auto enable node access: "new users will be able to connect on the nodes".
  • Recursive group search and Autocreate blacklist.

A detail that is not Pandora FMS's, but explains many calls: Windows allows the old password to be used for 60 minutes after a change in Active Directory. Windows controls that, not the console.

docs.title: Double authentication (2FA)
docs.text:
Double authentication adds a second factor on top of the password. In the global authentication configuration there are three settings:

  • Double authentication. Enables the option so that users can turn it on.
  • Force 2FA for all users. Makes it mandatory for everyone.
  • Display name in the authentication app. The name the user will see in their code app, so they do not confuse Pandora FMS with other services. It is worth setting.

Each user turns it on in Operation → Workspace → Edit my user.

It needs a code-generating app (Google Authenticator and similar) on the user's own phone, and the server and the phone to have synchronized time; without that, the codes do not match.

To disable it for a specific user without going through the console, there is the CLI:

/usr/share/pandora_server/util/pandora_manage.pl /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf \
    --disable_double_auth '<user>'

docs.title: SAML
docs.text:
SAML is an open XML-based authentication standard: Pandora FMS acts as a service provider and delegates to an identity provider. Here too, administrators always authenticate against the local database.

Three pieces are needed to use it: a working SAML server (SimpleSAMLphp), the Pandora FMS configuration and, if the provider is Azure, the configuration on the Azure side. The SimpleSAMLphp technical annex covers the installation step by step; here are the fields on the Pandora side.

Field What it is for SimpleSAML path Directory where simplesamlphp is installed SAML source Name of the configured authsource SAML user ID attribute Attribute taken as the identifier. The ID cannot contain the characters > < " ` & / * ( ) º ° or spaces SAML email attribute Attribute with the email address (for autocreation) SAML group name attribute Attribute with the group (for autocreation) Simple attribute / multi-value attribute Whether the attributes come as a single value or as a list Profile attribute and Tag attribute Where the user's profile and tag come from SAML profile and tag prefix Prefix to match the attribute value with the profile or tag

With Advanced Config SAML enabled, Advanced SAML permissions appear, with the same attribute-rule mechanism as LDAP and AD.

docs.title: Sessions and API tokens
docs.text:
Two settings govern when a session is closed:

  • Session timeout (mins). How long the session lasts.
  • Session timeout based on. What the time is counted from: the last login (it restarts on every login) or the user's inactivity (it restarts with every action). A screen left open with auto-refresh does not count as inactivity.

Apart from the session, each user has their API token, which is generated and used as a bearer token in the HTTP header to call the API without a username and password.

docs.title: Authentication in a Command Center
docs.text:
When there is a Command Center, user administration is handled centrally, and that affects login. A user whose authentication is not local (AD, LDAP or SAML) needs, in order to enter the nodes, either their password to be saved (Save Password) or the node to have Auto enable node access enabled. Otherwise, the user exists on the node but cannot log in.

The first time a centralized user accesses a node, the console warns that you have to wait for the Command Center to synchronize and log in again with the same credentials. That is normal behavior, not an error.

docs.title: Advanced security and visibility (advanced ACL)
docs.text:
The groups and profiles from the previous chapter decide what a user can do. But there is a question they do not answer: which pages they see. An administrator profile gives access to everything, and many times that is not what you want; you want someone to be able to touch one part of the console and not the rest. That is what the advanced ACL system (formerly called Enterprise ACL) is for: it defines, profile by profile, which pages each user has access to.

Two rules worth knowing before touching anything. The first: superadmins are exempt from the system, and everyone else is bound by it, even if they have the Pandora Administrator profile. The second: the advanced ACL and the classic one (groups and profiles) are parallel and compatible, but the classic one is evaluated first. If the classic ACL does not allow something, the advanced one does not open it.

docs.title: What the advanced ACL system adds
docs.text: The classic model is Unix-style: role, action, group, user. The advanced one goes a step further and allows restricting administration page by page: which sections and which specific screens each profile can open. It is the tool for granting very specific low-level permissions without opening the whole hand.

docs.title: Enabling the system
docs.text:
The system comes disabled. It is enabled like this:

  • On a node: Management → Settings → System Settings → General setup → Features → Use Advanced ACL System, enable it and click Update.
  • In a Command Center: Configuration → Metasetup → Use Advanced ACL System.

In a Command Center, the system is configured independently in the Command Center itself and on each node.

You can lose access to the console

When you enable the advanced ACL, all pages are restricted for all groups, including the administrator group, and only the pages you have defined remain allowed. If an administrator profile has no page included, it will see nothing. Before enabling it, leave the rules defined for the profile you are going to log in with.

If you get locked out by mistake, there is no need to reinstall: from the server, the system is turned off via the CLI.

pandora_manage /etc/pandora/pandora_server.conf --disable_eacl

And to turn it back on, --enable_eacl.

docs.title: How rules are defined
docs.text:
They are configured in Management → Profiles → Advanced ACL Setup; in a Command Center, in Centralized management → Management → Advanced ACL Setup. There are two ways to add pages, and a button next to Add switches between them: Wizard and Custom.

The wizard works with drop-downs: choose the user profile, the Section, Section 2 and, if needed, Section 3. If you choose All in the section, that profile will see the whole section; with All in every one, it will see everything, as if the system were not active. Three things that surprise you the first time:

  • The drop-down only lists pages accessible from the menu. For a page reached another way, you have to use the custom editor.
  • It shows all menu options, whether or not the profile has access. Adding one the profile cannot use does not make it appear.
  • The default profile in the drop-down is Chief Operator. Change it before adding anything, or you will be giving permissions to the wrong person.

The custom editor is for pages that are not in the menu: you paste the page's sec2 parameter by hand. For example, to give access to an agent's main view, open any agent's view, copy the sec2 from the URL (operation/agentes/ver_agente) and put it in the Section 2 box.

A detail that explains menus that "do not show up": for a section to appear in the menu, the user needs access to at least its first page. And to check at any time which pages a profile is allowed, there is Filter by profile.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The system is not decorative. A restricted page is not shown in the menu and cannot be used, not even by typing the URL by hand. Moreover, a page that the classic ACL does not allow will not be allowed by the advanced one either.

There is an extra check that verifies whether a page belongs to its section, which reinforces security against tampered URLs. That check skips pages added with the custom editor and entire allowed sections, so as not to penalize load.

docs.title: Visibility permissions on shared elements
docs.text:
There are elements that are not agents or modules and behave differently: reports, visual consoles, network maps and dashboards act as containers. A user with visibility over all data creates a report and assigns it to a general group. From then on, anyone with access to that group will see the report and all its content, even if they do not have permission on the individual elements that make it up. It is convenient, and that is why it is worth knowing before sharing a report.

There are exceptions to keep in mind:

  • Some dashboard widgets, such as the treeview or the event control, because they allow interacting with the data.
  • Elements of a visual console, which can be restricted to a specific group.

And a coexistence rule for anyone with read and write access: when editing a container, they can only add elements they have access to and can delete elements they do not have access to, but cannot add them back.

The rest of the shared elements are governed by their menu and their permission:

  • Servers: Manage servers, Manage consoles and Manage HA database.
  • Credential store: each credential is seen according to the group assigned to it.
  • Scheduled downtimes, audit log and local server logs.
  • Database management from the console and external tools.
  • Plugin registry, Insert data, resource registry and resource export and import.
  • String translator, workspace and EndPoint repository.

docs.title: Customization and examples
docs.text:
The advanced ACL does not only close doors; it also opens the right ones. Three examples that always come up when it is enabled:

  • For a user to change their own data, they need access to Workspace → Edit my user → All.
  • For them to generate their own tokens, Workspace → Edit my Tokens → All.
  • For them to read their notifications, Workspace → Messages → All; and if they also have to reply to a message, add the sec2 operation/messages/message_edit in the custom editor.

The same mechanism works for any individual page: find its sec2 and add it by hand. It is the way to adjust the console to what each role needs, without opening entire sections.

docs.title: Strict ACL
docs.text:
The user record has a Strict ACL checkbox. It is not the default option and the console itself warns that it is not recommended, because it affects performance. What it does, in short: a user with strict ACL does not see any tag, that is, the tag permission system stops showing them modules. Enable it only if you know why you need it.

For the use and best practices of tagging and naming, see the next chapter in Part 04.

docs.title: Naming and tagging best practices
docs.text: The previous three chapters explain how groups, profiles and tags work. This one is about how to use them well. There is no single right way, but there are decisions that become expensive later: a badly chosen name or one tag too many sticks around for years, and changing it afterwards costs more than thinking about it on day one.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A small installation organizes itself. An installation with hundreds of agents does not: if the names are a mess, every search is a lottery and every report, a negotiation. Naming and tags are what allow you to find an element, group it for reports and delegate it with permissions without exposing what should not be exposed. The sooner the convention is fixed, the less there is to undo.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
The golden rule is boring and it works: a predictable name is worth more than a pretty one. These are the guidelines that prevent real problems.

Agents. A pattern that usually works is SERVICE-ENVIRONMENT-NN, for example WEB-PROD-01 or DB-PRE-03. It does not matter which pattern you choose; what matters is that it is consistent and that the name says at a glance what it is and where it lives. Avoid spaces in the name of the group they go into (see below) and be consistent with capitalization: the console search may normalize the alias, and a Web-Prod-01 does not appear the same as a WEB-PROD-01.

Modules. The module name should say what it measures and in what units, not what the metric is called in the source system: CPU usage (%) is easier to understand than hrProcessorLoad. If the module belongs to a service, include it in the name (Apache requests/s).

Groups. Here there is a recommendation that is not aesthetic, it is functional: to use the group name in automatic agent provisioning, it should not have spaces or extended characters. It is supported, but it is a known source of failures: there are documented cases where a group with spaces in its name is not assigned when the agent is autocreated. A Networks-DC1 avoids the problem; Networks DC 1 invites it.

Other identifiers. The same criterion applies to anything used as a key in integrations or scripts:

  • The group password (to restrict agent self-creation) must not have spaces or symbols.
  • The credential store identifier goes without spaces or special characters.
  • In the CLI, group and calendar names do not accept spaces or special characters.
  • Custom fields with very long names are cut off in some views: a short, descriptive name is better.

And two details that surprise:

  • In visual consoles, a name that starts with _, ,, [ or ( makes the element appear in the left menu. It is a feature, not a whim: if you do not want that behavior, do not start the name with those characters.
  • Control characters and some accents cause problems when saving depending on where (custom fields, policies with a specific encoding). If a name has to travel through the API, the CLI or scripts, leave it in plain ASCII.

docs.title: Using tags
docs.text:
Tags complement groups, they do not replace them. The way to get it right is to be clear about what each one is for:

  • Groups organize the hierarchy and permissions. They are the main structure, and the ones used to delegate (secondary groups included).
  • Tags fine-tune. They mark modules with a cross-cutting criterion that does not match the hierarchy: by technology, by criticality, by owner.

Criteria that save trouble:

  • Do not turn tags into a second hierarchy. If a tag reproduces a group, it is redundant.
  • Few and stable. The tag security mode has a performance cost and the console recommends not going beyond two or three per combination of user, profile and group. A tag nobody uses is just debt.
  • Name them the same as in the rest of the installation. If you call production tags prod, do not call them Production somewhere else.
  • Remember where they apply: to modules (and policy modules), not to agents or groups.

docs.title: Anti-patterns and an example
docs.text:
The mistakes that repeat the most:

  • The name that says nothing. Agent1, test, test2: a month from now, nobody knows what they are or whether they can be deleted.
  • The date or the name of whoever set it up as an identifier. The system changes hands; the name stays.
  • Mixing languages and capitalization in the same inventory (web, WEB, Web).
  • Using spaces or symbols in anything that will go through an integration.
  • Tagging for the sake of tagging, until the tag permission system starts to slow down.
  • Duplicate groups with almost identical names.

An example convention, applied to an environment with two sites and two environments:

Element Convention Example Agent SERVICE-ENVIRONMENT-SITE-NN WEB-PROD-MAD-01 Group SERVICE-SITE (no spaces) WEB-MAD Module What it measures (unit) CPU usage (%) Tag Technology or criticality, in lowercase apache, critical

It is not the only valid one, and it does not need to be. What matters is that it exists, that it is written down and that everyone follows it. That is the real work of this chapter.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
A GIS map is a visual representation of where each agent in the installation is, geographically. On a base map (streets, satellite image or a map of your own), agents appear as markers at their last known position, with the color of their status. A glance shows where each machine is and how it is doing. Agents that do not report coordinates of their own are not left out: they are drawn at the map's default position for agents without GIS data, a point that is set when the connection or the map is created.

It is the geographical view of Part 5. The chapter 5.7 Network topology maps draws relationships: who depends on whom, how machines connect. A GIS map draws places. They do not compete: one answers "what goes down with what" and the other, "where is what goes down".

For a GIS map to show anything, three pieces have to agree. The EndPoint provides the position, the Pandora FMS server processes it and stores it, and the web console defines the map connections and the maps. The chapter goes through the three in that order and ends with the reference of the parameters involved.

docs.title: Requirements and activation
docs.text:
Requirement Detail Server with GIS enabled Token activate_gis set to 1 in pandora_server.conf. It defaults to 0 and, with that value, the server discards all the position information it receives Console with the feature enabled Enable GIS features switch in the general configuration of the web console A default map There must be a map marked as default; it is the one the agent view uses to place the agent Internet access OpenStreetMap and Google Maps connections load the base map tiles from the user's browser Google Maps API key A valid key; it may take a few minutes to become fully active Reverse geolocation Internet (Google or OpenStreetMap) or a local MaxMind GeoLiteCity file

The web console switch is in Management → Settings → System Settings → General setup, on the Features tab: "Enable GIS features" → Update.

Remember that they are two different switches: the console one decides which parts of the interface are shown; the server one decides whether the position information is processed and stored. The console may be showing the maps while the server ignores what it receives.

docs.title: Configuring the position of EndPoints
docs.text:
The EndPoint configuration file, pandora_agent.conf, accepts fixed position parameters. With them the agent is placed without depending on anything else:

latitude 40.37346827
longitude -3.6418548
altitude 637
position_description Madrid, Vallecas
Requirement Detail latitude Latitude in decimal degrees longitude Longitude in decimal degrees altitude Altitude in meters; it is optional position_description Readable description of the place (for example, "Madrid, Vallecas"); it is optional gis_exec Path of a script that returns the coordinates

gis_exec points to a script that, when run, prints a single line with the coordinates separated by commas: latitude,longitude,altitude. Altitude is optional. An example of valid output would be 41.377,-5.105,2.365. The script must exist on the system; if the path does not resolve to a real file, the EndPoint ignores gis_exec and uses the manual values. When gis_exec is defined and executable, it takes precedence over latitude and longitude.

The output of gis_exec is not read the same way in every piece

The EndPoint reads the string as latitude,longitude,altitude; the satellite server, on the other hand, reads it as longitude,latitude,altitude. If the same script is going to feed both, keep in mind the order each one expects: the same 41.377,-5.105 means different coordinates depending on who reads it.

docs.title: Reverse geolocation and Discovery
docs.text:
The Discovery server can calculate the position of the agents it discovers without them reporting anything: it geolocates their IP address and places them on the map. To do so it uses a reverse geolocation algorithm and a database that relates IP addresses to positions. The token recon_reverse_geolocation_file points to the file with that information, in MaxMind GeoLiteCity format (GeoLiteCity.dat). If the file does not exist or cannot be read, the server warns and discards it.

Because the position deduced from an IP address is approximate, the token recon_location_scatter_radius scatters the agents at random around the calculated point, with a radius in meters, so that they do not all pile up in the same place. A value of 0 leaves them exactly at the deduced point.

Besides the local file, the server can resolve the address online:

  • google_maps_description, set to 1, enables reverse geolocation with the public Google Maps API.
  • openstreetmaps_description, set to 1, enables it with the public OpenStreetMap API.

Online reverse geolocation costs performance

The two options above reduce the performance of the server and need Internet access: the address of every position received has to be resolved. They also depend on the service provider being available.

The last token in the processing is location_error, a radius in meters. Two positions less than that distance apart are considered the same. It keeps a motionless agent from appearing to move because of GPS receiver noise: if the jump does not exceed the threshold, the server updates the current position but does not record it as a movement. When the agent does move beyond the threshold, the server records the previous position in the history and sets the new one. The current position and the position history are stored in the database; their schema is in 10.1 and 10.2.

docs.title: Map connections
docs.text:
A map connection defines where the base maps come from: the tile server, the Google key, the static image or the WMS service. They are created from the web console in Management → Settings → System Settings → Map connections GIS. The list shows the existing connections and the Create button opens the new connection form.

Every connection shares a few basic fields before the type is chosen:

Requirement Detail Connection name Name used to identify it and to select it later when building a map Group Group the connection belongs to Number of zoom levels Zoom levels available on the map Default zoom level Level the map opens with, unless the map itself overrides it

Once the type is chosen, its own fields appear. The four possible types are Open Street Maps, Google Maps, Static Image and WMS Server.

Open Street Maps. It only asks for the URL of the tile server, with the ${z}, ${x} and ${y} markers in place:

http://tiles.example.com/${z}/${x}/${y}.png

The installation ships two OpenStreetMap connections ready to try, "OpenStreetMap (MapQuest Open)" and "OpenStreetMap (Standard)".

Google Maps. It asks for the base map type (Google Hybrid, Google Physical or Google Satellite) and the Google Maps API key.

Static Image. It uses an image of your own as the base map. The image must be in the EPSG:4326 (WGS84) projection. Its URL, its corners (left, bottom, right and top) and its size in pixels (width and height) are given.

WMS Server. The service URL and the list of layers to be obtained from it are given. It is the way to use a map server of your own (for example, GeoServer) when an online service cannot be used.

Once the type is set, the map center and the default position for agents without GIS data remain: the point where the map opens and the point where agents that do not report coordinates are placed. The console offers two ways to set them. The map is previewed with Load preview map and clicked on it, after choosing with the Change in the map selector which of the two points is being moved; or the values are typed by hand in their cells, with a dot as the decimal separator.

The connection is saved with Save.

docs.title: Creating and defining a GIS map
docs.text:
GIS maps are managed in Operation → Topology maps → GIS Maps → GIS Maps list. The list allows creating, editing, viewing and deleting maps, and marking which one is the default map with the radio button in the "Default" column.

A default map is needed

The agent view places the agent on the default map. Without one marked as such, that view warns that there is no default map and shows no position.

The Create button opens the map builder. The first fields are the Map name, the group, the Default zoom and the coordinates of the center and of the default position. Then one or more map connections are added, to be used as base layers: they are selected in Add Map connection and are added to the list. Only one of them can be active as a base layer at a time.

When a connection is marked as the default one of the map, or when it is changed, the console asks whether its default data is to be used. If accepted, it fills the center coordinates, the default position and the zoom with the values of the connection; if rejected, it changes nothing and only adds the connection.

Layers. A layer decides which agents are painted on the map. Each layer can show the agents of a group, a specific list of agents or a group with a representative agent. They are created from New layer, where its name, whether it is visible, the group it takes the agents from and the list of agents are set, and they are added to the list of layers of the map. Layers can be sorted, edited and deleted, and all of them are saved with the rest of the map.

A group with a representative is not repeated

Once a layer has a group with its representative agent, another layer cannot be created with that same group and a different representative.

The map is saved with Save map. If the map is going to be the default map, there is no need to define layers: it is used to place the agent in its view.

docs.title: Operating the map
docs.text:
The map viewer shows the map with its layers and its controls. The name of the map appears in the title and, in the top bar, the operation controls.

Navigation. The arrows in the top left corner move the map in each direction; the + and - icons and the zoom bar change the zoom level. The map can also be dragged with the mouse.

Layers. The layer control allows choosing the base layer (when the map has more than one connection) and marking which layers are visible and which are not. Among them is the system layer Hierarchy of agents, which draws dotted lines between an agent and its parent when both are visible.

Status filters. The Filter by status selector reduces the agents shown to those in a specific status: None (all), Critical, Warning, OK or Other.

Refresh. The Refresh selector sets how often the map is refreshed (from 5 seconds to 2 hours, 1 minute by default). The refresh is done over AJAX, without reloading the page.

Clicking on an agent expands its information, and the agent name links to its agent view. If the user has management permission, the bar also includes the gear button to edit the map and the link to the public map, which opens the viewer without signing in.

docs.title: Agent view and GIS data
docs.text:
In the agent view, the GIS data tab shows the default map and the position of the agent. With GIS enabled in the console, the tab bar includes that section, which, besides the position in latitude, longitude and altitude, presents a table with the information reported by the agent in the chosen period (including the place description, resolved by reverse geolocation) and the position history.

In the agent administration, the GIS data tab is used to set the position by hand: the map is clicked or the latitude, longitude and altitude fields of the lower form are filled in. When the position is changed by hand, the console turns on the Ignore new GIS data option by itself, so that the next data packet does not readjust what has just been set. If that is not what is wanted, it has to be turned off before pressing Update.

The other end of that setting is in the agent management, in the Update new GIS data option. When it is on, the server applies the position information it receives; when it is off, it keeps the last valid position. It is the option to use when an agent reports a wrong position or when it has to be left at a fixed position. If the position is set by hand on the GIS data tab, it is worth reviewing this option afterwards: it is the same setting seen from the other side.

The GIS data tab is shown even if global GIS is off

The agent administration forces the global switch to build the GIS data tab, so that interface appears even if "Enable GIS features" is disabled. The GIS view button in the agent view, on the other hand, does depend on the global switch and is not shown if it is off.

docs.title: Parameter reference
docs.text:
The complete detail of each token, with its context, is in 9.3 Full server configuration reference and in 9.1 Full EndPoint configuration reference.

Server (pandora_server.conf)

Parameter Default value What it does activate_gis 0 Enables (1) or disables (0) the processing of GIS information in the server location_error 50 Radius in meters below which two positions are considered the same recon_reverse_geolocation_file empty MaxMind GeoLiteCity file for the reverse geolocation of the discovered agents recon_location_scatter_radius 50 Radius in meters of the circle in which the discovered agents are scattered at random google_maps_description 0 Enables (1) reverse geolocation with the Google Maps API openstreetmaps_description 0 Enables (1) reverse geolocation with the OpenStreetMap API

EndPoint (pandora_agent.conf)

Parameter Format What it does latitude Decimal degrees Fixed latitude of the device longitude Decimal degrees Fixed longitude of the device altitude Meters (optional) Altitude of the device position_description Free text Readable description of the place gis_exec Path of a script Script that returns latitude,longitude,altitude on one line

docs.text:
